#6528. The 2026 Chefs of the Year

Five U.S. chefs making waves in their communities with compelling menus

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Each of the chefs featured in our new national Chef of the Year category made news in a major way. But their most recent projects are just one part of their story.

This year we celebrate five chefs who are making an impact both on the city where they cook and on the larger culinary conversation. — Missy Frederick, editorial director

Learn more about this year’s Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, and how editors selected them, here.

San Francisco diners became acquainted with powerhouse couple Laura and Sayat Ozyilmaz through their championing of Eastern Mediterranean cuisine at Dalida. That restaurant told the story of Sayat’s upbringing and influences in Istanbul, Turkey, opening in 2023 inside a historic building within the lush environs of the Presidio and earning critical acclaim for the duo’s cooking.

In the years since, diners came to know Laura outside of Dalida. She completed an impressive run on Top Chef in 2024, where viewers saw her deftly plant one foot in Mediterranean food and another in Mexican cuisine, showcasing her skill in both fields throughout the season. With the 2026 debut of the Ozyilmazes’ restaurant Maria Isabel, the food feels like an even fuller expression of Laura’s heritage and personal history.

Named after Laura’s sister (Maria) and her mother (Isabel), the restaurant steeps in Mexican matriarchy, highlighting female winemakers, ceramics made by Mexican producers, and indigenous Mexican ingredients. The menu channels Laura’s upbringing in Guerrero and her family’s Sinaloan roots, as recounted through mariscos and maiz, moles and salsa macha. The ceviche Acapulqueño reimagines the Fanta- and ketchup-laden version instead with marigold flowers and preserved Seville oranges dressing tender shrimp and raw scallop; petals — and three fried shrimp heads — adorn the top. Duck enmoladas showcase the power of mole negro against a seasonal mole (sometimes a peach manchamanteles, other times a rhubarb rendition, but always compelling). Chochoyotes, a lesser-seen dish in San Francisco, demonstrates the restaurant’s ability to apply masa in different ways — in this case, dumplings — while harnessing the earthy flavor of huitlacoche. Maria Isabel is both a conduit for diners to connect with complex Mexican flavors and a view into Laura’s vision of the Mexico of her past and future. — Dianne de Guzman, editor, Eater SF

Chef Carlos Delgado’s meteoric rise in D.C. began in 2022 with the opening of tiny tasting room Causa, located in Shaw, where he sends diners on a seafaring voyage along the Peruvian coastline and into the Andes he grew up around, and its accompanying upstairs pisco destination Bar Amazonia. His meticulous sourcing and culinary skills quickly drew critical acclaim.

2026 might be the Lima native’s biggest year yet: His breakout project, Maru San, commanded instant Capitol Hill buzz upon opening in February for its orchestra of Nikkei-style hand rolls, sashimi, and other polished seafood plates he and fellow José Andrés alum Simon Lam pass across a 25-seat black marble counter under a big pink octopus mural, as his favorite tropical house blasts in the background. A rare few get to sample the restaurant’s elaborate tasting menu full of ingredients like high-end uni and dry-aged fish; reservations for the 15-course feast are nearly impossible to get.

The ambitious chef, at 36, isn’t afraid to stretch in many directions. He linked up with the Eaternity Group last year to give the Mediterranean-themed La Vie a needed menu makeover at D.C.’s Wharf development — meanwhile, at least one more Maru San is in the works elsewhere in D.C.

Sounds a lot like his former mentor: Before Causa, Delgado honed his craft under José Andrés as the longtime executive chef at Penn Quarter’s Peruvian mainstay China Chilcano. They still text frequently. — Tierney Plumb, Northeast editor

While Amir Hajimaleki has had American-leaning restaurants in Austin for well over a decade, he hasn’t had the opportunity to fully express himself as an Iranian-born, Texas-raised chef. That is until he opened Roya, his most personal restaurant and a project that has been in the works for more than eight years. Here, he manifests the depth and diversity of Persian cuisine, a bold feat for the middle of Texas. The space, designed with his brother Ali Hajimaleki, feels transportive with intricate tile mosaics, burnished gold and dark blue hues, and delicate chandeliers.

There’s been an electric energy to the Philly restaurant scene in recent years. The city, ever the underdog, has long punched above its weight; now, the rest of the world has come to the same realization. Amid this buzz, two newer restaurants have outrun the shadow cast by the city’s big names: Cambodian noodle house Mawn, which opened in 2023, and Southeast Asian oyster house and raw bar Sao, which opened last September.

At their helm is the slick, stylish Phila Lorn. The restaurants he runs with his wife Rachel feel singular, blending the influences of his Philadelphia upbringing with his Cambodian background in food that feels playfully free and emboldened by a lack of boundaries between cuisines. At Mawn, funnel cake meets coconut macaroons, and vinegar peppers enhance scallops in red curry. At Sao, the crispy rice in the nam khao salad, which features Italian sausage, feels analogous to arancini. Tuna carpaccio is served with crispy shallots and jalapeños, then cured in lime until it picks up the aura of the bowls of beef pho on Washington Avenue.

Hear Lorn talk, with his South Philly-bred bravado (and requisite uses of “jawn”) giving him a commanding presence, and it’s clear that the city’s culinary community is listening, rallying, and getting stoked to eat more of his food. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter

Tucson-based chef Aaron Lopez had a vision that started in his small California city of El Centro, an agricultural city near the U.S.-Mexico border. There, he hatched a plan to create a menu imbued with the techniques and flavors of the Sonoran Desert that spans northern Mexico, Arizona, and southeastern California. Trained at top kitchens in Los Angeles and beyond, Lopez researched by going deep into the desert, armed with a camera and his wits. A year later, he and his wife June Chee carried the project to Tucson, a larger venue still deeply embedded in the desert, but with a new audience.

Inside the high-ceilinged, brick-walled downtown space, Ursa serves as a hushed gallery for Lopez and his team’s $150 tasting menu, which merges Indigenous cooking techniques with foraged and locally farmed ingredients. Barrel fruit (a yellow cactus) topped with the tang of pickled chiltepin leaves is the first bite, a luscious treat you may never see on a European plate. Quail breast arrives on a metal skewer dressed in pickled yucca, hovering over a jujube broth like a quiet offering. Goat roasted in agave, pit barbacoa-style, is unveiled tableside and served over softened tepary beans.

At every turn, with no extraneous adornments, the kitchen lets the produce and meats boast their innate nature. Lopez eschews conventional comfort, reimagining a meal of cactus, corn, sunflower tea, and beans as true luxuries, and the results are evocative and powerful. His message — seeing the value and beauty of this landscape, its people, its ingredients, and the way it all comes through the cooking — is the luscious pith of the cactus you find beneath the surface of the American Southwest. — Matthew Kang, correspondent

#6527. Researchers Discover New Lace Bug Species on Japan’s Remote Ogasawara Islands

DNA uncovered a hidden species among Japan’s lace bugs and hints that a tree introduced by humans could help give rise to another.

Lace bugs living on two groups of Japan’s remote Ogasawara Islands had been classified as a single species, despite differences in their diets and coloring. Comparisons of their DNA have now revealed that they belong to two species, a distinction supported by subtle physical differences.

The archipelago lies roughly 900 to 1,000 kilometers (560 to 620 miles) south of Tokyo and is a UNESCO World Natural Heritage site. Its land snails and plants are celebrated for including species found nowhere else. About 440 insect species are also known to be unique to the islands, but their evolution has received far less attention.

Among those insects is Omoplax, a genus of lace bugs thought to have diversified rapidly across the islands. Jun Souma, of Hirosaki University’s Shirakami Research Center for Environmental Sciences, investigated these insects with Naoyuki Nakahama, of the Graduate School of Agriculture at Osaka Metropolitan University.

“The reason I took a particular interest in Omoplax desecta is that it feeds on both the native plant Rhaphiolepis indica var. tashiroi and the introduced plant Calophyllum inophyllum in the Chichijima island group,” Souma said. “This is quite unusual for lace bugs, which typically exhibit high host specificity. I was also intrigued by the fact that it is distributed across multiple island groups, which is different from other Omoplax species.”

To investigate relationships among the insects, the researchers analyzed 52 specimens using MIG-seq, a method that provides DNA data from across the genome. Populations classified as Omoplax desecta on the Chichijima and Hahajima island groups were genetically distinct. The study is published in the open-access journal ZooKeys.

The genetic evidence helped explain differences Souma had noticed in the Hahajima insects.

“I had wondered why it fed exclusively on Rhaphiolepis indica var. tashiroi and why there were no individuals with dark brown to black pronotum, which are sometimes seen in the Chichijima island group,” Souma explained. The pronotum is the plate just behind an insect’s head. “After conducting population genetic and phylogenetic analyses, I began to suspect that this population might be a distinct species. Upon closely observing their morphological characteristics, I was certain of this.”

Subtle differences in male genitalia confirmed the distinction. The Hahajima population is now described as Omoplax sandoru, named after the local name of its host plant.

For Omoplax desecta in the Chichijima group, the introduced tree offered another clue to how these insects might diversify. The DNA data indicate that its shift to feeding on Calophyllum inophyllum happened once, and recently. Whether that change will eventually produce another species remains a possibility rather than an established outcome.

“I also find it interesting that the introduction of Calophyllum inophyllum by humans may have led to a budding of future speciation in Omoplax desecta,” Souma added.

The researchers also reconstructed an evolutionary tree to trace relationships among the insects. That allowed them to test whether species with similar appearances and food preferences were one another’s closest relatives.

“The most surprising finding of my research was that species feeding on the same plant and appearing very similar are not necessarily sister groups,” said Souma, referring to groups that are each other’s closest evolutionary relatives. “Adaptive radiation among insects on oceanic islands may be more complex than comparisons of morphological characteristics and life histories would suggest at first glance.”

Adaptive radiation is the diversification of related organisms into species adapted to different ecological roles. Here, the findings point to both geographic isolation and shifts between host plants as drivers of species formation.

The researchers could not obtain DNA from two rare species, leaving gaps in the evolutionary picture. Further sampling will be needed to trace how these insects reached the islands and diversified.

Reference: “Genome-wide SNP data reveal phylogenetic relationships and further new species of lace bugs (Hemiptera, Heteroptera, Tingidae) endemic to the Japanese oceanic islands (the Ogasawara Islands), providing insight into their speciation” by Jun Souma and Naoyuki Nakahama, 8 October 2026, ZooKeys. DOI: 10.3897/zookeys.1294.205145

#6526. A Common Food Emulsifier Could Solve One of Rocketry’s Oldest Fuel Problems

In propulsion system design, engineers have long faced a trade-off between solid and liquid rocket fuels. Each has advantages and disadvantages, and in an effort to try to min/max the efficacy of different types of fuel, researchers have long placed an emphasis on a hybrid between solids and liquids - in other words theyâve been working with gels. Unfortunately, gels have their own sets of problems to deal with. But a new paper published by Pranay Mudaliar and Jerin John of Concordia in the journal Langmuir uses an uncommon ingredient to elegantly solve some of those problems, but which is typically used in a completely different area of human activity - lecithin.

Solid rocket boosters, like those that powered the Space Shuttle, are very stable, durable, and quick to ignite. However, they are also impossible to turn off - you have to burn through all the propellant at once.

Liquid fuel, on the other hand, is much more flexible, much like automotive fuel. Liquid fueled engines can be throttled up and down, restarted multiple times, and generally are much more controllable than their solid cousins. However, they also float and slosh around in tanks, which is a particular problem in zero-gravity environments, as that sloshing can cause vapor pockets that can break a turbopump if not filtered out beforehand. Liquids also have a tendency to leak or evaporate over long periods, making them less than ideal for multi-year journeys through the solar system.

Fraser talks about some of the difficulties of orbital refueling.

On paper, gels offer a great solution to that. While sitting in a tank, they would act like a dense solid, but can also act like a liquid when forced into a combustion chamber. However, they suffer from their own challenges, such as shelf life and temperature dependent phase changes.

The paper details a new type of fuel that uses an unexpected special ingredient. Lecithin might sound familiar, but not in the context of rocket fuel. Itâs commonly used as an emulsifier in food. Itâs commonly used to keep chocolate smooth, and salad dressing cohesive, and can be found on thousands of supermarket food labels. In the context of rocket fuel, lecithin acts simply as an organic gelling agent.

When combined with a trace amount of calcium chloride salt, lecithin molecules self-organize into microscopic worm-like structures called micelles. Chains of these form an invisible 3D mesh that can trap and hold kerosene molecules, a more traditional type of rocket fuel, in place. Lecithin also has the added advantage of being an organic compound made up of carbon and hydrogen, so it will burn right alongside the kerosene rather than acting as simply dead-weight like may other non-combustible thickening agents previously used to create gel fuels.

Scott Manley talks about the engineering behind solid rocket boosters. Credit - Scott Manley YouTube Channel

But perhaps the most interesting feature of the new fuel is a physical phenomenon known as shear thinning. When the gel is sitting under normal conditions in a tank, it holds it shape firmly like a gelatin, eliminating the sloshing features that cause so many problems in liquid-fuel rockets. However, as soon as thereâs a mechanical pressure or shear force applied - such as when the spacecraft pressurizes the fuel lines - the micellar mesh breaks apart, causing the gel to temporarily quickly collapse into a liquid.

Measurements detailed in the paper show the gelâs viscosity dropping by a factor of more than 100, creating an easily pumpable liquid that can be sprayed through injector nozzles. But when the pressure stops, the material snaps back to its rest state as a gel. There are also two other environmental stimulants that can cause this liquid transformation - if the gel is heated up to between 59 and 68 degrees C, or splashed with a small amount of ethanol. In other words, localized thermal or chemical triggers could easily intentionally force specific amounts of fuel to liquefy without requiring the bulk of the fuel to do so.

Another appealing feature of the gel, from an experimental standpoint anyway, is that itâs clear. Therefore researchers can watch it with optical high-speed cameras and lasers to analyze its structure as well as its spray patterns. And a final appealing feature is its shelf life - the gel stayed stable in a tank for over a year, with no visible signs of a phase separate that plagues many other gelatin-like fuels.

It is still a very long road from the benchtop to the launchpad though. The new fuel hasnât actually been sprayed through the high-pressure injectors that would be used on an actual rocket engine. Nor has it shown that itâs capable of withstanding the vibrations and temperature shocks that come from being launched into space. But as the Concordia researchers continue its development, this new gel is looking promising for potentially powering a future mission.

Concordia University - RESEARCH: New gel fuel could make rocket and satellite propulsion easier to control

P. Mudaliar & J. John - Rheology and Thermal Characterization of Lecithin-Based Kerosene Gels for In-Space Propulsion

#6525. 9 NYC Christmas Markets for Food, Fun, and Getting All Your Gift Shopping Done

New York City is electric any time of year, but few months on the calendar are as magical as the final two. In the run up to Christmas in New York, the Big Apple transforms into a holiday winter wonderland: think twinkling lights on street posts, elaborate department store window displays, and marquee theater events like New York City Ballet’s The Nutcracker or the Radio City Rockettes. It’s also probably the best time of the year to shop, thanks to a flurry of NYC Christmas markets that set up everywhere from Bryant Park to Grand Central Terminal.

But with so many to choose from, and locations all over the boroughs, how do you know which one is best for you to visit? That’s where we come in. Not only are we yearly visitors to all the annual markets, we’ve already done the research to scout the best newcomers to the field for 2026. Below, find our New Yorker-vetted NYC Christmas markets worth a holiday visit, from favorite and famed ones like Union Square’s, to newer events like Eater Under Wraps and Field + Supply.

Read our complete New York City travel guide here, which includes:

The rink at Bryant Park is tied only with Wollman in Central Park for the title of most famous in the city, and it's part of the Winter Village that runs here every year.

Location: Bryant Park, New York, NY 10018

Why we love it: There’s something for everyone at the massive Bank of America Winter Village at Bryant Park in the heart of Midtown. Gift givers will love The Holiday Shops by Urbanspace, a European-style market made up of “jewel box” kiosks filled with 180-plus vendors stocking everything from cozy winter hats to artisanal ornaments, while outdoor food stands at The Lodge provide plenty of fuel like s’mores and sausages for your shopping escapades. The Winter Village is also home to one of the city’s most famed ice rinks, which is free to use (though skate rental fees apply if you don’t bring your own).

The Grand Central Holiday Fair is celebrating its 21st year within the iconic terminal's shuttle passage.

Location: Vanderbilt Hall, Grand Central Terminal, 89 E. 42nd Street, New York, NY 10017

Why we love it: If you’re not exactly a fan of the cold weather, we have good news: New York City is also home to a handful of fantastic indoor holiday markets. The longest-running is the Grand Central Holiday Fair inside the city’s transportation crown jewel, Grand Central Terminal. The train station’s annual Holiday Fair inside Vanderbilt Hall features over thirty small businesses selling handmade gifts, plus an Uncommon Goods pop-up and an outpost of the Grand Central Gift Shop for all the train lovers on your list. And speaking of trains: after you’re done shopping, stick around the Terminal to watch the famed Holiday Train Show, featuring model trains trundling along decorated tracks that feature NYC landmarks and even the North Pole.

Union Square Holiday Market remains the gold standard classic for most New Yorkers, with 185 vendors spiraling out in a seemingly endless array of booths.

Location: Union Square, New York, NY 10003

Why we love it: If you say “holiday market” to a New Yorker, chances are they’ll direct you to the bustling Union Square Holiday Market. With nearly 200 vendors spread across concentric half-circles of booths, we’re not exaggerating when we say you can find the perfect present for everyone on your list at this sprawling pop-up. Some buzzy vendors to look out for this year? The MB Edit for vintage accessories and silk scarves, Hudson Valley Seed Company for organic bulbs and seeds, and make sure to save time to explore the many food purveyors for snacks, like Fan-Fan Donuts from James Beard Award nominee Fany Gerson. Pro tip: As the city’s most famous market, it can get quite crowded on nights and weekends, so try to opt for daytime weekday visits if possible.

Location: 100 W. 77th Street, New York, NY 10024

Dates: Every Sunday from November 29 until December 30 (and Saturdays December 12 and December 19)

Why we love it: While many of New York’s most famed holiday markets have the polish so closely associated with the city, one of the reasons Grand Holiday Bazaar is beloved is that it feels like a proper neighborhood event. Held every Sunday in a combo indoor-outdoor space on the Upper West Side, the Bazaar hosts over 150 independent, rotating local vendors who sell everything from handmade holiday decor to vintage accessories to skincare. Plus, 100 percent of the event’s profits are donated to four local public schools that serve over 2,000 kids.

FAD Market Holiday Pop-Up will set up shop in the lobby of Empire Stores in Dumbo, also home to Time Out Market.

Location: Empire Stores, 55 Water Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201 (Dumbo) and St. Paul, 190 Court Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201 (Cobble Hill)

Dates: November 30 – December 20 (Dumbo) and December 5–6, 12–13, and 19–20 (Cobble Hill)

Why we love it: FAD (which stands for Fashion, Art, Design) will host double the markets this year, in two separate locations in Brooklyn. Dumbo, which will run continuously from November 30th until December 20th inside Empire Stores, will have a rotating selection of jewelry makers, ceramicists, and small-batch food purveyors, with about 35 vendors on weekends and 14 during the week. Cobble Hill’s pop-up, meanwhile, will run over three weekends in December at St. Paul church, with a brand-new crew of 70-plus makers selling giftables like apparel, home decor, and skincare.

Turkish jewelry, fondue baguettes, and artisan soaps are on offer at Columbus Circle's Central Park-adjacent Christmas market.

Location: Columbus Circle, New York, NY, 10019

Why we love it: Situated at one of the prettiest corners of Manhattan—smack between Columbus Circle and Central Park—this market would be worth the trip even if the vendors were hawking only touristy souvenirs. Luckily though, the selection here is carefully curated, with makers this year ranging from Seyahan’s Turkish-inspired jewelry to Fairy Greens Lavender Farm’s fragrant collection of candles, soaps, and body oils made with the dreamy plant. There’s also plenty to snack on: don’t miss first-time vendor Fondue Baguette selling—you guessed it—baguettes filled with cheese.

Location: Herald Square, New York, NY 10001

Field + Supply, one of upstate New York's premier makers' markets, has landed in the city for the first time this year with a weekend pop-up in the Starrett-Lehigh Building.

Location: Starrett-Lehigh Building, 601 W. 26th Street, New York, NY 10001

Why we love it: One of upstate New York’s premier makers’ markets returns to the city this year, much to the delight of anyone looking for chic home goods, artisanal jewelry, and much more. There will be 140-plus vendors at the two-day Field + Supply event in Chelsea, with products ranging from ceramics to textiles to specialty foods. And even if you’re shopped out, there’s plenty else to lure you, including a visit from Santa himself and retro tintype portraits.

Location: Iron23, 29 W. 23rd Street, New York, NY 10010

Why we love it: The ultimate one-stop-shop for foodies, Eater Under Wraps, returns for a one-day-only market this year in Chelsea. Brands like Pepsi, Reese’s, and Kahlúa will host activations, along with food and drink samples from local spots like Shania's Max Bet and Nishaan, and, naturally, a robust, curated selection of gifts chosen by Eater’s own editors.

#6524. NASA Warns a Monster El Niño Could Surpass the Historic 1997 Event

An El Niño that could beat 1997’s record is taking shape in the Pacific, leaving scientists watching for its next move.

El Niño is part of a natural climate pattern that returns roughly every two to seven years. Its most recent very strong events, in 1997–98 and 2015–16, disrupted weather worldwide. Consequences included fires in Indonesia and the Amazon, crop failures caused by drought in southern Africa, and heavy rain and coastal flooding in Southern California.

Satellite measurements show that the current El Niño resembles the 1997–98 event, with warm water stretching across the equatorial Pacific to South America. But that oceanic resemblance does not guarantee the same weather during winter 2026–27, as the outcome also depends on how the atmosphere responds.

Every El Niño starts with a change in the tropical Pacific’s winds. Trade winds normally push warm surface water westward, leaving sea levels higher in the western Pacific than in the east. When those winds weaken, warm water begins moving back toward the central and eastern Pacific.

As warmth spreads eastward, the trade winds weaken further and sometimes reverse, allowing still more warm water to follow. This feedback loop helps El Niño intensify.

But strength alone does not determine its effects. The location of the warmest water and the atmosphere’s response also shape the outcome. “The search for the ‘typical’ El Niño is very elusive,” said Josh Willis, project scientist for sea level missions at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). “They’re all different in terms of where they land and how their impacts play out.”

Scientists can track that developing pattern from space because warming water expands, raising the sea surface. Across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, unusually high water therefore provides a signal of El Niño’s heat buildup.

The maps compare sea surface height anomalies on October 13, 1997 (left), and October 12, 2026 (right). JPL scientists processed measurements from TOPEX/Poseidon and Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich, respectively. Red shows higher-than-average sea levels, white indicates normal conditions, and blue marks lower levels. Seasonal effects and long-term trends have been removed to highlight El Niño and other short-term natural changes.

“What’s unique about altimetry is that we have a 35-year record from nearly identical satellites flying almost the same ground track, with each mission overlapping the next,” Willis said. “That lets us look back in time and compare this El Niño to what happened in 1997. And right now, this one is on track to be even bigger.”

Although the 2026 El Niño developed much more abruptly, by October it shared two defining features with 1997: lower sea levels in the west and higher levels in the east, with warm, elevated water reaching South America. Willis thinks that resemblance could translate into similar impacts, including the abundant rainfall seen across California and the southern United States in 1997–98.

The powerful 2015–16 event shows why the arrangement of that heat matters. A map based on Jason-2 measurements from October 12, 2015, appears alongside the 1997 and 2026 comparisons. In 2015, the exceptionally warm, high water along the equator did not reach as far against South America. That winter, rainfall effects were concentrated more over Central America and the southeastern United States, with significant flooding in Mexico.

NOAA’s October 8, 2026, El Niño outlook assigned an 83 percent chance of a strong to very strong event through the first three months of 2027. Still, its effects during winter 2026–27 and beyond remain uncertain. El Niño’s influence passes through a chaotic atmosphere, and its signal becomes harder to distinguish beyond the tropics.

“There’s always a bit of a dice roll here,” Willis said. “Just because this El Niño looks like 1997 doesn’t mean it will be exactly the same—it’s just our best guess at the moment.”

“Scientists can track that developing pattern from space because warming water expands, raising the sea surface.”

The sea surface is moved by tides, drifting air masses with different pressures, prevailing winds, random gusts, constructive interference of waves from all over the world, and ubiquitous, local waves. Those influences, many with short temporal duration, have to be averaged to obtain an estimate of the mean surface elevation. I have never seen an estimate of the standard deviation, often used as an estimate for the uncertainty of the mean. Things like “rogue waves,” (constructive/destructive interference) are probably usually missed, despite their great height, because of their short duration and narrow width.

Why the preference for altimetry instead of a direct measure of temperature? Because of surface mixing and the thermal inertia of water, it would seem to me that thermal IR would be a more direct measurement of the influence of El Niño on weather.

Once again, it appears necessary to remind these authors, and others, that “could” is a qualitative, not quantitative, word used to describe a low-probability event that is not, however, impossible. That is, it is permissive, not obligatory. In fact, the way it is commonly used, it has less probability of occurring than not occurring. Given that it is not associated with a numeric probability, there isn’t much else about it that can be said that is actionable. It is a word best used by a defense attorney trying to convince a jury that it is possible that his/her client is innocent of the charges brought. Our jurisprudence system is purposely designed to minimize wrongful convictions. It is embodied in the guiding principle that it is better that 10 guilty criminals are set free rather than one innocent person be punished. Science is not supposed to have such biases.

If this developing El Niño turns out to not be as strong or long-lasting as it ‘could’ be, will we hear any more about it after the fact? Will we get an explanation for why it didn’t live up to the arm waving? Probably not, because meteorologists don’t really know what triggers an El Niño. About the best they can do is predict that they will occur episodically every two to seven years. They are like a great earthquake or volcanic eruption in that respect.

#6523. An Artificial CORTEX to Guide Satellite Rescue Missions

The growing problem of satellites crowding one another is generating concern in the space community, for good reason. Almost 20,000 satellites orbit Earth now, and with more satellite constellations and other satellites being launched every year, Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) is starting to look like it's reaching its limit. Of particular concern are the 3,500+ plus satellites that are basically zombies. They are either completely non-functional or not sending any signals alerting other satellites to their presence.

A collision between two satellites could be catastrophic. Satellite constellations have some built-in redundancy which would help deal with the loss, but there's an additional risk. A collision could also create a debris cloud, multiplying the ongoing risk. The Kessler syndrome describes a cascade of collisions generated from debris created in a single, initial collision, that goes on to create even more collisions. It's like a feedback loop that keeps getting worse.

Somehow, this problem must be dealt with. The existing debris is one thing, but intact zombie satellites are another. These have lost the ability to communicate and warn other satellites of their presence. These can be repaired, and that's the subject of new research in Acta Astronautica. It's titled "CORTEX: An autonomous, end-to-end, convex-based framework for close-range rendezvous trajectory design and guidance with hardware testbed validation," and the lead author is Minduli Wijayatunga, a new aerospace engineering faculty member in The Grainger College of Engineering, at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

This work is all about the growing idea of Rendezvous and Proximity Operations (RPO). Spacecraft docking operations have been custom-designed solutions for individual situations, like docking with the ISS. But with thousands of zombie satellites, custom docking solutions aren't realistic.

"Rendezvous and Proximity Operations (RPO) are shifting from bespoke demonstration missions such as Northrop Grummanâs Mission Extension Vehicles, Chinaâs Tianyuanâ1, and Astroscaleâs ADRAS-J, to routine missions due to the growth of in-orbit assets and the resulting demand for inspection, servicing, assembly, and debris mitigation," the authors write. They point out that while there were only about 13,700 tracked objects in LEO in 2019, there were more than 24,000 in 2025. That's a shocking increase, and there's no signs of it slowing down.

That's forcing scientists to develop autonomous ways to deal with the overpopulation. The growing population of satellites isn't the only thing dictating an autonomous solutions. Autonomous repair is also critical because of the time delay in communications between the ground and LEO, and because satellites are best observed in and maneuvered with in windows when they're illuminated by sunlight.

âThese spacecraft must be able to track the trajectories of uncooperative objects autonomously but also make go/no-go decisions without waiting for the ground to decide,â Wijayatunga said. âSuppose your thruster fails or you encounter high-order orbital perturbations that push you away from your nominal trajectory. In those instances, how do you make those decisions?â she added.

That's what CORTEX is being designed to do.

"This paper presents CORTEX (Convex Optimization for Rendezvous Trajectory EXecution), an autonomous framework for close-range rendezvous trajectory design and guidance under sensing, actuation, and dynamics uncertainties," the authors write.

"Among RPO phases, the close-range rendezvous, where the servicer locates the docking port axes and approaches the client, is particularly safety-critical. It must satisfy strict operational constraints (e.g., keep-out zones, approach corridors, plume/line-of-sight constraints, illumination/eclipses) under limited actuation authority and imperfect relative navigation," the authors write.

Wijayatunga's PhD involved trajectory and guidance using something called convex optimization. Convex optimization is a method that lets a spacecraft approach a target using math and trajectories, not input commands. It basically solves a math problem of trajectories and thruster commands until the lone, best answer is arrived at. The answer should mean a successful docking. The idea is to reach that docking state with minimal fuel use while also following constraints like the targets no-go zones or keep-out zones. Those are places on the target satellite that might house sensitive equipment like sensors or antennae.

This work expanded to include the idea of sunlight windows. Cortex also includes options other than aborting if things went sideways. Instead of calling the docking off, CORTEX can reconsider its options. It even takes into account situations that arise where thrusters can't be fired.

âI wanted to bring that same idea into developing CORTEX and expand it, taking into consideration sunlight windows so we don't have to operate in darkness. That, and the replanning versus abort architecture, are novel in CORTEX,â Wijayatunga said.

âCORTEX has trajectory design and guidance, so if you deviate significantly from your nominal mission trajectory, it replans the trajectory and re-approaches unless you are in severe violation of your keep-out zone, in which case it returns to a passively safe orbit. It's an algorithm to recover from the unexpected. We tried instances where you're supposed to use your thrusters, but you can't for whatever reason. And CORTEX was very robust to that.â

CORTEX is being tested in a particular modelled docking scenario. It's what's called an ISAM, an In-orbit Servicing Sssembly and Manufacturing. It's designed for what will most likely be fairly typical in the future. It involves a Client Spacecraft Object (CSO) in LEO and is designed to test autonomous approach, servicing, and inspection of the CSO by a servicing spacecraft with a Guidance Navigation and Control (GNC) system for proximity operations.

Hold positions are an important part of CORTEX. In the modelled scenario, there are two of them that let the servicing spacecraft pause and re-evaluate in a fixed relative position. One is at the beginning of the fly around, and the other is at the start of the final approach. They are there to let the servicer pause during eclipses, a new idea in CORTEX.

This figure shows some aspects of CORTEX controlling a servicing spacecraft while it approaches and rendezvous with a client satellite. Blue shows the Rendezvous Sphere, orange shows the Approach Sphere, and red is the Keep Out Sphere. The approach axes is identified as CORTEX's successful solution to the docking problem. Image Credit: Wijayatunga et al. 2026. Acta Astronautica.

One way of looking at CORTEX is as a flow chart governed by four things. "The goals of CORTEX are: (i) minimize fuel and time consumption, (ii) ensure that both the fly-around and final approach occur entirely in sunlight, (iii) avoid the KOS during the fly-around phase, and (iv) satisfy the approach corridor constraint and avoid plume impingement during the final approach," the authors write.

This schematic flow-chart shows how CORTEX works. CORTEX has the ability to abort its approach if necessary, and instead of giving up, it can determine how to re-approach its client. Image Credit: Wijayatunga et al. 2026. Acta Astronautica.

In the tests, the servicing spacecraft was forced into an odd, unexpected situation and CORTEX had to deal with it. Its orbit was unexpectedly perturbed, and thruster operation was impaired, not firing when they were supposed to. Other errors were also introduced, corresponding to unexpected factors like solar storms and thrust errors.

CORTEX fared well in the tests and was able to deal with the unexpected situations in the models. "In all cases, the framework either recovered successfully while respecting safety constraints or executed a safe retreat before entering unsafe regions," the authors write.

âIn some of the hardware tests, if the servicer violates the approach corridor, it leaves the keep-out zone and retreats to a safe position and in others, the servicer is able to recover and carry on with its mission,â Wijayatunga said.

Satellite close approach and recovery isn't purely hypothetical. The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAX) launched Astroscale's ADRAS-J in 2024. It successfully maneuvered within 50 meters of a typical piece of space debris, a spent rocket stage, considered to be an 'uncooperative target.' It flew around the object, catching multiple images from different angles. It used sensors and autonomous navigation to accomplish this.

Astroscale's ADRAS-J autonomous spacecraft approached a spent rocket booster, a typical piece of space debris, and captured images of it from multiple angles. It's a step toward eventual servicing of zombie satellites. Image Credit: Astroscale/JAXA.

The hallmark of the past few decades is rapidly-advancing technology. Among other things, it's led to a crowded LEO and a growing population of zombie satellites.

Maybe we'll end up using technological tools like CORTEX, enabled by AI and machine learning, to manage the problems technology has helped generate in the first place.

Using machine learning, astronomers developed a new way of looking at James Webb telescope data that allows far-off planets to emerge from their stars' glare.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When it comes to spotting planets orbiting distant stars, the biggest hurdle is often separating the signal from the noise — specifically, trying to distinguish a planet from the stellar glare around it. That's true even for the most sophisticated telescopes, including the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST).

Now, astronomers have developed a new way to spot planets that were formerly drowned out in a sea of light. Using a combination of modeling and machine learning techniques, they picked out a previously hidden giant exoplanet in data from JWST. The results were published Nov. 4 in the journal Nature.

"Planets are a million times fainter than their stars," study first author Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, an astronomer at Northwestern University, said in a statement. "So, to image exoplanets, we need to remove that glare."

Telescopes like JWST use instruments called coronagraphs to block out some of this excess light, similar to the way the moon and a pinhole camera operate during a total solar eclipse. But even the best coronagraphs have limitations — for example, they can't block all the glare, and the telescopes themselves move.

Even the most stable telescopes vibrate almost imperceptibly as they collect light, so the images a telescope produces contain ever-so-slight mismatches compared with what the instrument actually sees. These slight shifts can be enough to obscure even very large exoplanets.

To address this, Ferrer-Chavez and his team developed a "digital twin" of JWST that virtually recreates how light travels through the telescope's detectors, minus any movement-based imperfections. To fine-tune this digital replica, the researchers used computational models based in real-world physics alongside machine learning techniques similar to those used to train AI. But the authors stressed that this is not an AI model.

"Because we already know the physics, we don't need AI to understand what's happening," study co-author Jason Wang, also an astrophysicist at Northwestern, said in a statement.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The researchers named their approach Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets, or FLIP.

Using FLIP, the team analyzed data from three stars, including 51 Eridani, which is located around 97 light-years from Earth and was already suspected to have a giant exoplanet orbiting it. Although the planet, called 51 Eridani b, had been detected by ground-based telescopes, it was drowned out by light in previous JWST observations. With FLIP, however, 51 Eridani b popped out from the dataset.

The scientists hope this approach will help astronomers pick out even more hard-to-spot exoplanets, especially ones that look like the planets in our own backyard. In the nearly 35-year history of exoplanet hunting, the vast majority of planets we've found have been radically different from those in our own solar system, partially because larger and more reflective worlds are easier to spot with current telescopes.

"It's not that [solar-system-like planets] don't exist," Ferrer-Chavez said. "It's that we can't see them."

Ferrer-Chavez, R., Wang, J. J., Bouman, K. L., Freeman, W. T., Pueyo, L., Feng, B. Y., & Perrin, M. D. (2026). Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit. Nature, 659(8139), 58–62. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11213-z

#6521. The 2026 Restaurant Dishes of the Year

From an earthy curry crab callaloo dip to a plate of pickled walleye cheeks, these were editors’ most memorable bites

Our editors ate in hundreds of restaurants across the country this year, but certain dishes left a lasting impression, and we’re recognizing them in this new national Eater Award category.

From a textbook execution of the ubiquitous 2026 entree — roast chicken — to an innovative fish preparation offering Midwestern diners a new way to experience a familiar ingredient, these dishes are all worth celebrating. — Missy Frederick, editorial director

Learn more about this year’s Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, and how editors selected them, here.

When experiencing a five-course tasting menu ($145), I wasn’t expecting toast to be a main attraction. But even with competition from luxurious courses featuring everything from a complex Hokkaido scallop to an assertive charred rib-eye with peaches, All Well’s puffed grain toast left a lasting impression.

After three years at two-Michelin-starred Oriole, Larry Feldmeier partnered with Noah Sandoval, fellow Oriole alum and James Beard winner for Best Chef: Great Lakes, to open the ambitious West Loop restaurant All Well, which offers both a la carte bar options and the aforementioned tasting; the toast is only available as part of the latter experience.

The dish arrives to the table amplified with nutty buckwheat butter sweetened with honey, the backdrop for a pasta stuffed with triple-cream Délice de Bourgogne and a cauldron of salty chicken brodo. You’ll dive into the pasta, of course, using the bread to sop up the rich beurre blanc. Like a performer waiting in the wings for their monologue, the puffed grain toast takes center stage. The toast effectively offsets the creaminess and saltiness of the rest of the dish, but can stand on its own even without the accompanying pasta. Its subtle sweetness almost acts as a mid-meal dessert, a distinctive break in a seamless dinner you don’t quite want to end. — Isaiah Reynolds, audience editor

The only thing about Oklahoma City that feels even vaguely reminiscent of the Caribbean is the sheet-pan-flat horizon. And yet inside a gaping industrial dining room downtown, there’s Dougla Kitchen, where diners sip fruity rum drinks out of plastic bags and acclaimed chef Andrew Black digs deep in his past to bring OKC locals a taste of his Indo-Jamaican upbringing. I fully admit this Midwestern-born, California-raised girl doesn’t encounter ruddy callaloo greens as often as she’d like (my hunch is neither do most Oklahomans). No matter. What Black manages to do with this deceiving pile of greenish-brown mush, dank with hand-picked crab and sparkling with curry spices, translates the soul of Caribbean home cooking in a single scoop. I didn’t know it was possible to be overwhelmed by a sense memory from a life that’s not your own, but this heady appetizer does that, served with a side of crisp taro chips and worth lingering over all afternoon with a couple of Red Stripes. — Lesley Suter, brand director

To understand California cuisine in 2026, look no further than Henrietta, a neighborhood bistro that has struck a just-right balance of precision and ingenuity while imbuing a feeling of nostalgia that begs locals and travelers alike to return. The restaurant’s intentions come across most clearly in its roast chicken, served as a just-salty-enough half chicken hunked into handheld pieces with deep, smoky char marks. The prize chicken pile gets tucked onto a plate alongside a scorched lemon half and a heaping, chicory-heavy Caesar panzanella blanketed under a layer of Parmesan that could be a snowcap on a stretch of the San Gabriel Mountains. With the chicken, Henrietta nods to forebears (namely San Francisco’s Zuni), while making the dish its own with a Baja-born Caesar salad that feels distinctly Los Angeles, dotted with torn fistfuls of bread from the neighboring local Clark Street Bakery. Of course, 2026 continues to be the year of the Great Chickening, where roast chicken has become many a restaurant’s calling card — and an easy way into the cultural cache. In Los Angeles alone, Sqirl (with its new dinner menu) and Pasjoli have both put out progressive, near-intoxicating spins on the dish, but Henrietta’s has lodged itself into the collective imagination with its brazen simplicity. — Rebecca Roland, deputy editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest

The striking cantaloupe and verjus terrine at Nashville’s Junior offers a glimpse into the minds of chef Philip Krajeck and chef de cuisine Brian Mejia, the duo behind the high-technique kitchen. A “terrine” slice arrives with pieces of cantaloupe suspended in a clear gelatin made with verjus, the pressed juice of unripened grapes. One corner is covered in tiny, diced cubes of cantaloupe dressed in citrus-forward turmeric oil; another gets draped in chamomile-steeped cream. The mix of textures and flavors comes together in a dynamic symphony: the bright, acidic cubes of summer-ripened fruit against the calming mellowness of chamomile and gelatin layers that meld cantaloupe juice sweetness with crisp verjus.

The dessert’s structural elegance, which highlights a French variety of melon grown by a local farmer, may not immediately reveal its full complexity: Clear gelatin features a layer of clarified cantaloupe juice with encased melon slices, stacked between two layers of verjus gelatin. The melon gets compressed to intensify its flavors. Somehow, Junior managed to make Jell-O cool again — and dare I say, even sophisticated? — an example of Junior’s steady confidence that makes the restaurant an irresistible experience. — Dianne de Guzman, lead editor, Eater SF

Though people outside the Midwest may not be familiar with freshwater whitefish walleye, there it’s a classic comfort food, a staple of Lenten fish fries, state fair booths, and Lake Erie fishermen’s freezer stashes. At Rosy, chef Vinnie Cimino leans on that familiarity to help convince his customers to experience a beloved ingredient in an entirely new way. Pickled walleye cheeks ($17) have been a recurring staple — if a fleeting one — on Rosy’s Eastern European-leaning menu since the restaurant opened in February 2026. Kate’s Fish in Cleveland’s historic West Side Market provides walleye filets for sister restaurant Cordelia; when breaking down and fileting each fish, the fishmongers save the cheeks until they have a formidable stash. About every three weeks, Rosy can offer pickled walleye cheeks for around four days at a time. It’s a thoughtful move for sustainability, but also for succulence, as fish cheeks are a prized cut for their luscious texture.

Cimino conceived the dish as a nod to Jewish fish-pickling practices (for me, the results also brought to mind a tender ceviche). Seasonal vegetables are pickled with lemon — an earlier version invoked German-style potato salad, spring brought asparagus, and, when I went in June, bell pepper, carrot, and dill were in the mix. They’re then combined with the cheeks, which get a separate hot-pickling treatment involving red wine vinegar, salt, sugar, bay leaf, peppercorns, and coriander. “People really gravitate toward it,” Cimino says. “We’ve built up a great trust with our diners.” While the dish won’t be replacing fried walleye at area fish fries anytime soon, Cimino feels proud that when at Rosy, diners have been more than willing to go along with him for the ride. — MF

#6520. Antarctica’s Melting Ice Has Triggered a Sudden Shift Deep in the Ocean

Ocean measurements show a vast Southern Hemisphere water layer growing saltier and denser, a shift that could send more heat into deep waters than climate models predict.

Every Antarctic summer, melting sea ice sends a vast pulse of fresh water into the ocean. That seasonal supply helps sustain Antarctic Intermediate Water (AAIW), a layer of relatively fresh seawater that spreads across much of the Southern Hemisphere’s ocean. The AAIW helps store carbon, supply oxygen, and drive global currents, redistributing heat, fresh water, and carbon around the planet.

From 1995 to 2015, summer ice melt helped maintain this layer. But from 2016 to 2024, reduced freshwater input left it saltier, denser, and deeper, abruptly reversing its long-term trends in salinity, or salt content, and density.

The findings, published in Nature Climate Change, provide the first direct observational evidence of this change in the AAIW’s properties. The international research team analyzed data from the global Argo program, a network of around 4,000 robotic floats that sample the upper oceans, alongside satellite and atmospheric datasets.

The study was led by Associate Professor Bishakhdatta Gayen, of the University of Melbourne and the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), and Kaushik Mishra, a PhD student at IISc. Gayen said:

“The Antarctic region is the freshwater engine of oceans around the globe. Melting Antarctic sea ice influences circulation thousands of kilometers away. Until 2016, the seasonal summer melt was triple the Amazon River’s entire annual flow of roughly 6,600 cubic km.

“From 2016, Antarctic sea ice shrank to record lows. This abruptly choked off that critical seasonal surge, and the meltwater delivery dropped to roughly double the Amazon’s annual flow.”

Co-author Professor Alberto Naveira Garabato, of the University of Southampton in the United Kingdom, described the changes as an urgent reminder that climate change is affecting almost every part of Earth’s surface.

“As this altered, saltier and denser water mass travels north, it moves across the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans. Because this water layer forms part of the upper limb of the ocean’s global ‘overturning circulation’, a sustained shift could, over years to decades, feed into the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation – the deep-ocean current system often linked to climate stability in the North Atlantic.

“It could also ultimately influence atmospheric circulation, weather, and storm tracks in the Southern Hemisphere. However, the impact can cascade globally.”

The globe shows sea ice around Antarctica month by month. The first time-series graph shows whether sea-ice area was above or below normal (the 1993-2024 mean), based on satellite observations. The bottom graph tracks the saltiness of Antarctic Intermediate Water, a layer that sinks from the surface into the ocean’s interior, using Argo float data from 2004. From 1993 to 2015, Antarctic sea ice slowly expanded (blue trend line), releasing more freshwater, making the waters beneath it fresher. After 2016, sea ice dropped sharply (red trend line), and the layer turned saltier. Less melting ice means less freshwater reaching the ocean interior. Credit: Kaushik Mishra

Changes in how water moves between the surface and deeper layers could also affect the oceans’ role as a “climate buffer,” as Gayen described it. Oceans absorb and redistribute most of the excess heat and a large share of human CO₂ emissions, storing them for decades to centuries. This slows and moderates atmospheric warming and its immediate effects.

Mishra said the abrupt reversal revealed a critical missing feedback loop.

“The ocean absorbs over 90 percent of all heat released into the environment by human activities, with most of that heat stored in the upper ocean. A weakened AAIW layer could push more excess heat deeper. That would mean existing models are underestimating deep-ocean warming and therefore miscalculating regional sea level rise and long-term ocean and land surface temperatures.”

“If the altered AAIW changes the way surface water is carried down into deeper layers, it could affect how much carbon the ocean locks away – although the magnitude and timing are uncertain,” Gayen said.

“This could be the tipping point for the Atlantic Ocean and the AAIW current, leading to larger, longer-lasting changes to the climate in the Southern Hemisphere.”

According to Gayen, the last time the AAIW switched was at the end of the last interglacial period, around 130,000 years ago, when there was very little ice in Antarctica.

“That transition took thousands of years, not two decades,” he said.

Reference: “Reversal of Antarctic Intermediate Water trends triggered by sea ice decline” by Kaushik Mishra, Bishakhdatta Gayen and Alberto C. Naveira Garabato, 28 October 2026, Nature Climate Change. DOI: 10.1038/s41558-026-02758-y

MOES/11/2024) and the Australian Research Council Discovery Grant (grant no. DP240102823). A.C.N.G. acknowledges U.K. Research and Innovation guarantee funding for a European Research Council Advanced Grant (grant no. EP/X025136/1).

“Every Antarctic summer, melting sea ice sends a vast pulse of fresh water into the ocean.”

Inexplicably, the authors don’t mention why the melting sea ice is ‘fresh.’ Obviously, there is some snow on top of the ice. However, the main reason is that as sea water freezes, the dissolved salts are extruded from the crystal lattice of the forming ice, and cold, dense plums of concentrated brine sink into the depths. They have ignored half of the cycle and focused on the melting half, and implied that recent behavior portends a change in the long-term trend. Predictions are difficult when a system isn’t rigorously characterized and understood, which is the case with Antarctica. Antarctic shelf ice is is notoriously variable, and thus highly unpredictable. This is Chicken Little behavior of the wet feathers variety.

“That would mean existing models are underestimating deep-ocean warming and therefore miscalculating regional sea level rise and long-term ocean and land surface temperatures.”

Water is incompressible. Therefore, thermosteric expansion of the deep water by the speculated warming will be communicated to the sea level surface. Where is the evidence that this is happening?

#6519. A Perseverance Experiment Could Help Astronauts Prepare for Dust Storms on Mars

Martian dust is a major hurdle for human missions to Mars. Like Moon dust, its fine size and electrostatically charged nature allow it to stick to spacesuits, metal, and just about any other surface they come into contact with. Dust storms are also common on Mars, ranging from small whirlwinds that happen daily to global dust storms that occur once every 3 Martian years (~5.5 Earth years) and envelop the entire planet. Due to the low density of Mars' atmosphere, these storms don't generate much physical force.

The danger lies in how the dust plays havoc with instruments, machine parts, and astronaut health and safety. Given how well it adheres to surfaces, Apollo astronauts found that lunar dust accompanied them back into their landing modules, degrading mechanical joints and seals and causing respiratory problems. A recent study led by Washington University in St. Louis (WashU) highlights the need, using data from NASA's Perseverance rover, for sufficient astronaut training to prepare for the Martian environment.

Assistant Professor Scott VanBommel led the research effort along with staff scientist Abigail Knight, both of whom are fellows of the McDonnell Center for the Space Sciences (MCSS). They and their colleagues were joined by an international team of scientists from the U.S., Canada, Australia, and Europe, the MIT Haystack Observatory, Research Institutes of Sweden, the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO), the Space Science Institute (SCI), the Astromaterials Research and Exploration Science (ARES) division at the NASA Johnson Space Center, and NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

A very large Martian dust devil. This one reached 20 km high. Image Credit: NASA/JPL/University of Arizona

In addition to its array of sensors, cameras, drilling equipment, and sample cache, Perseverance also carries small swatches of spacesuit material that are constantly exposed to Mars' atmosphere. Using data acquired by the rover's Planetary Instrument for X-ray Lithochemistry (PIXL), the team examined the swatches for signs of wear and tear. They also applied a method developed by VanBommel to estimate the size of each particle in the PIXL data, providing the first direct characterization of fine (â²2.5 Âµm) and ultrafine particles (â²0.1 Âµm).

Their analysis found that the swatches showed little visible wear after 1,645 Martian days (sols) of exposure, largely because the particles observed were much smoother than the jagged grains found on the Moon. In summary, the results showed that Martian dust may be less likely to be abrasive to equipment or harmful to astronaut health than lunar regolith. The PIXL data also allowed the team to analyze the chemical composition of the particles that had caked the swatches.

From this, the team confirmed the presence of perchlorates and other toxins, as well as high levels of sulfur, iron, and silica in the dust grains. In addition, Martian dust can be exceptionally fine, with some ultrafine particles measuring as little as 100 nanometers (nm) in diameter. On Earth, ultrafine particles typically come in the form of smoke and air pollution, which can cause significant health problems because they can sink deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. With Martian dust carrying perchlorates and other toxins, the health risk is magnified.

There's also the way it is electrostatically charged like its lunar counterpart. "The electrostatic properties of Martian dust are likely causing it to preferentially adhere to some surfaces," Knight added, who helped conceptualize and conduct the analysis while a Ph.D. student at the MCSS. So while Martian dust may be less abrasive to surfaces and irritating to the lungs, it poses a hazard because of its toxicity and how easily it can be tracked into habitats where astronauts will not have the protection of a spacesuit.

Mars Perseverance rover - PIXL studies a rock (artist concept). Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

These considerations must be taken into account when mission planners are designing space suits and infrastructure for Mars. As astronauts will be passing in and out of vehicles and habitats regularly, small amounts of dust will likely be introduced that (if left unchecked) will constitute a mounting health hazard. Fortunately, the level of health risk largely depends on dose and duration. With proper mitigation strategies, both can be limited to a point where they do not pose a significant threat.

The particles in the Martian atmosphere have been blowing in the wind for potentially billions of years, so they tend to be well-rounded, like pebbles in a river. We've been operating rovers on the surface of Mars continuously for more than 20 years at this point. We know that dust will be a challenge, but it's something we can prepare for and overcome.

These results highlight the effectiveness of rover missions in advancing human spaceflight and the exploration of extraterrestrial bodies. In addition to providing immense insights into the geological history and conditions on Mars, they've also served as test beds for technologies that will be crucial to human exploration when it begins.

#6518. Brick Kilns Became Cleaner and More Profitable, but Workers Saw No Benefits

Bangladesh’s brick kilns found a way to pollute less and earn more, but workers saw no measurable improvement in their pay or working conditions.

Simple adjustments to how coal is fed and bricks are stacked helped traditional kilns burn less fuel, release less pollution, and produce better bricks. Yet a companion study found no measurable improvement in wages, health, child labor, or coercive working conditions during the study period.

The findings expose a gap between improving an industry’s performance and improving life for its workforce. They also suggest that protecting workers requires measures aimed directly at their needs.

The multiyear research effort involved Nina Brooks, an assistant professor at the University of Michigan’s School for Environment and Sustainability and a faculty affiliate of its Center for South Asian Studies.

Bangladesh’s rapid urban growth depends on an industry with a substantial environmental footprint. The country is the world’s fourth-largest brick producer, and roughly 8,000 traditional kilns supply more than 90% of its domestic brick consumption. Alongside carbon emissions, the kilns release fine particles known as PM2.5. Ambient air pollution causes 4.9 million premature deaths globally, with South Asia accounting for 32% of them.

Brooks began investigating brickmaking about eight years ago during her doctoral studies. She and her collaborators mapped kilns with satellite imagery and machine learning, studied regulation, and examined health effects in communities downwind. Their work revealed why restricting kiln locations alone could not solve the pollution problem.

“Bangladesh is one of the world’s most densely populated countries,” Brooks said. “It is not feasible to move brick kilns away from all schools, health facilities, and urban centers that may be harmed by the pollution.”

Instead, researchers worked with owners, managers, and workers to improve existing operations. They introduced more continuous coal feeding, brick-stacking arrangements that improved airflow, and measures to reduce heat loss. None required replacing kilns or purchasing major new equipment.

After a small pilot, the team expanded the approach to hundreds of kilns. Results published in Science showed that training and technical support reduced energy use by about 10.5% across kilns assigned to the program. Estimated emissions fell by 171 metric tons (about 188.5 US tons) of carbon dioxide and 0.45 metric tons (about 990 pounds) of PM2.5 per kiln over a firing season.

Among kilns that adopted the practices because of the program, energy use dropped about 23%, while carbon dioxide and PM2.5 emissions each fell roughly 20%. Owners spent less on fuel and produced a greater proportion of higher-quality bricks.

Adoption had increased when researchers returned the next firing season, suggesting the changes had staying power. “Because the changes are economically beneficial for owners, they had a strong incentive to continue following them,” Brooks said.

For businesses facing expensive equipment upgrades and authorities struggling to enforce environmental rules, the findings offered a practical route to cleaner production.

The researchers then examined whether those business benefits reached workers. Bangladesh’s brick industry relies on a large, mostly informal workforce whose employment can involve debt, advance payments, long hours, hazardous conditions, and restrictions on leaving. A companion study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences examined 246 kilns in the Khulna Division and included private interviews with 1,442 workers.

Seventy percent of workers reported having no personal protective equipment, and 71% lacked a formal labor contract. Forty-two percent described restrictions on movement or communication. Across the sample, roughly 20% met the U.S. Department of State’s definitions of labor trafficking. At nearly half the kilns, at least 1 in 6 workers met those definitions.

Adult workers also reported child labor at more than 70% of the kilns, with most reported cases involving children ages 14 to 17.

The intervention lowered fuel costs by 9.6% and improved brick quality by 8.1%, but researchers detected no corresponding improvement in trafficking, child labor, wages, health, or working conditions. Although changes were possible within the study period, the economic gains did not produce measurable benefits for workers.

Higher productivity is often expected to help employees through better pay or conditions. The kiln studies show why that outcome cannot be assumed when coercion and limited bargaining power shape the labor market.

“In many countries, not just Bangladesh, labor laws are hard to enforce, particularly in informal sectors. So, it’s critical to find other ways to protect workers from exploitation,” said Grant Miller, a professor of medicine at Stanford University. “Our study shows that we cannot rely on productivity gains alone to do that, at least not in the short run. Finding approaches that work beyond regulation is a central goal of our ongoing research.”

Expanding the cleaner production program revealed that kiln owners in other regions were more reluctant to adopt the changes. In districts around Dhaka, owners were considerably less likely to adopt the practices than those in Khulna. Yet participating kilns achieved comparable reductions in fuel use and emissions, Brooks said. “So, we’re seeing greater hesitation,” she said. “But once they adopt, we see the same benefits.”

Sameer Maithel, the research team’s lead technical expert, said the reasons are still being investigated. Owners operating on narrow margins may hesitate to change familiar methods while facing unpredictable coal prices, brick demand, and regulation. Differences in kiln size, land, and production practices can also make adoption easier in one location than another.

“Informal brick production in South Asia faces a lot of uncertainty: weather, energy prices, market demand, and regulation all shift unpredictably. Many kiln owners also have limited technical and managerial support, and conditions vary from region to region,” Maithel said. “All of this makes scaling up slow and complex, and it takes sustained, dedicated effort.”

The lack of improvement for workers has prompted the team to test more direct measures. During the most recent brickmaking season, researchers returned to Khulna with recommendations developed through pilot work and conversations with workers.

They recommended masks for people crushing coal, goggles and protective footwear for fire workers, and head protection for brick carriers. Other measures included sanitation and cooking facilities, shaded rest areas, clean water, heat-stress awareness, and information about child labor.

“None of the owners I interviewed objected to improving conditions for workers, though some disagreed with specific components. They saw the cost as negligible compared to what they spend running a kiln. As they put it, if workers do better work because of it, it’s worth doing,” said Mohammad Saeed Munim, a research officer in the Health Systems and Population Studies Division of the International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research in Bangladesh.

Researchers had expected more resistance. Owners’ willingness to consider these changes now gives the team an opportunity to test whether targeting workers’ daily needs can deliver improvements that greater productivity alone did not.

“Reducing emissions and air pollution from informal brick kilns: Evidence from Bangladesh” by Nina Brooks, Debashish Biswas, Sameer Maithel, Grant Miller, Aprajit Mahajan, M. Rofi Uddin, Shoeb Ahmed, Moogdho Mahzab, Mahbubur Rahman and Stephen P. Luby, 8 May 2025, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.adr7394

“Productivity gains and work conditions in coercive labor markets: Experimental evidence from the Bangladesh brick sector” by Grant Miller, Debashish Biswas, Aprajit Mahajan, Kimberly Singer Babiarz, Nina Brooks, Jessie Brunner, Sania Ashraf, Jack Shane, Alvise Scarabosio, Sameer Maithel, Shoeb Ahmed, Moogdho Mahzab, Mohammad Rofi Uddin, Mahbubur Rahman and Stephen P. Luby, 16 July 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2528388123

#6517. Mars' Molten Heart is Long Gone, but Some Magma Chambers May Persist

We'll never stop being fascinated by Mars. It's kind of like a failed Earth. It appears as if billions of years ago Mars was warm, wet, and habitable. That ended when its interior cooled and its geodynamo failed.

When its geodynamo failed, its magnetic shield failed. The full force of the Sun bore down on the unfortunate planet, and its warming atmosphere was lost to space.

The loss of atmosphere wasn't the only change. Mars had a powerful volcanic past, and the prominent volcanoes in Tharsis Montes prove that. But the planet is largely believed to have left its volcanic past behind as a consequence of cooling.

But there's growing evidence that the planet isn't totally dormant. Recent evidence from missions like InSight and the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter suggest some ongoing activity. InSight detected more than 1300 Marsquakes, and the Trace Gas Orbiter detected hydrochloric acid.

Hydrochloric acid (HCl) is a highly corrosive acid with multiple natural sources, including atmospheric ones. The ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) collected widespread observations of HCl in Mars' atmosphere at parts-per-billion levels, but initially, it was only detected during perihelion. The HCl detections were attributed to aerosol-atmospheric sources driven by greater warmth from the Sun, a naturally-occurring, seasonal pattern.

But new research in Science Advances shows that not all of the TGO's HCl detections can be traced to perihelion. It's titled "Enigmatic HCl detections as a potential signature of igneous activity on Mars." The lead author is Alexander Trokhimovskiy from the Space Research Institute at the Russian Academy of Sciences.

This Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) image shows Alba Mons near the top, with the three Tharsis Montes volcanoes below it, and the massive Olympus Mons to their northwest. Though not as tall as Olympus Mons, Alba Mons is larger by area. The new HCl detections are curiously close to Alba Mons. Image Credit: NASA/JPL/GSFC

The authors acknowledge that Mars is believed to be volcanically dormant, and that Marsquakes and other evidence of more recent volcanic activity is accumulating. However, there's no clear understanding of Mars' modern activity. For instance, many of the InSight lander's detections were attributed to meteorites.

If we were to witness an actual eruption, and the gases that go with it, a new understanding of Mar's interior would arise. But that hasn't happened, and we have to rely on less obvious evidence for Mars' internal state.

"While sulfur dioxide, so far undetected, could testify to ongoing eruptive activity, evidence of active magma chambers may be better identified by seepage of halogen gases, such as hydrogen chloride (HCl)," the authors write. "Here, we report HCl detections during the cold aphelion season that are isolated in the Alba Mons region." Could these new HCl detections be a window into Mars' interior?

Olympus Mons is known as the largest volcano and the tallest mountain in the Solar System. But Alba Mons is actually the largest volcano by surface area. Like Olympus Mons, it's also in the Tharsis region. (And neither are part of Tharsis Montes, the iconic row of three volcanoes). Alba Mons' volcanic flows reach further than 1300 km from its central summit. One of Alba Mons most significant features is its enormous system of fractures. For multiple reasons, detecting HCl over Alba Mons is intriguing.

"Strongly localized in space and time, aphelion HCl detections, amidst an otherwise absence of HCl at that season on Mars, exhibit marked contrast with prolonged and widespread detections at perihelion," the authors write.

âDetections of HCl at low altitudes, unexplained by observed atmospheric state and models, together with the geological context of the region, hint at an igneous origin of this gas,â Trokhimovskiy et al. write. These most recent HCl directions were in 2025.

This figure show HCl detections by the Trace Gas Orbiter. Blue ones represent perihelion detections, which can be explained by seasonal warming and atmospheric interactions driven by the Sun. Red ones are more enigmatic. They could come from tiny fissures near Alba Mons, almost directly under the detections. Image Credit: Alexander Trokhimovskiy et al. , Enigmatic HCl detections as a potential signature of igneous activity on Mars. Sci. Adv.12, eaeb9422(2026).

The HCl detections alone may not be enough to oveturn the idea that Mars is dormant. As the authors say, they're just a hint. But there's more. "We also identify fresh and narrow (<1 meter) fissures in this area, which we interpret to be potential HCl pathways rooted into magmatic bodies at depth," the researchers explain.

"These structures have not been identified on Mars in earlier works. For instance, systematic geomorphologic mapping of the northern hemisphere did not consider these landforms," the authors explain.

These panels shows some of the important points in the research. (A) shows Alba Mons and the HCl aphelion detections in yellow. (B) is a CASSIS image from the TGO showing a fractured ridge, while (C) and (D) are HiRISE images from NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter showing smaller fissures the researchers identify as potential HCl sources. (E) and (F) are geological models that can explain HCl is seeping from these fissures. Image Credit: Alexander Trokhimovskiy et al. , Enigmatic HCl detections as a potential signature of igneous activity on Mars. Sci. Adv.12, eaeb9422(2026).

The researchers calculated the seepage rate necessary to account for the HCl abundance in the aphelion detections. They compared it to the perihelion detections, and included the expected lifetime for HCl to persist in the Martian atmosphere. Their work rules out atmospheric-aerosol interactions as the source for the HCl detected during aphelion. But it also rules out those same interactions for the source of HCl detected during perihelion. That makes sense, since non-seasonal seepage from magma chambers would be happening no matter the season.

"Thus, perihelion HCl is unlikely to be directly volcanic in origin," they write. There could still be a link between igneous HCl and perihelion HCl. "However, a connection between igneous and seasonal HCl may still exist via a mechanism complementary to heterogeneous production," the authors write.

Planets are complicated, as we Earthlings know. Multiple interrelated factors contribute to the whole, and everything changes over time. This work further emphasizes how that's true, even on so-called dormant Mars. "The overall cycle of hydrogen chloride includes irreversible sinks," the authors write, and sinks have to be included in any modelling or understanding of Mars.

"Introducing a volcanic source of HCl, we can propose that a fraction of the perihelion HCl observed in the Martian atmosphere is ultimately of igneous origin," the researchers explain. "Localized igneous sources may therefore act as continuous primary contributors of chlorine, which is subsequently redistributed between atmospheric and surface reservoirs."

But despite the complicated picture of seasonality and surface sinks, their conclusion is clear: "Our results are best explained by ongoing igneous processes in the Martian interior."

Evan Gough is a science-loving guy with no formal education who loves Earth, forests, hiking, and heavy music. He's guided by Carl Sagan's quote: "Understanding is a kind of ecstasy."
