#6516. The 2026 Best New Bakeries in America

Precision pastries are sweeping the nation. These bakers are leading the charge.

If there’s one thing we’ve noticed over the past several years, it’s how much bakeries have stepped up their game.

Some embody a personal expression of a baker’s identity, while others push the envelope beyond expected flavor combinations; all excel at a time when “little treat” culture is at its peak. — Missy Frederick, editorial director

Learn more about this year’s Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, and how editors selected them, here.

If one new place in Chicago needs no further hype, it is Bad Butter. You’ll know you’re there when you spot the line cascading out of the whitewashed storefront along West Cortland Street, a queue that doesn’t let up until the pastry case is empty. Formerly a head baker at Soho House Chicago, Dan Koester was stuck at home like the rest of us in 2020, handing off excess home-baked sourdough loaves to friends and family and making some available for free pickup. After he was officially laid off that summer, he launched his own online bakery business, earning a massive following along the way.

One residency at the Emily Hotel later, Koester debuted his Bucktown bakery, demonstrating the full range of his skill. Still warm, charred, and dimpled flats of focaccia showered with scallion furikake rest on its shelves. Impossibly crisp and exquisitely laminated twice-baked almond croissants burst with subtle, aromatic almond paste. A spicy harissa monkey bread with a cloudlike texture is cooled by a pool of creamy labneh drizzled with silky olive oil.

The bakery’s menu has breadth and also manages to arc with the season. Customers snake along the floor waiting their turn to claim a towering cruffin, dusted in fine grains of sugar and piped full of ginger plum jam, or a seasonal tart piled with plump, lacquered blueberries. A pastry box filled with these confections is well worth the wait. — Brenna Houck, dining editorial manager

Born as an underground dinner party operated out of Karla Subero Pittol’s Echo Park garage, Chainsaw finally got its own digs in November 2025 in the form of a lively cafe in Melrose Hill, an unquestionably gentrifying neighborhood that has become home to some of Los Angeles’s best independent restaurants. At the cafe, Subero Pittol channels her Venezuelan heritage through a menu of arepas plump with beans, limey guasacaca, and cheese; a Venezuelan hot dog (“perro caliente”) buoyed by an acidic slaw; and her bracingly tart passionfruit-lime icebox pie, which commands a cult following all its own.

Stepping into Chainsaw feels like you could be in Subero Pittol’s own kitchen as she greets regulars and newcomers as if they are old friends. Customers study a handwritten menu that changes daily — it doesn’t help to come in too attached to any one dish (save the ever-present icebox pie) when you may get tempted by another. The cafe’s impact on Los Angeles feels clear in the near-constant crowds that hover outside, reading their newspapers over an espresso or tucking into the latest of Subero Pittol’s ideas, such as a full English breakfast served for a single day. In a city lacking in untamed Venezuelan cooking, Chainsaw offers a home for Subero Pittol to celebrate the cuisine in a way that feels distinctly Los Angeles. — Rebecca Roland, deputy editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest

With both Afghan and Latin American influences, Diljān gives New Yorkers a bakery with a point of view and innumerable reasons to become a regular. Ali Zaman and Mohamed Ghiasi, owners of Astoria’s Little Flower Cafe, teamed up with Bryan Ford, Honduran American baker and cookbook author, to conceptualize the bakery, now perched on a corner near Atlantic Avenue in Brooklyn Heights.

Their combined talent makes for some of the city’s most compelling baked goods. For the Saffron Shah, laminated pastry holds delicate saffron cream in the shape of a crescent, an important Islamic symbol. Halwa tops the sticky bun, while a swirl of samosa pastry wraps halal lamb under a dusting of powdered sugar. Don’t miss the enormous Afghan flatbread crowned by toppings such as halal beef bacon with scallions or sour cherry cream cheese. The team has also branched into pizzas topped with cheese and Afghan cumin, kofta kebabs, or beef pepperoni. Look for specials like the flan with cardamom-poached apricots and conchas stuffed with firni, a rice pudding. — Nadia Chaudhury, deputy editor, Eater New York

San Francisco’s pastry game is stronger and more competitive than ever before, and Parachute Bakery steps to the forefront of a crowded field with a mix of patisserie standards and seasonal standouts. At his Ferry Building bakery, pastry chef Nasir Armar marries his fine dining training, honed at Michelin-starred Sorrel and Saison, with flavors that make everyone sit up and take notice (and snap a food photo or two for their socials).

Vegetables and savory complements are given their own footing on the menu. Stalks of grilled asparagus shine in a baton-shaped croissant shell, with fennel jam, sheep’s milk ricotta, and ramp pesto alongside them; one brief, bordering-on-gimmicky croissant got piped with clam chowder, a reference to the soup in a bread bowl famously served on the city’s wharf. Even potato-laden samosas and bright tomato shakshuka get interpreted into pastry form. Parachute succeeds with its experimental vision, a hype well-earned that leaves fans clamoring for what they’ll come up with next. — Dianne de Guzman, editor, Eater SF

#6515. Where to Find 15 of Philly's Best Cheesesteaks, According to a Longtime Local

The City of Brotherly Love is filled with meat-and-cheese sandwich lovers. Philadelphia is defined by the big three: Hoagies (loaded Italian and chicken cutlet sandwiches), roast pork (with garlicky broccoli rabe and sharp provolone), and cheesesteaks.

The cheesesteak's story began in the 1930s in South Philadelphia but has become a staple at corner shops across the region, given the gourmet remix by award-winning chefs, and even inspired international outposts in Tokyo and London. I've been eating cheesesteaks since my college days, and as a Philly lifer, I've got plenty of opinions. Consider this your beginner’s guide.

Cheesesteaks are as much a part of Philly's late-night food culture as they are a daytime attraction, especially on weekends and game days. Expect long lines, limited seating, and plenty of takeout orders at popular spots, and bring cash—many old-school shops don't accept cards. Like New York's pizza slice culture, cheesesteaks are typically eaten on the go or at a nearby outdoor table. Grab extra napkins and come hungry.

A classic Philly cheesesteak starts with thinly sliced ribeye steak, melted cheese, and a long Italian roll. But no two shops make it exactly the same, and everyone has their preferences.

The meat: Some shops finely chop their ribeye on the grill, while others leave it in thin slices or longer strips. It comes down to whether you prefer a finely chopped, cheesy mixture or more substantial bites of steak.

The cheese and toppings: American, Cheez Whiz, and provolone are the traditional choices. In Philly, you'll hear people order their preferred cheese "wit" or "without," referring to fried onions. For example, "Whiz wit" means Cheez Whiz with onions, while "American without" means American cheese without onions. Other popular toppings include mushrooms, sweet or hot peppers, which you can often request on the side.

The bread: A good cheesesteak roll is typically long and Italian-style, sometimes seeded, with a lightly crunchy crust and soft interior—similar to New Orleans French bread. Some shops scoop out the excess bread to make more room for the steak and cheese, while others leave the roll intact. Either way, the bread needs to hold up to all that juicy filling.

John's Roast Pork has a signature sandwich of the same name.

John’s on East Snyder Avenue has been a neighborhood fixture for nearly a century, thanks to the Bucci family. The James Beard Award-winning shop has also been voted Best Cheesesteak multiple times, known for its hefty portions of finely chopped, crispy ribeye steak served on crusty rolls sourced from nearby Carangi’s or Sarcone’s. Choose from American, provolone, or Cooper Sharp cheese. Expect long lines, but there’s outdoor seating and a semi-enclosed dining area where you can dig in. And if you’ve got the appetite, don’t leave without trying their signature roast pork sandwich.

You’ve probably heard the hype or seen the long lines on 9th Street. Every cheesesteak at Angelo’s is made with house-baked, crusty bread and fresh, peppery ribeye steak, with your choice of Cooper Sharp or the increasingly popular long-hot-pepper-infused Cheez Whiz. Since its Italian Market debut, the Michelin Bib Gourmand-recognized shop has expanded beyond its Italian Street location, including an outpost at a food hall in Wilmington, Delaware and a ghost kitchen deeper in South Philly, with more locations on the horizon.

400 South St. Philadelphia, PA 19147431 N. 62nd St. Philadelphia, PA 19151

Philadelphia is lucky to have two Jim’s Steaks, each with its own personality. The 50-year-old Jim’s South Street is where all walks of life congregate late into the night, plotting their orders (definitely get the famous Whiz wit), scrambling for cash (there’s an ATM inside that sometimes works), and hollering at motorbikes cruising by. Inside, there’s a first-floor diner-style dining room and a second floor adorned with rare mosaics by the late legendary Philadelphia artist Isaiah Zagar, whose Philadelphia’s Magic Gardens is just a few blocks west. Over in West Philly, Jim’s West—the original location, now under different ownership—sits on a residential corner where O.G.s line up to bring cheesesteaks home to family and friends or score a $20 combo special: a beef or chicken cheesesteak, a drink, and a side of banana pudding.

517 South St. Philadelphia, PA 19147337 South St. Philadelphia, PA 19147

Recently featured in season six of Abbott Elementary, the nearly 50-year-old Ishkabibble’s has long attracted celebrities, locals, and tourists alike, often captured on camera by local photographer South Street Sam. The shop helped popularize chicken cheesesteaks and hot pepper-and-onion Spanish fries, eventually expanding to a second, larger location with additional seating just two blocks away. Chicken cheesesteaks are the name of the game here, with nearly a dozen variations, including Pizza (mozzarella and pizza sauce), South Philly (roasted peppers, spinach, and provolone), and Broccoli (melted cheese and steamed broccoli). Wash it all down with their famous Gremlin, a half-grape soda, half-lemonade concoction. Trust us.

What began as a Northeast Philly corner shop in 1949 has changed owners, locations, and names over the decades, but one thing remains: its signature thinly sliced ribeye cheesesteaks, grilled to order with or without onions on fresh Liscio's rolls delivered daily. In 2013, the renamed shop landed at Fishtown's buzzy corner of Girard and Frankford avenues, transforming into a family-friendly, '50s-style diner with an expanded menu. Alongside its classic cheesesteaks, you'll find vegetarian versions with onions and mushrooms, gluten-free roll options, crinkle-cut fries, egg creams, and sundaes.

1338 S. 10th Street Philadelphia, PA 19147

Got cheesesteak FOMO because you're vegan? Or have plant-based loved ones who want in on the Philly experience? Triangle Tavern, a neighborhood bar on East Passyunk Avenue, has you covered. Most of the menu is vegetarian or vegan, including its only cheesesteak, which was crowned Best Vegan Cheesesteak in Philly by the American Vegan Center in 2019. The winning sandwich features locally owned Blackbird Foods' seitan, fried onions, and a Carangi Bakery roll, all smothered in house-made vegan Whiz (a blend of Daiya vegan cheddar, Tofutti cream cheese, miso, nutritional yeast, and seasonings).

For decades, Robert Perry has cultivated a community of artists, musicians, creatives, and beer lovers at this two-story rock-and-roll bar known for its sticker- and graffiti-covered walls. Affectionately called TMoms by locals, Tattooed Mom welcomes meat lovers and plant-based eaters alike with a savory, gooey vegan cheesesteak. Chunks of seitan and plant-based smoked Gouda replace the traditional steak and Whiz, all tucked into a crusty roll from local bakery Merzbacher's of Germantown. Even better, you can snag one for just $7 on Meatless Mondays.

4540 Baltimore Ave. Philadelphia, PA 19143

A West Philly institution, this husband-and-wife-run Ethiopian restaurant and bar is known for its mashup of East African and Philly staples, particularly its berbere-spiced beef cheesesteaks, served since 1996. Thinly sliced beef is coated in an earthy, fiery blend of chili peppers, coriander, ginger, cardamom, nutmeg, and allspice, then tossed with onions and melted American cheese. The result is a juicy, boldly seasoned cheesesteak with a kick.

1600 W. Girard Ave. Philadelphia, PA 19130

Fairmount may not be the first neighborhood that comes to mind for a Philly cheesesteak, but it's home to an 8,500-square-foot indoor mini golf course serving pan-Asian-inspired bar food. Opened in 2021 by three longtime friends, Libertee Grounds has a playful menu to match, including an Indian-inspired Lamb Kheema cheesesteak made with a masala-rubbed lamb and ribeye blend, melted Cooper Sharp, caramelized onions, and cilantro-lime aioli on a seeded long roll. It comes with fries, but for an extra kick, add pickled Fresno peppers or miso Cooper Sharp cheese Whiz.

3101 Tasker St. Philadelphia, PA 191453401 Walnut St. Franklin's Table Food Hall, Philadelphia, PA 191042563 Trenton Ave. Philadelphia, PA 19125

What began as a food cart in 2022 has grown into multiple Philadelphia locations for Korea Taqueria, where chef-owners Alexander Sherack and Rene Lopez blend traditional Korean flavors with Mexican street food staples. Their Korean-Mexican mashups include a signature slow-burn spicy bulgogi cheesesteak featuring thinly sliced halal ribeye marinated in bulgogi sauce, melted Cooper Sharp, gochujang mayo, and scallions on a seeded Liscio's hoagie roll. Add cucumber kimchi for an extra tangy crunch.

Dalessandro's sits in Roxborough, in the city's northwest outskirts.

Husband-and-wife team Steve and Margie Kotridis have kept this Northwest Philly cheesesteak shop humming with hungry customers since taking over in 2008. Now one of three Michelin Bib Gourmand-recognized cheesesteak shops in Philadelphia, alongside Del Rossi's and Angelo's, Dalessandro's is known for its juicy, gooey, squishy sandwiches. Finely minced ribeye, melted cheese, and generously diced onions meld together inside Amoroso's hearth-baked rolls (another local favorite bakery), which soak up all that goodness. Better yet, toppings are free. Grab your cheesesteak to go and, weather permitting, enjoy it beneath the trees at the park across the street.

3653 Germantown Ave.Philadelphia, PA 19140

This North Philly cheesesteak shop is a celebrity in its own right, having appeared in Creed and Creed II and attracted famous fans like Philly's own Colman Domingo. Since 1994, crowds have lined up beneath its glowing red neon sign near the Broad and Erie transit hub for finely chopped "100% sirloin steak," served in half, whole (12-inch), or Giant (two-foot) portions. Order yours Whiz wit (ketchup is a popular addition here), grab some cheese fries, and join the regulars eating off the hoods of their cars. Those in the know head next door to Eagle Bar for a beer before calling it a night.

3020 S. Broad St. Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19145

Heading down to the stadiums for a game? Consider Skinny Joey's your pre- or post-game cheesesteak fix. Former inmate turned podcaster turned restaurateur Joey Merlino has entered Philly's competitive cheesesteak scene, offering six beef and chicken variations that draw long lines of customers and parked cars along Broad Street on weekends. And he's not stopping there: Merlino has expanded to the Jersey Shore with a Wildwood outpost.

Competition and tradition run deep in Philly's cheesesteak scene, a challenge Nish Patel embraced when he took over Del Rossi's in 2020. He helped usher in a new wave of cheesesteak making by focusing on better ingredients and technique rather than reinventing the classic sandwich. First came a house-baked roll with a crunchy crust and pillowy-soft interior. Next, pasture-raised, hormone-free, hand-cut ribeye steak, followed by melted Cooper Sharp American cheese and onions. The upgrades paid off: Del Rossi's earned Michelin Bib Gourmand recognition in 2026.

One of Philly's newest cheesesteak sensations, Sal Burgese's Backyard Cravings began as pandemic-era home cooking for friends, family, and a few lucky guests at his South Philly rowhome. What started in his backyard grew into tailgating parties and, eventually, his first brick-and-mortar shop in October 2026. Like Del Rossi's, the focus here is on quality ingredients and cooking from scratch. The $20+ cheesesteak has a generous portion of finely chopped, salt-and-pepper-seasoned beef, onions, and creamy Cooper Sharp cheese on a long, crisp, sesame-seeded roll with a soft, scooped-out center. Burgese's cheesesteaks have drawn sold-out crowds wherever he's served them, so for now, the Eagles “Kelly Green” and cream-colored corner spot sells them only on weekends.

#6514. A Common Plastic Could Solve a Major Problem With Living on the Moon

The same plastic that keeps marathon runners warm could help future moon bases withstand extreme temperatures and years of rough treatment.

Engineers at the University of Pennsylvania have developed an insulating material by stacking hundreds of thin sheets of Mylar. In laboratory tests, the stacks combined effective insulation in a vacuum with flexibility and resistance to repeated compression, qualities that could make them useful for long-term lunar construction.

Their study, published in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces, calls the material hybrid layered insulating film stacks (HyLIFS). The approach addresses a persistent engineering problem: materials that resist heat flow often struggle to withstand physical damage.

“These stacks of Mylar can bend, withstand substantial compression, and maintain their insulating performance,” says senior author Igor Bargatin, an associate professor in Mechanical Engineering and Applied Mechanics (MEAM), “potentially allowing them to be packed, transported, and survive rough treatment over many years of use.”

On the moon, insulation must protect against temperatures ranging from hundreds of degrees below zero to the boiling point of water. But surviving those extremes is only part of the job. Materials must also endure transportation, installation, maintenance, and accidental impacts.

Some leading insulators are poorly suited to that treatment. Aerogels contain mostly empty space, making them lightweight and effective at slowing heat transfer in applications from industrial pipelines to NASA’s Mars rovers. Their porous structure, however, can also leave them susceptible to mechanical damage.

Multilayer insulation, widely used in space, takes another approach: reflective sheets separated by insulating spacers reduce heat transfer by radiation. These assemblies work well thermally, but they are not built to carry substantial loads and can tear during handling.

Making an insulator stronger can compromise its thermal performance. “For lunar infrastructure, we would ideally like both,” says Bargatin. “The ideal material is both resistant to damage and to the loss of heat.”

Mylar offered the researchers an accessible starting material. Formally known as biaxially oriented polyethylene terephthalate, or BoPET, the plastic already appears in food packaging and aerospace equipment. Combined with aluminum, it reflects infrared radiation, which is how shiny emergency blankets help marathon runners retain body heat.

The team tested several film thicknesses and coated some sheets with an extremely thin layer of aluminum oxide, also called alumina, to increase stiffness. Researchers then assembled the films individually into stacks.

“At the moment, the process is very time-consuming,” says first author Danielle R. Levin, a recent Penn chemistry doctoral graduate who also earned a master’s in MEAM. “We use two pairs of tweezers and small weights to handle and stack the delicate films. Even breathing near the stack can send the layers flying.”

Once assembled, however, the films were far tougher than their delicate handling suggested. Under vacuum conditions and compression representative of a lunar habitat with indoor air at atmospheric pressure, the best stacks matched the thermal conductivity of other high-performance vacuum insulation technologies while remaining flexible.

In separate mechanical tests, the coated stacks retained their insulating performance at the highest compressive stresses the laboratory equipment could produce. Researchers repeatedly squeezed samples to approximately 20 megapascals (about 2,900 pounds per square inch), roughly equivalent to concentrating 200 pounds onto an area the size of a fingertip.

“We were concerned about the material failing under such high compressive stress,” recalls Levin. “But the stacks didn’t survive just one high-stress cycle—they survived 10 in a row.”

That durability could make the material easier to transport and reuse, as well as more forgiving once installed. “You could use these stacks to insulate a lunar habitation, but astronauts will inevitably have little accidents where they bump into them,” says Bargatin. “When we’re talking about long-term habitation on the moon, it’s really important to have tough materials that can last long enough.”

“The combination of thermal and mechanical robustness is critical for long-term use on the moon,” says Levin. “This material could open a pathway to inexpensive, durable, and reusable lunar insulation.”

The study also identified an overlooked feature of commercial Mylar that could help explain its performance: microscopic particles added to keep the plastic from sticking to itself. These “antiblocking” particles protrude slightly from the surface, separating neighboring sheets and making thin films easier to manufacture and handle.

Their industrial purpose was already understood, but their influence on heat flow through stacked films had received little attention, according to the researchers. Because conventional multilayer insulation primarily targets radiation, there had been less reason to investigate how these particles affect heat conducted directly between sheets.

The researchers built models of heat transfer across the interfaces between layers and compared their predictions with experimental measurements. The results suggest that, in a vacuum, heat passes between sheets mainly at the tiny contact points where antiblocking particles touch neighboring films.

Those contacts could become a design tool. Instead of working around whatever particles commercial Mylar happens to contain, future insulation could use carefully selected particle sizes, numbers, and distributions to regulate heat transfer.

The particles also helped explain a result that contradicted the team’s initial expectations. Thinner sheets should allow more layers to fit into a given space, creating more interfaces that impede heat transfer. The researchers therefore expected their thinnest films to provide the strongest insulation.

Instead, the thinnest films they successfully characterized performed similarly to medium-thickness films when both received an alumina coating. The team suspects that particles in the thinner films create additional contact between neighboring layers, opening more pathways for heat to flow.

“As you compress the layers, the contact landscape changes,” says Levin. “It’s not just a matter of minimizing the film thickness or the number of particles; we must also account for how the contacts change and the films deform as pressure increases.”

Improving the material will therefore require balancing film thickness, stiffness, and particle distribution. Simply making each sheet thinner may provide little benefit if the resulting contacts allow more heat through.

The current samples cover only about one square centimeter (0.16 square inches), and manually cutting and stacking them takes hours. Producing practical insulation at the scale of a meter (about 3.3 feet) will require a much faster assembly method.

The researchers see potential in manufacturing techniques such as continuously coating large rolls of Mylar. Eventually, film thickness, coatings, and particle distribution might be adjusted before the material is wound into large stacks.

Larger versions still need testing, including whether they can withstand repeated bending, bumps, and scuffs. If the laboratory results carry over to practical production, HyLIFS could provide flexible insulation for lunar habitats, spacesuits, rovers, electronics, and other equipment that must operate for years in space.

For Levin, the findings show how much remains to be discovered in familiar materials. “The simplest configuration ended up being the best one,” she says.

Reference: “Robust Layered Thermal Insulator Film Stacks for Vacuum Applications” by D. R. Levin, M. F. Campbell, G. Aldan, O. H. Omodior and I. Bargatin, 1 September 2026, ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces. DOI: 10.1021/acsami.6c09126

This work was supported by the National Science Foundation Division of Chemical, Bioengineering, Environmental and Transport Systems (grant number 1845933) and Penn Engineering.

#6513. Using Vibrations and AI, Future Robotic Missions Could Handle Buried Rocks Autonomously

Knowing a planet's surface and subsurface structure is vital when planning robotic and crewed missions to explore it. Before landers, rovers, or crew modules reach the surface, astronauts and mission controllers need to know what they will be landing on. For rovers with a limited energy budget, it's also crucial that they can determine how far rough, rocky terrain extends beneath the surface. That way, they won't waste time and energy trying to clear obstacles they can't possibly move.

In short, scientists and astronauts need to know what's on a planet's surface (and beneath it) before they attempt to land there and conduct science operations. Thanks to a team from Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University (Virginia Tech), scientists could soon have a new set of tools that will allow robotic missions to make these determinations autonomously. These AI-powered tools measure vibrations in surface terrain to determine what lies beneath and how deep structures extend.

The study was led by Yiyan Ruan, a Ph.D. candidate at Virginia Tech, and Erik Komendera, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering (and Ruan's advisor) who once worked as a researcher at NASA's Langley Research Center. The paper detailing their findings was published in IEEE Sensors Journal. The tools they have developed could have profound applications for both space exploration and life on Earth.

View generated from the digital terrain model and the nadir and color channels of the High Resolution Stereo Camera on ESA's Mars Express. Credit: ESA/DLR/FU Berlin

As they indicate in their paper, estimating the burial depth of partially embedded rocks is a key capability for energy-limited robotic excavation. When obstacles like rock formations are in the way, mission teams need to know how deep the rock extends so they can decide whether to remove the obstacle or avoid it. Ruan and Komendera's solution leverages AI to interpret vibrational data, allowing robots to make those decisions autonomously. As Komendera said in a Virginia Tech press release:

For as long as humans have built things on Earth, we have had to deal with large and heavy obstacles that cannot simply be ignored or scooped out of the way without careful planning. It's easy enough for us to just look at rocks and make some quick, testable judgments. Is this rock resting or partially buried? Can I move this alone or do I need help and tools? But what if robots need to do this? How can robots make those judgments? Now we have an answer.

To test their approach, their team buried 18 concrete blocks of different shapes and sizes in sand at different depths. They then struck the exposed portions of the blocks with an instrumented hammer and remotely measured the vibrations using a device known as a Laser Doppler Vibrometer (LDV). The results were then input into a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), a type of neural network that learns to identify complex, non-linear patterns from data.

Their MLP mapped 11 measurable features to identify the relationship between impulse excitation, exposed rock geometry, and burial depth. Given the range of factors to consider, the task was rather complex. But by teaching their AI to account for them, Ruan and Komendera created models that could reliably determine the blocks' depth.

When the future rovers set down on Mars, they could determine rock depth and obstacle clearance autonomously. Credit: NASA/JPL

"Estimating how deep a rock is buried using vibrations can be tricky," said Ruan. "The feedback is affected by the rock's geometry and the way the soil holds it. By carefully selecting features from vibration measurements and exposed geometry, we were able to produce reliable data using a compact neural network with just two hidden layers."

These models could help robotic missions excavate subsurface rocks, caches of water ice, and remove obstacles along their travel routes. In the meantime, the team plans to keep building datasets and testing their approach for applications on Earth, such as analyzing construction sites and natural disasters to locate where potentially hazardous materials are buried. They could also be used to study unstable rock formations and underground caverns, assisting with resource and construction planning, and advancing exploration of Earth's subsurface.

Further Reading: Virginia Tech, IEEE Sensors Journal

About half of people with long COVID see meaningful improvement in their symptoms after three years, a new study found.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Symptoms of long COVID ease in half of patients within three years of the infection that kicked off their illness.

That's the primary conclusion of a new study that tracked over 1,000 patients with long COVID, a chronic condition that can emerge after an infection with the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Among the patients, the chance of improvement varied sharply depending on how the condition affected their bodily systems.

In the study, published Tuesday (Nov. 3) in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, roughly 60% of patients whose predominant symptoms were changes to their ability to taste or smell had significantly improved three years after their first positive test. But less than 20% of those with a multisystem presentation had improved in that time frame.

This latter group had symptoms that affected their cardiac, nervous and gastrointestinal systems, among others. An expert told Live Science that the condition resembled myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), which often arises after an infection and similarly impacts a wide range of bodily systems.

The new study's findings could help direct the structure of future clinical trials of treatments for long COVID, experts said.

The patients in the study were enrolled in the long-term RECOVER Adult Study. Funded by the National Institutes of Health, the project has recruited thousands of adults across the United States who previously tested positive for COVID-19.

Researchers scored patients based on how they were affected by a range of symptoms, including fatigue, brain fog, shortness of breath and heart palpitations. The study included patients who scored more than 10 points on a 30-point scale — called the 2024 LC Research Index (LCRI) — which attempted to capture these different symptom combinations.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Nearly 1,020 patients met this requirement and were tracked over time; they had in-person appointments and filled out symptom surveys every three months. Scientists marked patients as "improved" once they recorded LCRI scores of 10 or less at two consecutive visits. They found that 36% of the participants had improved two years after their inciting COVID-19 infection, and that figure rose to 50% after three years.

LCRIs hit zero for 26% of the participants after three years, meaning all of their symptoms were gone at the time of the survey.

Reeder said he was careful to avoid describing the participants as "recovered." This decision was influenced by input from the long COVID community to the RECOVER Adult Study, he said. They highlighted that their symptoms can wax and wane, whereas "recovery" implies a permanent resolution. The new study didn't capture, for example, whether individual patients who recorded meaningful improvement later relapsed.

The researchers analyzed which SARS-CoV-2 strain was associated with the most long COVID cases, controlling for patient vaccination status.

Some patients' journeys were far less straightforward than the top-line data might suggest. Although men and women improved at similar rates, adults under 46 were more likely to improve than older participants were. Patients affected by the Omicron variants of SARS-CoV-2, which emerged in 2021 and quickly became the dominant strain of the virus, were more likely to improve than those infected with earlier strains.

Some of the starkest differences in improvement rates were seen between patients with different symptoms.

In a previous study, RECOVER researchers had grouped participants into five subtypes, using an algorithm to connect patients with similar predominant symptoms:

In the new study, patients in the last three groups were less likely to get better within three years. The final group's rate was particularly low, at just 19%.

Dr. Carmen Scheibenbogen, an immunologist at Charité University Medicine Berlin, said these patients' progress resembles that of people with ME/CFS.

"It looks as if at least a major subgroup is suffering from ME-CFS," Scheibenbogen said, noting that COVID-19 may have triggered their condition. "This is a disease which is triggered by different infections, but in the end, the disease [itself] is very similar," she said.

Like long COVID, ME/CFS can affect a wide array of bodily systems, and it remains poorly understood despite recent advances in research.

The team's new findings highlight the need for clinical trials to test possible treatments for long COVID. Both Scheibenbogen and study co-author Harrison Reeder, a biostatistician at Massachusetts General Hospital, said these subtypes would be important to consider in the design of these potential trials.

The multisystem subgroup, Reeder said, "might be a group where an effective intervention can make a bigger difference than people who stand to potentially have a higher chance of improvement regardless."

Future work would need to further scientists' understanding of people affected by long COVID at the level of their genes and proteins, both scientists said.

"There's a lot of work to do in RECOVER and in the world of long COVID research," Harrison said. "There's a lot of opportunity."

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#6511. Tiny Solar Whirlpools May Hold the Secret to the Sun’s Blistering Corona

For the second time in a few weeks, weâre writing about research into the temperature gap between the Sunâs surface and its corona. More and more data from various missions continue to feed this wave of discovery. A new paper by Katariina Nykyri of Embry-Riddle, recently published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, adds to this growing body of work. She argues that millions of tiny whirlpools scattered across the Sunâs surface could be the energetic engine driving that temperature difference.

Earlier this year, the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST), located atop HaleakalÄ on Maui, took extremely high resolution images of the Sunâs surface. For the first time, scientists could make out whirlpools of plasma, a few dozen kilometers across, dotted around the Sunâs surface. When this research was published in August, Dr. Nykyri had a bit of a âEureka!â moment, according to a press release from the University.

Her research had focused on Kelvin-Helmholtz waves. On Earth, these are most commonly seen in broken ocean swells or ripple-pattern clouds. However, they are also present elsewhere in the solar system, driving gas patterns on Jupiter. On the Sun, they occur when fast-moving plasma passes slower, magnetized plasma. They contain an absurd amount of mechanical energy. The vortices created by these waves are the very structures DKIST resolved on our starâs surface. As these vortices churn across the solar surface, their vast kinetic energy transfers into the Sun's magnetic fields, converting mechanical motion into magnetic stress.

Fraser talks about the features of the Sun that we are only now getting a glimpse of thanks to new technologies.

Dr. Nykyri set out to answer how much energy these vortices carry and whether it equals the total energy needed to heat the corona. After accounting for the velocity shear, density difference, and vertical heights of the tornadoes, she reached a conclusion. On average, each vortex contains around two septillion ergsâa unit of energy commonly used in solar physics. Across the Sunâs 1.4-million-kilometer surface, millions of these vortices spin up and dissipate every few minutes.

When these vortices dissipate, their energy must go somewhere. According to Dr. Nykyri, it appears to enter the corona through magnetic reconnection. Solar physicists have long thought this process plays a key role in coronal heating. As each KH vortex spins, it squeezes nearby magnetic field lines together. This forms ultra-thin current lines ranging from a few centimeters to meters across.

Once theyâre squeezed past a certain point, they start to violently snap and rearrange. That is the process of magnetic reconnection, and it converts the stored magnetic energy into heat and high-speed plasma jets that are fundamental components of the solar corona. In other words, the KH vortices are the driving force behind the process of reconnection of the Sunâs magnetic field lines.

Frase talks about how hot the Sun actually is.

When the energy they store is released, it has to have somewhere to go, though. And these vortices donât always cause reconnections only in the corona - they also do so on the surface. So why does the corona seem so much hotter? Particle density.

When a magnetic line snaps on the surface, the energy is immediately distributed between trillions of neutral atoms. Each atomâs temperature is commensurately raised, but only by a tiny amount. In the corona, though, atoms are much less plentiful, but the same amount of energy is released. So each magnetic snap increases the temperature of an individual atom by much more in the corona than down on the surface.

According to the paper, only five to eight percent of the mechanical energy stored in the vortices needs to make the journey upward to the corona to replenish the heat that is otherwise radiated away. Even in darker âcoronal holesâ, a max of 21% of the energy from the vortices would be capable of maintaining the temperature of the corona.

This work is a major step toward understanding the heating process, but more research is needed. Scientists still must track wave transmission and polarization through the chromosphere. This will confirm whether as much energy reaches the Sunâs chromosphere as Dr. Nykyri suggests is necessary to maintain coronal temperatures. If her theory holds, some of the high temperatures on our star will be proven to stem from relatively small plasma tornadoes floating across its surface.

#6510. A Planet 11 Times Bigger Than Jupiter Is Challenging What We Thought About Planet Formation

New observations of the giant exoplanet Beta Pictoris b are challenging assumptions about how and where massive planets form.

New observations of Beta Pictoris b, a massive planet orbiting a young star, are challenging a method astronomers hoped could reveal where giant planets form. More precise measurements of the planet’s atmosphere have overturned an earlier result, raising doubts about whether a particular chemical signature can reliably trace a planet’s birthplace.

Located in a 23-million-year-old planetary system, Beta Pictoris b is approximately 11 times Jupiter’s mass. It orbits about 10 astronomical units (approximately 930 million miles) from its star, completing one revolution every 23 years. Earlier atmospheric measurements suggested the planet might have formed much farther away before migrating inward, but the latest evidence points to a different possibility.

Astronomers have proposed using the relative abundance of two forms of carbon monoxide (CO) to determine where giant planets formed within their original disks of gas and dust. These molecules contain different carbon isotopes, 12C and 13C, which have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Their slightly different masses can influence how they behave during chemical processes.

The method relies on the carbon monoxide snowline, the distance from a young star beyond which temperatures become cold enough for CO gas to freeze onto dust grains. Planets forming beyond this boundary may accumulate carbon monoxide ice, potentially leaving a different isotopic signature than planets that develop in warmer regions where CO remains gaseous.

Earlier observations of Beta Pictoris b using the original GRAVITY instrument produced a relatively low ratio of 12CO to 13CO. That result appeared consistent with formation beyond the snowline, followed by inward migration to the planet’s present orbit. However, the researchers cautioned that instrumental limitations could have affected the measurement.

A team led by Antonia von Stauffenberg, a doctoral student at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy (MPIA) in Heidelberg, Germany, has now revisited the planet using GRAVITY+. The upgraded instrument operates at the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI), managed by the European Southern Observatory (ESO) in Chile.

The new observations reveal a substantially higher 12CO/13CO ratio than previously reported. While 12CO produces a readily detectable signal, its less abundant counterpart, 13CO, is considerably harder to measure accurately. GRAVITY+ provides improved adaptive optics and greater observational precision, allowing researchers to better distinguish the two molecules.

“The GRAVITY+ interferometric instrument is highly stable […], making it uniquely capable of high-fidelity characterization of directly imaged exoplanets,” says co-author and MPIA scientist Jonas Sauter.

The revised ratio agrees with independent measurements reported by González Picos et al. (2026) using a different instrument. This agreement supports the new result and indicates that systematic uncertainties affected the earlier GRAVITY measurements.

The researchers also detected tentative variations in the planet’s observed brightness. These fluctuations appear to follow a period of approximately 8.7 hours, close to the planet’s rotation period.

If confirmed, the variations could arise from atmospheric clouds or chemical differences moving in and out of view as the planet rotates. However, the evidence remains statistically weak, and more sensitive observations will be necessary to establish whether the changes are real.

“The ability to accurately constrain both isotopologues and potential rotational variability using ground-based observations of a bona fide planet such as Beta Pictoris b demonstrates the exceptional data quality achieved with the updated GRAVITY+ instrument,” says von Stauffenberg.

Under the proposed formation model, the revised carbon monoxide ratio would favor an origin inside the snowline, consistent with Beta Pictoris b’s current orbital distance. Yet the measurement also closely resembles ratios observed throughout the Solar System and the interstellar medium, the gas and dust occupying the space between stars.

Similar values have been measured in most of the roughly dozen young giant planets studied using this technique. This widespread consistency suggests that differences in carbon isotope abundances across planet-forming environments may be too small to distinguish reliably, limiting the method’s usefulness for reconstructing individual planetary histories.

“It is still difficult to utilize 13CO as a formation tracer of giant planets, due to the uncertainties that still persist in the models and measurements,” explains von Stauffenberg.

Current models may be missing important details of carbon monoxide ice chemistry in planet-forming disks. Until those processes are better understood, atmospheric carbon isotope ratios alone cannot establish whether a giant planet formed in a warm, gas-rich region or farther out among frozen materials. More precise observations and additional chemical indicators will be needed to reconstruct these planets’ origins, with GRAVITY+ offering a powerful tool for investigating both their formation and atmospheric behavior.

Reference: “13CO and potential variability in β Pictoris b with GRAVITY+” by A. von Stauffenberg, J. Sauter, P. Mollière, M. Ravet, D. Trevascus, W. Brandner, A. Berdeu, M. Bonnefoy, G. Bourdarot, J.-B. Le Bouquin, G. Chauvin, F. Eisenhauer, M. Houllé, L. Kreidberg, E. Matthews, F. Millour, J. Scigliuto, J. Wang, J. W. Xuan and Y. Zhang, 9 July 2026, Astronomy & Astrophysics. DOI: 10.1051/0004-6361/202660275

#6509. I Visited China as an American Without a Visa—Here’s How You Can Do It Too

Last month, I visited China as an American—without going through a multi-week visa application process. This is thanks to a recent policy introduced in 2024 that allows certain travelers to visit China for a maximum of 10 days while transiting between one country and another. Though the rule can feel intimidating in theory, it’s relatively straightforward in practice as long as you prepare accordingly.

Officially called the “240-Hour Visa-Free Transit Policy," the program is part of China’s goal to attract more inbound international travelers, according to Mei Zhang, the founder of WildChina and a Condé Nast Traveler travel specialist. “The idea is to make visiting China an easier decision,” Zhang says. “Most people are daunted by the idea of queuing for a visa at the Chinese consulate. Removing that step makes it easier for people to come.”

And even though the policy is designed for transiting between countries, 10 days is still enough time for a meaningful visit. “Beyond the quick business visits or short stopovers people may associate with China, ten days gives travelers time to explore several destinations, experience the culture, and develop a deeper appreciation for the country,” says Catherine Heald, CNT specialist and founder of Remote Lands, which specializes in travel to Asia.

However, because the program is relatively new, not all airline or airport staff are familiar with it—which almost resulted in me being denied boarding. To help you avoid ending up in a similar situation, here’s what travelers should know before booking your flight to China, so you too can see the Forbidden City in Beijing, the futuristic skyline glowing along the Bund in Shanghai, the terracotta warriors in Xi'an, and the mountainous megacity of Chongqing.

Officially called the “240-Hour Visa-Free Transit Policy,” this new rule was first introduced by China’s National Immigration Administration in December 2024. It permits a traveler to visit China without obtaining a visa ahead of time as long as the total length of their stay in the country does not exceed 240 hours. “It’s a great policy that has driven the growth of international travelers to China,” says Zhang, “but you do need to read the fine print before using it.”

The fine print: First of all, the operative word is transit. You have to enter China from one country, then leave it for another, different country. For example, flying from the US to China, then from China to Japan is allowed. However, going from the US to China, then back to the US, is not. Hong Kong, Macao, and Taiwan count as separate destinations for this policy, so a trip that goes from Hong Kong to mainland China to Taiwan would qualify for a visa-free transit in China that does not last longer than 10 days.

Second: Only holders of passports from 57 countries, including the United States, can take advantage of this policy. See the full list here. And third: You have to enter and exit via designated ports. The full list is here, and it conveniently includes the cities you might visit on a first-time visit to China, like Beijing, Shanghai, and Chengdu. If you want to travel beyond the areas permitted by the transit policy, you’ll have to apply for a Chinese visa.

“Remember that you can enter and leave through the same eligible Chinese city or choose different eligible cities,” says Heald of Remote Lands. So you could come to China through Shanghai, spend three days there, then take the high-speed train to Beijing, stay for another three days, then depart for a third destination like nearby South Korea to make the most out of your trip.

The Forbidden City was the Chinese imperial palace from the Ming dynasty to the end of the Qing dynasty (1420-1912).

To try the transit policy for myself, I kept my first-ever trip to China simple. I arrived in Shanghai on September 30 and departed on October 5, entering and exiting through the same qualifying port, Shanghai Pudong International Airport (PVG). I stayed in the country for a total of five nights, well under the 240-hour limit. (For what it’s worth, I stayed at the good-looking PuLi Shanghai, the very cool Upper House Shanghai, and the historically rich Capella Shanghai, Jian Ye Li, to explore different parts of the city.)

I’m an American citizen, so my US passport made me eligible for the transit policy. As for my routing, I departed from Paris, where I live, on a direct flight to Shanghai; from there I flew onward to Manila. The logic is that this made my visit to China count as a long layover since my final destination was actually the Philippines.

As you prepare your itinerary, check—and double check—that your passport, routing, entry and departure ports in China, and destinations within China all qualify under the 240-hour visa-free transit policy before you make your bookings. The list of qualifying passports and entry-exit ports in China can be found here.

Once you have all your confirmation info, it’s a good idea to get organized and put together a folder with all your bookings as proof of your plans to stay no more than 10 days in China. “Carry printed copies of your confirmed onward tickets, hotel reservations, and itinerary,” Heald says. She also recommends calling your airline before departure and confirming your transit eligibility with them. You might even print the official page describing the policy (again, here!) so you can present it to anyone you encounter, like a check-in agent, who might be unfamiliar with the relatively new 10-day rule.

Consider this your heads up, says Zhang: “It’s a great policy but sometimes the implementation on the ground can be uneven.” For an added layer of security, consider booking your travel to China with local tour operators or travel specialists like WildChina or Remote Lands. They can design a trip that will definitely qualify for the transit policy, and can help you out in case you run into issues while you’re traveling.

Well, I did none of the above. I arrived at Paris-Charles de Gaulle for my flight to Shanghai without any printed confirmations of my onward ticket to Manila, my three hotel stays, or the official policy from the Chinese National Immigration Administration’s official website.

The Air France check-in agent asked me to present my Chinese visa, which, of course, I did not have. I tried to explain in French that I could go to China through this new policy, but the agent insisted, “Non, c’est pas possible.” Foolishly, I plugged “10-day visa-free transit China” into Google on my phone and presented the results to him. He sighed, switched to English, and said, “That is not official. That is AI Overview.”

I asked if there was anyone at Air France I could talk to, and the agent shook his head. Maybe he softened when he saw the panic creep across my face because he then phoned a colleague, an Air France agent who was Chinese. The other agent explained that I was correct, there is indeed a new 10-day transit policy, and all I had to do was present my onward ticket to the Philippines, which I did have saved as a screenshot on my phone.

May my failure to properly prepare be your reminder to print out everything, including your flight and accommodation info, as well as the official visa-free transit policy. If there was ever a time to be a type-A traveler, it’s this.

Once in China, the process becomes much smoother. All international travelers are required to fill out a digital arrival form, whether they have a visa or not. The form asks if you have a visa for China and, when you select no, offers a drop-down menu where you can declare that you are visiting through the 240-hour visa-free transit policy. Once that’s done, the form gives you a QR code that confirms you’ve completed the form; screenshot this code, just in case. Then go through the immigration line, approach the immigration officer, and present whatever is asked of you, like that QR code or your onward ticket, when prompted. That’s it!

For my journey, I got to Pudong Airport in Shanghai, logged onto the airport Wi-Fi, completed the form, and went into the immigration line. They didn’t ask for the QR code but they did ask for my ticket to Manila. Once everything looked good to them, they stamped my passport with a transit visa—a little sticker that declared my date of entry into China and when they expected me to leave. I was cleared to go, and I stepped into the duty-free shopping area, located right before baggage claim, feeling giddy and satisfied that it all worked out.

Zhang says working with a travel company could help relieve some of the stress on the arrival side too: “WildChina normally would book a VIP airport pickup if any of our travelers are using the 10-day transit visa. This way, an airport concierge would meet the guests at the gate and walk them through the visa step-by-step. This eases the stress of facing an unfamiliar bureaucratic process.”

One of the things that greatly intimidated me about visiting China was how different the tech is. There’s no Uber or Google Maps, which has been very helpful for me on my solo travels in new-to-me countries. The very fine teams at PuLi Shanghai and Upper House Shanghai helped me get set up with the right apps, and I was zipping around the city in no time. (For a map app, Apple Maps worked like a charm, to my surprise.) Here are tips for what Chinese apps to download before traveling.

First, set up Alipay, which is a do-it-all app and a total lifeline in China. You can link an international bank card and use it for all payments everywhere you go; call a DiDi car (China’s equivalent of Uber or Lyft), use its translation tool, and more. “Alipay is part of everyday life here,” Zhang says. “At most restaurants, you can scan the QR code on your table with Alipay, choose your dishes—already translated on the interface—and pay through the app.” Be sure to set it up and link your bank account or card before you arrive in China; some verification steps require authorization via your phone number, which you may not have access to while in the country.

Second, everyone in China is on WeChat, so you’d do well to download that too; it’s how I communicated with the guest experiences team at Capella Shanghai, Jian Ye Li, who took me on cultural tours in the hotel’s neighborhood. Think of it as Chinese WhatsApp.

And to stay connected online, Heald suggests checking if your existing carrier offers roaming in mainland China (helpful for any verification texts you may need to receive). Otherwise, get a compatible travel eSIM that explicitly covers it. A home carrier or a travel eSIM will allow you to connect to sites like Google Workplace and apps like Instagram that you would not be able to normally access through the internet while in China. For my phone, Airalo, a travel eSIM, and Free, my French home carrier, worked perfectly.

“If you'll be using a laptop or tablet on Wi-Fi and need access to services such as Google, WhatsApp, or Instagram, install a VPN and arrange any paid subscription before you leave,” Zhang says. “Downloading and setting it up can be much trickier once you're in China.” I, for one, used Astrill VPN to stay connected on my laptop to sites like Gmail and YouTube.

And finally, both Zhang and Heald recommend keeping an open mind. “China can feel very different from what you know,” Heald says. “Give yourself the chance to observe, ask questions and learn, rather than expecting everything to feel familiar.” Zhang adds, “That's part of getting to know a place. Don’t be afraid to ask for help or start a conversation, even if you only have a few words in common. You'll often find people are curious about you too, and pleased that you've come to see where they live.”

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6508. Why Aging Stars Suffer A Sudden Luminosity Dip

From a naked eye perspective, stars are stable and predictable. Not much goes on but shining. The Sun itself is fairly plane and nondescript and will shine relatively steadily for billions of years. It's considered a low-mass star compared to the most massive stars, which are rarer and contain many times its mass.

Powerful telescopes bring millions of stars of different types and ages into view. Astrophysicists and astronomers watch the Sun and its low-mass brethren, and note changes in their shining, just as they do all types of stars. Their observations reveal the changes stars experience during their long lifetimes.

As low-mass stars like the Sun exhaust their hydrogen supplies and evolve, they become Red Giant Branch (RGB) stars. This is not only theoretical, it's an observational conclusion. RGB stars are easy to observe and study for two reasons: they're bright, and they're numerous. Arcturus, Aldebaran, and Pollus are all bright, naked-eye stars and are all RGB stars. (Well-known Betelgeuse is a Red Supergiant, not quite the same.)

As RGB stars age and cool, they swell in size and become more luminous. It's a pretty steady change. But for some reason, there's a brief and abrupt dip in their brightness known as the RGB luminosity bump. The bump is called that because of how it appears in the colourâmagnitude diagrams of stellar clusters.

Astrophysicists know why the bump ends. But what initiates the bump is still unexplained. Astrophysicists don't like this gap in their knowledge and they've been trying to fill it in.

New research in The Astrophysical Journal Letters has an explanation for the bump. It's titled "The Role of Specific Entropy in the Onset of the Luminosity Bump," and the sole author is Saskia Hekker. Hekker is a Professor of Theoretical Astrophysics and the Group Leader of the Theory and Observations of Stars Group at the Heidelberg Institute for Theoretical Studies.

"During their evolution, stars follow a distinct path in luminosityâtemperature space. Low-mass stars that have exhausted hydrogen in their core follow the so-called red-giant branch (RGB), which is predominantly in the direction of increasing luminosity and decreasing surface temperature," Hekker explains. "The luminosity bump is a temporary decrease in luminosity against this otherwise increasing trend."

The inset grey box is the Hertzsprung-Russel diagram for a 1 solar mass star progressing from the subgiant branch to the tip of the Red Giant Branch. The tiny grey box inside it is magnified in the larger part of the image, highlighting the RGB luminosity bump. Image Credit: S. Hekker 2026 ApJL 1008 L61

The bump is understood theoretically and also confirmed with observations. But there's one discrepancy between theory and observation. In models, the bump appears at higher luminosities than the observed bump, meaning it appears later. "To understand why the bump appears later in the models than in observations, the physics of the bump needs to be unravelled," Hekker writes.

Stars, including our Sun, are layered, and RGB stars are no exception. But unlike the Sun, RGB stars have exhausted the hydrogen in their cores, and most of what's left is in their envelopes. Since the core has exhausted its hydrogen by fusing it into helium, the core is inert helium. An RGB's fusion occurs in a thin shell. In both these regions, energy is transported via radiation.

Above this radiative region is a convective outer envelope.

As an RGB star ascends the branch, the core contracts and the surface expands. Since the core is inert helium, it exerts no outward pressure and is forced inward. "This causes the deepest layer of the convective envelope to move inwards, reaching layers that have changed their chemical composition due to (burning) processes earlier in the evolution of the star," Hekker explains.

This is when dredge-up occurs, as deeper layers are forced into the convective zone. Since the convective zone is convective, the material from the radiative zone mixes into the convective zone, changing its composition.

Now there's a situation where there's a shifting boundary deep inside the star called the Base of the Convective Zone (BCZ). It's organized around a thermodynamic property called specific entropy. It basically measures how disordered the gas is at the BCZ. As the BCZ moves deeper inside the star, the entropy difference across the boundary shrinks. Past a certain point, entropy across the boundary layer drops past a critical value, and that triggers the luminosity bump.

This diagram shows the interior of an RGB star (not to scale). An inert helium core is in the center, and it's contained in a thin hydrogen-burning shell. Above that is a radiative zone separated from the star's convective envelope by the base of the convective zone (BCZ). Earlier dredge-up and mixing created this boundary between helium-enriched and hydrogen-rich gas. This work ties the RGB luminosity bump to this boundary. The author argues that the onset of the bump occurs when the entropy across this boundary crosses a critical value. (Image Generated with AI)

Previous explanations for the bump rested on mechanics. In those explanations, the thin hydrogen-burning shell reaches the boundary and something inside the star changes, triggering the bump. In this explanation, the bump happens when an entropy threshold is crossed inside the star's thermodynamics. It's not simply that layers meet.

We can't see inside stars. Astrophysicists use physics to try to understand what's going on there, and they test those physics against the only part of the star they can really see, the outside. It's a constant back and forth to refine theories until they match observations.

âThis succinct explanation of the onset of the bump, is the first quantitative description proposed so far,â said Hekker.

This new work will make its way into the larger body of astrophysical theory.

"This viable description of the mechanism behind the onset of the bump provides crucial and new insights for the exploitation of the bump as an anchor point in stellar evolution theory," Hekker writes. "Such added knowledge of the onset of the bump could potentially be used to make more informed choices for changes to the physics in stellar models that go beyond calibration of the overshoot, to place the bump in stellar evolution models at the correct luminosity while at the same time aligning them with measured surface abundances."

Evan Gough is a science-loving guy with no formal education who loves Earth, forests, hiking, and heavy music. He's guided by Carl Sagan's quote: "Understanding is a kind of ecstasy."
