A new study points to testosterone and proteins in the skin as reasons why males and females experience temperatures differently.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's a common observation that women often prefer warmer temperatures and feel cold more easily than men do, and the same trend appears among females of other species. Now, a study offers new clues as to what drives this preference — and testosterone may play a part.

Skin carries sensors to detect heat and cold that influence each organism's decision to stay in or move out of an environment. The new study, published Oct. 28 in the Journal of Physiology, found that these sensors activate at higher temperatures in female mice, which appears to shift their preferred temperature roughly 7 degrees Fahrenheit (4 degrees Celsius) higher than that of male mice. Testosterone seems to influence this difference in activation.

"You could say it's just a cute observation of no particular importance," said study co-author Peter McNaughton, a pharmacologist at King's College London who studies pain, thermal sensation and thermoregulation. "[But] it's got practical ramifications," in that it might be important in designing buildings and spaces that accommodate people, he told Live Science.

Proteins in the skin's nerve endings activate in response to warmth or cold. "You can look at them like little electrical generators in the nerve endings," said Dr. Michael Caterina, a neuroscientist at Johns Hopkins University who was not involved in the research.

When activated, these proteins allow charged ions to enter sensory nerve cells, which, in turn, transmit electrical signals to the brain. The circuits a given nerve cell connects to determines our perception of heat or cold, Caterina told Live Science.

Beyond humans, it is known that many female animals, including mice and birds, prefer slightly warmer temperatures than their male counterparts do. So the researchers set up an experiment to investigate these differences.

They put 30 male and 27 female mice on two adjacent plates of different temperatures — one at 91.4 degrees Fahrenheit (33 degrees Celsius) and another that varied between lower and higher temperatures. A camera tracked the mice's movements and calculated how much time they spent on each plate.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Both male and female mice spent more time at the 91.4 F plate when the second plate was cooler. However, when put next to a plate measuring 100.4 F (38 C), female mice spent significantly more time on the warmer plate than male mice did. The average preferred surface temperature was approximately 89.6 F (32 C) for male mice and 96.8 F (36 C) for female mice.

"Since the top of the cage was completely open, there was no question of the air temperature affecting the mice," McNaughton said, so the preference was driven solely by the sensors in their skin. The researchers also measured the internal and skin temperatures of the mice and confirmed that there were no significant differences between the sexes on those fronts.

The scientists explored what would happen if they genetically deleted the warmth-detector protein. In male mice, this reduced their avoidance of the warmer plate, suggesting this protein normally sends a signal that discourages them from staying on warmer surfaces. The mice's preferred temperature also rose to about 95 F (35 C), closer to that of females.

The study suggests that testosterone somehow tweaks the function of heat-sensing nerves in the skin.

In female mice, deleting or blocking the protein did not have any significant effect.

The team then tried eliminating or blocking the coolness-detecting protein, finding that males and females didn't avoid the cool plates as strongly as they did before. Female mice also spent less time on the warmer plates, but males' preference for the warmer plates didn't change.

"Females are a little bit more responsive to activation of the cold receptor," Caterina said, "and a little bit less responsive to activation of the warmer receptor." That's despite the temperature-sensing neurons in both sets of mice working identically, the team found.

The researchers suspected that sex hormones might help to explain this difference.

They gave a group of male mice a drug that blocks the production of testosterone. Weeks after the treatment, these mice spent more time on the 38 C plate than males with normal testosterone. Meanwhile, female mice given testosterone lost their preference for warmer temperatures.

Interestingly, giving male mice female hormones, including forms of estrogen and progesterone, did not affect their temperature preferences. And blocking the hormones in female mice also had no effect. These hormones are known to influence other aspects of temperature regulation in the body, though, such as heat dissipation through the skin; but in this case, they didn't seem to affect animals' perception of temperature.

"So it really seems as though testosterone is the most important determinant," McNaughton said. But these changes were only partial; testosterone did not completely reverse the differences between the sexes. "So there is something else going on that we weren't able to identify," he added.

The exact mechanism for how testosterone impacts the sensor proteins is not clear. Because the effect happened over weeks, researchers suggested that it did not directly affect the temperature-sensing proteins. It might instead act indirectly by influencing the activity of genes, but further studies would be needed to confirm this idea.

Although the researchers did not conduct any tests in humans, McNaughton noted that the same sensor proteins are present in people and that studies with humans suggest that they behave in a similar way.

This research provides "valuable information" for understanding how the proteins responsible for sensing temperature work, Caterina said. Understanding these mechanisms could be useful for studying conditions like neuropathic pain, in which people's sensitivity to heat and cold is enhanced.

"What kinds of signals create our daily experiences around temperature is by itself very important," he told Live Science. "It's a big part of understanding ourselves as living beings."

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#6470. This $10,000-a-Pound Spice Could Help Save Colorado Farmers

Beneath Denver’s solar panels, a spice nicknamed “red gold” is yielding a promising harvest that could help Colorado farmers earn more with less water.

At Colorado State University Spur, horticulture graduate student Reece Bailey is investigating whether saffron could become a profitable addition to the state’s farms. His experiments in the campus’s urban gardens and green roof research areas are testing how the crop handles Colorado’s climate, how much water it needs, and whether growing it beneath solar panels improves production.

The appeal starts with its extraordinary value. A pound of saffron typically costs between $600 and $5,000, with some varieties reaching $10,000. Vanilla, the second most expensive spice, sells for roughly $90 to $225 a pound. Those prices caught Bailey’s attention, but the research must establish whether the potential earnings justify the work.

Colorado may seem an unlikely home for a spice closely associated with the Middle East. Yet Iran, which produces roughly 85% of the world’s saffron, has mountainous, semiarid conditions that resemble parts of the state. Bailey sees that overlap as a reason to investigate whether “red gold” could find a foothold on Colorado’s high plains.

The crop also offers an unusual combination of low water demand and late production. Saffron typically blooms in November, potentially bringing farmers income after other harvests have ended. Under suitable conditions, Bailey said, it could provide that additional crop without requiring extra irrigation.

“One thing that’s always been interesting to me is new ideas and novel ways of integrating crops into our environments,” said Bailey, who grew up in Aurora and has worked on Spur’s green roof for three years.

The world’s most expensive spice comes from a remarkably small harvest: the three slender red stigmas inside each purple saffron flower. Collecting enough to produce a pound of dried spice requires roughly 75,000 flowers.

That harvest is painstaking. Flowers open for only a few hours each morning, and workers carefully extract the stigmas, often with tweezers. The amount of hand labor helps explain both saffron’s price and the challenge of turning it into a profitable crop.

“It’s certainly not the easiest crop to grow or the easiest crop to work with, but the investment can be well worth it,” Bailey said.

The Colorado Department of Agriculture has committed $80,000 through its Specialty Crop Block Grant Program to investigate that possibility, particularly as a source of supplemental income late in the season and during dry years.

“For a lot of farmers, the price for their goods isn’t keeping up with the price of inputs, so what we’re really trying to do is find new crops that will work with Colorado’s climate and for our producers’ bottom line,” said Sam Hahn, the department’s next generation and specialty crops program manager. “Saffron has a high labor input, but it could really be a boon for our farmers.”

Successfully growing the flowers would answer only part of the business question. Farmers would still need to assess startup costs, bulb suppliers, equipment, labor availability, and buyers. A valuable spice does not automatically translate into a profitable harvest.

Its labor demands could nevertheless create another benefit. Hahn said the November bloom might provide agricultural jobs during a period when many farmworkers are typically unemployed, while helping farms adapt to a changing climate.

“It’s so important that we experiment with these high-value crops to see if it can supplement the market in our state and keep us competitive,” Hahn said.

Some of the most promising results are emerging 75 feet (23 meters) above the ground. Bailey’s plots occupy the roofs of two CSU Spur buildings, with Denver’s skyline and the Rocky Mountains in view. One grows among native Colorado plants, including sunflowers. Another sits beneath solar panels in an agrivoltaic system, where the same space supports crops and electricity production.

“I’m always curious about how different plants evolve and how they adapt to green roofs, and lately, I’ve come to realize that saffron is almost the ideal plant for these environments,” said Jennifer Bousselot, Bailey’s faculty adviser and an associate professor of horticulture and landscape architecture at CSU.

Spur’s rooftop gardens have carefully selected soil characteristics and are designed to use water efficiently. Saffron also tolerates some shade, and Bailey’s research so far has found that yields nearly double beneath the partial shade of solar arrays.

“This could provide cash flow value for farmers who want to use solar as an energy source, or who happen to be in an urban agriculture setting,” Bailey said.

Water use offers another reason to keep testing. Bailey said saffron requires roughly half as much water as corn and could potentially survive on rainfall alone, making it an appealing candidate for a region where irrigation water is under pressure.

“This crop is incredibly drought resistant,” Bailey said.

The experiments extend beyond Spur’s rooftops to CSU’s Foothills Campus and Denver Botanic Gardens Chatfield Farms, at the base of the mountains south of Denver. At Chatfield Farms, Lauren Hazlett, one of the head growers working at the solar array, has welcomed the sight of flowers appearing as other plants fade.

“I never thought I’d ever be able to see saffron growing, especially in Colorado—it’s something I always associated with the other side of the world,” she said.

Bousselot and Bailey have also sent bulbs to farmers in Paonia, Pueblo, and Montrose. Their reports will help show how saffron performs in working farm operations and whether its potential benefits carry beyond the research plots.

There is already a long history of finding uses for the spice. Alexander the Great, king of the ancient Greek kingdom of Macedon, reportedly bathed in saffron to help heal battle wounds. Doctors once prescribed it for bubonic plague, and Cleopatra used its fragrance to attract potential suitors. Today, it flavors dishes such as paella and risotto and is increasingly sought after in perfumes.

Modern research is also exploring its medicinal properties. Some studies suggest saffron may support mental health and help alleviate depression, while others have investigated its possible anti-inflammatory effects. Those research areas could add to its commercial appeal, although Colorado’s trials are focused on whether farmers can grow and sell it successfully.

“Up until now, we haven’t really been able to study saffron in Colorado at a deeper level, but the demand is there, and I only think we’ll be talking about it more and more,” Bailey said.

#6468. Scientists Discover a Powerful Plastic-Eating Enzyme Hiding in an Ordinary Compost Heap

An enzyme found in compost broke down small amounts of polyurethane foam in laboratory tests, offering an early lead toward gentler ways to recycle a stubborn plastic.

The polyurethane used in mattress foam, shoe soles, and refrigerator insulation is notoriously difficult to recycle on an industrial scale. A very large share of the millions of metric tons produced worldwide ends up in landfills or incinerators, taking potentially reusable material with it.

Nylon presents a similar challenge. Used in clothing, bags, cars, ropes, engine components, and fishing nets, it is another plastic made from crude oil, a finite resource. Researchers want to break both materials down into their pure components so those ingredients can become new polyurethane and nylon. Chemical and biological approaches are making progress, but the solutions emerging from laboratories are not yet ready for industrial use.

Researchers from Aarhus University and the Danish Technological Institute went looking for help among bacteria. Their search took in a Kenyan landfill, a tropical zoo, the guts of wax moth larvae, and a compost heap near Aarhus. The best candidate came from the compost, where a bacterium produced an enzyme with an ability that could prove useful far beyond the heap.

Researchers collected bacteria from plastic-contaminated environments, including a tropical zoo, a landfill in Kenya, compost and larval guts. Using fluorescent probes and fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS), they isolated bacteria capable of cleaving chemical bonds found in polyurethane and nylon. The active enzymes were then purified and identified using chromatography, activity assays and mass spectrometry. In total, the researchers identified 10 polyurethane-degrading enzymes and 2 nylon-degrading enzymes. Credit: Rosie Graham / Angewandte Chemie

Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions. To find ones that can break down plastic, researchers conventionally search genome databases for gene sequences resembling those of enzymes already known to do the job. That approach has yielded useful enzymes, but there are relatively few known examples to guide the search.

This team used bioprospecting, which means searching nature for organisms and genetic material that could be useful in research or industry. It was the first time researchers had searched on such a large scale and across such varied environments for enzymes capable of degrading polyurethane, also called PUR, and nylon.

The idea came to Andreas Møllebjerg as he prepared to begin a postdoctoral position at what was then the Interdisciplinary Nano Science Center (iNANO) at Aarhus University. He was joining a new project investigating whether natural enzymes could break down plastic. Møllebjerg, a co-author of the resulting study, recently published in Angewandte Chemie, was responsible for collecting bacteria from different environments.

“I suggested looking for suitable enzymes in places where it is warm, because bacteria thrive and grow well there all year round. And preferably somewhere plastic has been present for a long time. A year and a half later, I was on a plane to Kenya, followed by half an hour on the back of a local student’s motorbike on the way to a huge landfill. He helped me collect samples and communicate with the hundreds of people who lived on and off the landfill,” he says.

Møllebjerg and PhD student and co-author Malthe Kjær Bendtsen also traveled 34 kilometers, about 21 miles, to collect plastic waste at Randers Regnskov Tropical Zoo. Møllebjerg bought a bag of wax moth larvae from a pet food shop so the team could investigate enzymes from bacteria in their guts. At a recycling center about 10 kilometers, or 6 miles, from the university, he collected a shovelful of compost.

Those samples gave the researchers millions of bacteria to examine. Finding a useful enzyme required more than showing that a bacterium could react with a convenient laboratory substitute for plastic.

“It was like a three-stage rocket, where we gradually narrowed them down. We started by finding bacteria that could break down the fluorescent model material. Then we isolated the enzymes capable of breaking down exactly that fluorescent material. And finally, we tested the enzymes on increasingly realistic materials,” Bendtsen explains.

This 90-hour time-lapse video shows enzymatic degradation of two different molecules that mimic nylon. The second and fourth vials show CCPUR1 breaking down the two molecules, while the first and third vials show an inactive enzyme. Credit: Samuel Peña Díaz, Aarhus University, and Andreas Sommerfeldt, Danish Technological Institute

For the initial screening, the researchers mixed bacteria with molecules designed to mimic chemical bonds in polyurethane and nylon. The molecules lit up when they encountered a bacterium containing a suitable enzyme. Using fluorescence-activated cell sorting, or FACS, a machine could screen the bacteria and pick out glowing cells at a rate of up to 10,000 per second.

The search identified 29 plastic-degrading bacteria and 12 enzymes with varying abilities to break down polyurethane and nylon. The most promising enzyme was CCPUR1, from the compost bacterium Chelatococcus composti. Its name takes “CC” from the bacterium and “PUR” from PURase, shorthand for polyurethane hydrolase, an enzyme capable of breaking down polyurethane.

Testing on more realistic materials showed both its potential and its limitations. Given polyurethane mattress foam in powdered form, CCPUR1 broke down just under 1% in three days. That leaves a substantial gap between detecting an enzyme’s activity and using it to recycle plastic on an industrial scale.

CCPUR1 nevertheless had several useful characteristics. Its unusually wide binding cleft, a groove where it accommodates the material it acts on, gives large polymer molecules room to fit. Polymers are the long molecules that make up plastics. The enzyme was also particularly stable, withstanding higher temperatures and a range of solvents better than the other candidates.

Its origins in compost offer an explanation for those abilities. Compost contains stubborn plant materials such as wax and lignin, and an enzyme that evolved to break down those substances can also happen to work on plastic. Compost heaps can reach 80°C, or 176°F, so enzymes functioning there need enough stability to withstand the heat.

The team has since worked to improve CCPUR1. In a follow-up study published September 11, 2026, in Chem Catalysis, the researchers collaborated with the University of Porto, using computer simulations and targeted edits to the DNA instructions for making the enzyme.

Within three days, the modified enzyme broke down around 1.4% of the polyurethane in foam from a real shoe sole, without any pretreatment of the plastic. That experiment used a different material from the powdered mattress foam in the original study. Postdoctoral researcher Rosie Graham, who was responsible for testing the enzymes on plastic materials in the laboratory, is the first author of the follow-up study.

The other 11 enzymes could also have a role. They work best on small pieces of plastic and may complement CCPUR1 in future combinations of processes. Because enzymes are selective about what they act on, the researchers envisage using an enzyme cocktail in stages. Polyurethane could first be broken down and washed away, followed by the addition of nylon-degrading enzymes. Chemical methods cannot separate those tasks in the same way.

Making these processes practical may require mechanical and chemical treatments that make the plastic easier for enzymes to attack. Chemical degradation of polyurethane and nylon is itself a major research field, including at Aarhus University. The scale of the remaining challenge is one reason the team compares efficient polyurethane recycling to finding the holy grail.

“But the research highlights the strength of enzymes. Their real advantage when it comes to recycling is that they work under mild conditions, meaning at lower temperatures and pressures than those used in most recycling technologies today,” Graham says.

Reference: “Environmental Identification of Novel Enzymes for Polyurethane and Polyamide Degradation” by Malthe Kjær Bendtsen, Andreas Møllebjerg, Samuel Peña-Díaz, Rosie Graham, Nicolai Claus Petersen, Bjørk Nolsøe Isaksen, Mathias Carstensen, Martin B. Johansen, Andreas Sommerfeldt, Allan R. Petersen, Iddi Khamisi Chuma, Cecilie Ryberg, Thomas Rea Wittenborn, Virginia Gichuru, Huabing Wang, Carsten Scavenius, Alexander Sandahl and Daniel E. Otzen, 26 June 2026, Angewandte Chemie International Edition. DOI: 10.1002/anie.6159643

This work is supported by the Novo Nordisk Foundation through the Challenge Grant NNF22OC0072891 to the Center EnZync.

A double subduction zone off the coast of Japan caused rifting halfway around the world to accelerate, fueling the formation of some of North America's most iconic features.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A geological reorganization near Japan may have led to the formation of one of North America's most recognizable features.

The birth of the Gulf of California, which rifted from Mexico and created the Baja Peninsula 6 million to 8 million years ago, was accelerated by the formation of a double subduction zone more than 6,000 miles (9,600 kilometers) away, near Japan. This reorganization led to a transfer of tectonic force across the Pacific tectonic plate, which, in turn, opened the Gulf of California and ultimately led to the Grand Canyon's formation, according to new research published Oct. 29 in the journal Science.

The findings will help researchers understand more about plate boundaries, which is where most of the strongest earthquakes on the planet originate.

"It's more than a regional curiosity," study co-author Thorsten Becker, a geophysicist at the University of Texas at Austin (UT Austin), told Live Science. "It's a reminder of the global connectedness of mantle convection and plate tectonics."

The Gulf of California is an example of a rift zone, a place where continental crust pulls apart and creates a spot so low that it can be filled by ocean water. There are many rift zones around the world; a currently active one is the Red Sea. But rifting can slow down, speed up or peter out entirely. In the Gulf of California, rifting not only persisted, but sped up. Rifting took about 6 million to 13 million years ‪—‬ much quicker than the typical speed of 30 million to 80 million years.

Study co-author Guido Gianni, a geophysicist at the Czech Academy of Sciences, wondered why that was. No previous research fully explained the rapid rifting, which changed the face of North America in many ways. Not only did the rifting transfer Baja California to the Pacific Plate, but it provided an outlet for the developing Colorado River, which subsequently carved the Grand Canyon on its way to sea level.

Gianni and Becker's doctoral student at UT Austin, Xiang He, used a global model of plate tectonics, run on supercomputers at the Texas Advanced Computing Center on campus, to find out if far-flung forces might provide an explanation. Around the same time the Gulf of California was pulling apart, Japan was undergoing its own geological changes. Off the coast of Japan, the Pacific Plate subducts, or pushes under, the Eurasian Plate. About 10 million to 12 million years ago, a single subduction zone near Japan transitioned into two separate subduction zones.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

A double subduction zone off Japan (left inset) accelerated the growth of the Gulf of California (right inset).

This transition at the western end of the Pacific Plate influenced the tectonic forces on the other side of the plate, He, Gianni, Becker and their colleagues found.

"It turned out — ta-da! — [with] the change in this pulling stress, Baja California was one of the few places outside the Japan region that were affected," Becker said. It was "unexpected and sort of a little bit too good to be true."

The researchers tweaked their model to see if the result held with different assumptions about stresses and mantle properties, and it did.

The Gulf of California was already rifting regardless of the situation across the Pacific. The initial rift was caused by the subduction of a tectonic plate called the Farallon Plate, located under the West Coast of North America. The Farallon slab stretched and thinned the continental crust of the North American plate as it moved. But such rifting might have ended with nothing more than the formation of a little valley or low spot if Japan's influence had not kicked in to give the rifting some extra oomph.

The findings have a direct effect on scientists' understanding of how plate boundaries form, Becker said. And this isn't just academic. The findings could have implications for understanding earthquake-generating faults such as the San Andreas in California and the Cascadia subduction zone in the Pacific Northwest, Becker said. Cascadia is what's known as a "megathrust" boundary, capable of triggering quakes of more than magnitude 9.

"If I'm asking what is the mantle doing underneath Cascadia so I get our megathrust correct," Becker said, "I need to include these effects."

Gianni, G. M., He, X., Becker, T. W., & Faccenna, C. (2026). Western Pacific double subduction drives Gulf of California rifting. Science, 394(6823), 515–519. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aef5187

Stephanie Pappas is a contributing writer for Live Science, covering topics ranging from geoscience to archaeology to the human brain and behavior. She was previously a senior writer for Live Science but is now a freelancer based in Denver, Colorado, and regularly contributes to Scientific American and The Monitor, the monthly magazine of the American Psychological Association. Stephanie received a bachelor's degree in psychology from the University of South Carolina and a graduate certificate in science communication from the University of California, Santa Cruz.

#6464. Scientists Discover a Hidden Immune System Difference That Could Explain Why Obesity Affects Men and Women Differently

Scientists have discovered that immune cells in fat tissue behave differently in males and females, potentially helping explain sex-specific responses to obesity.

A type of immune cell best known for its role in allergies and asthma may help explain why obesity affects males and females differently. Researchers at the University of California, Riverside found that certain immune cells in fat tissue appear to protect female mice from obesity-related inflammation, while others become more inflammatory in males fed a high-fat diet.

The findings, published in PNAS Nexus, challenge the long-held assumption that these cells, called eosinophils, perform a relatively narrow range of functions. Instead, their effects may depend on their molecular characteristics, biological sex, and interactions with neighboring immune cells.

Using high-resolution single-cell sequencing, scientists identified six distinct eosinophil populations in adipose (fat) tissue. Each population displayed different patterns of gene activity, suggesting that eosinophils perform specialized functions rather than acting as a single, uniform group.

“Eosinophils are more complex than we once thought,” said Meera Nair, a professor of biomedical sciences at the UCR School of Medicine who co-led the research with biomedical scientist Adam Godzik. “Some populations can protect against obesity, and if we can identify and activate the pathways that produce these protective cells, we may find new ways to improve metabolic health.”

In female mice, researchers identified a protective eosinophil population that communicated more effectively with macrophages, another class of immune cells found in fat tissue. This relationship appeared to be supported by RELM alpha, a protein produced by macrophages that may help maintain protective immune activity. Earlier experiments showed that supplying RELM alpha to mice had protective effects, providing additional evidence for its role in regulating the immune environment.

Male mice showed a different response to a high-fat diet. Their fat tissue tended to contain more eosinophil populations associated with inflammation, and these cells displayed gene-expression patterns that suggested weaker protective functions.

“This means the relationship between eosinophils and obesity is not simply a matter of how many eosinophils are present,” said Rebecca E. Ruggiero-Ruff, a postdoctoral researcher in Nair’s laboratory and co-first author of the study. “Their functional characteristics and how they communicate with other immune cells are also critical.”

Although eosinophils have been detected in the fat tissue of people with obesity, scientists have not yet established whether they perform the same protective or inflammatory functions observed in mice. Determining whether similar cell populations exist in humans could help researchers investigate treatments that influence specific immune pathways rather than broadly altering immune activity.

“A drug may not activate the same pathways or produce the same effects in males and females, particularly when it targets the immune system,” said co-first author Xinru Qiu, a postdoctoral researcher in Godzik’s laboratory. “We need to investigate sex-specific biology more thoroughly so that treatments can be optimized for different patients.”

The researchers are now developing three-dimensional adipose organoids, laboratory-grown structures that reproduce certain features of human fat tissue. These models could allow scientists to examine how eosinophils interact with fat cells and macrophages, and whether modifying those interactions can encourage healthier tissue responses.

“We ultimately hope to develop human adipose organoids that will allow us to investigate whether manipulating immune-cell communication can promote healthier tissue responses,” said Godzik, a professor of biomedical sciences and the Bruce D. and Nancy B. Varner Presidential Endowed Chair in Cancer Research.

Reference: “Single-cell heterogeneity of adipose eosinophils is shaped by sex and RELMα and linked to macrophage communication networks in obesity” by Rebecca E Ruggiero-Ruff, Xinru Qiu, Lauren Vance, Yuxin He, Djurdjica Coss, Adam Godzik and Meera G Nair, 24 October 2026, PNAS Nexus. DOI: 10.1093/pnasnexus/pgag365

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health, UCR School of Medicine, and California Institute for Regenerative Medicine.

#6462. Your Brain Chemistry Could Change How You Understand Language

A single word can overturn your understanding of a sentence, and your brain chemistry may shape how hard you work to make sense of it again.

Even a single word can change the meaning of an entire sentence, forcing the brain to rethink what it just read. But how efficiently the brain handles these grammatical surprises may depend partly on its chemistry.

A study published in PNAS found that increasing dopamine and noradrenaline (catecholamines) strengthened a brain response associated with untangling ambiguous grammar. Researchers led by the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics (MPI-PL) in Nijmegen observed the largest effects in healthy adults with lower baseline working memory capacity.

“Catecholamines are known to regulate attention, working memory, and cognitive control, but their role in language remains poorly understood,” says Peter Hagoort, senior investigator and director emeritus of MPI-PL’s Neurobiology of Language Department and the Donders Institute for Brain, Cognition and Behavior.

“Our earlier work suggested that catecholamines can affect semantic aspects of sentence comprehension. Whether these neuromodulatory systems also influence syntactic processing—how the brain combines words into grammatical structures—was largely unknown.”

Understanding a sentence involves more than knowing what its words mean. Readers also have to work out how those words fit together, sometimes revising an interpretation as new information arrives. The researchers used temporarily ambiguous “garden-path” sentences to examine that process.

Consider “The fan attacked the drummer, and the guitarist packed the instruments up.” When the words appear one at a time, readers may initially group “the drummer and the guitarist” together as the people being attacked. The word “packed” reveals that the guitarist is instead performing a separate action, requiring readers to rebuild their interpretation.

To test whether brain chemistry influences this revision, the team recruited 30 healthy adults. Each completed two sessions, once after taking methylphenidate, a stimulant commonly prescribed for ADHD that increases catecholamine levels, and once after taking a placebo.

Participants read ambiguous and unambiguous sentences and answered comprehension questions after each one. Meanwhile, researchers recorded their brain activity using EEG (electroencephalography), allowing them to examine the response at the precise word that exposed the grammatical ambiguity.

After methylphenidate, participants showed a stronger P600 response at the critical word, such as “packed.” This well-known EEG signal is associated with demanding grammatical processing and reflects increased cognitive effort. Its enhancement suggests that higher catecholamine levels changed how the brain recruited resources to resolve the sentence.

The increase was greatest among participants whose working memory capacity was lower before treatment.

“The findings suggest that catecholaminergic systems contribute to the dynamic allocation of cognitive resources during syntactic processing,” says Hagoort. “Their influence on language therefore appears to extend beyond semantic processing to syntactic unification, and the magnitude of this effect may depend on individual baseline working memory performance.”

“The results support the development of neuropharmacolinguistics as a field linking neuromodulatory systems to language processing.”

Reference: “Neuropharmacology of language: ERP evidence for catecholaminergic modulation of syntactic processing” by Yingying Tan, Ashley G. Lewis, Iris C. Schmits, Robert-Jan Verkes, Roshan Cools and Peter Hagoort, 22 October 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2606806123

Researchers found extreme levels of mercury in sediment cores in Mexico ‪—‬ and it’s all because the Maya loved red paint.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Maya used so much red paint that they accidentally poisoned their lakes and waterways with mercury, a new study finds.

The problem was cinnabar, a vivid-red mercury-sulfide mineral that can be used as the pigment vermilion in red paint. The run-off from the paint can enter waterways, where anaerobic bacteria then transform cinnabar into highly toxic methylmercury in the sediments of lakes. Over time, the methylmercury accumulates to higher levels in the food chain.

The ancient Maya, a people who lived in what is now southern Mexico and Central America and whose descendants are still around today, painted almost everything red. Archaeologists have found countless artifacts that the Maya reddened, including sculptures, monuments, walls, plazas, pottery and the dead for ceremonial funerals. Cinnabar was a common pigment in the paint they made, along with red ocher, which gets its color from a nontoxic iron mineral called hematite.

But the Maya passion for the color red — which to them represented the sun, blood and life — caused an environmental disaster when the nearby waters were poisoned by the cinnabar runoff, said study first author Matthew Waters, a paleolimnologist (a scientist who studies ancient waterways) at Auburn University in Alabama.

"They would have seen a strange color change in the water … and a drop in its productivity, such as fish for protein," he told Live Science. The Maya depended heavily on freshwater fisheries, including for freshwater shellfish.

Previous studies had already found evidence for high levels of mercury in the Maya's southern highlands and south-central lowlands, but no one had fully examined levels of the toxic mineral in Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula.

To investigate, Waters and his colleagues studied mercury levels in Maya-era mud in the Yucatán, and found overwhelming signs of mercury poisoning, probably from cinnabar paint, they reported in their study, published Nov. 4 in the journal Science Advances.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"We did not suspect [the Maya] used it in the quantities that we were seeing," he said.

The study found extreme levels of mercury in sediment cores from two Maya-era sites: Cobá Lake, a shallow lake beside the Maya city of that name, and Cenote Xcach (also spelled X-Canché), a flooded sinkhole beside a ruined city in the jungle that few have excavated.

The sediment cores chronicle the composition of earth and water over more than 2,000 years, and the times of mercury poisoning coincide with several periods during the Preclassic and Classic periods of the Maya civilization from about A.D. 40 to 820.

Waters explained that the Environmental Protection Agency in the U.S. has determined it is unsafe to drink water with mercury levels above 2 parts per billion, while the official limit for the level of mercury in fish, where it builds up over time, is 1 part per million — any number above that means the fish can be seized by authorities.

Severe poisoning occurs when the mercury levels in human blood exceed about 100 parts per billion, from drinking contaminated water or eating contaminated marine animals, such as fish. In humans, mercury poisoning can cause severe symptoms, including permanent lung damage, brain damage and death.

The reddish hue of the Maya sun god Kinich Ahau, made between the sixth and ninth centuries, now housed in Mexico’s National Museum of Anthropology, shows the Maya's love for mercury.

The most polluted parts of the Yucatan cores had a mercury level of 2.3 parts per million, the team discovered. "They experienced this for decades and, in one case, for centuries," Waters said.

The researchers then examined the sediment cores for signs of environmental damage caused by the mercury poisoning. They found that the cores lacked tiny fossils of freshwater shellfish, indicating that the high mercury levels were killing marine life. The team also noticed that the sediment cores had hardly any traces of algal blooms, which should have happened frequently, Waters said. That's likely because algae could not survive in the poisoned water nutrients.

Scholars debate why the Maya civilization collapsed in the eighth and ninth centuries, but a leading suspect is the disruption of food supplies caused by drought.

But although mercury levels were high during the Preclassic and Classic periods, the environmental damage caused by mercury levels had been falling in many places for hundreds of years by the time of the Maya collapse, Waters said, although it may have been a contributing factor.

Cinnabar does not occur naturally in the Yucatán, so it must have been imported there, probably from what's now Honduras, the researchers said. It seems these cinnabar imports eventually stopped at Cobá Lake, and the poisoning there fell to a background level of about 20 parts per billion by A.D. 520. However, the sediment cores showed that the mercury poisoning continued at Cenote Xcach until the collapse, they said.

#6460. Scientists Discover California Has Way More Bugs Than Anyone Imagined

California is teeming with thousands of insect species science has yet to name, and its wild places hold more distinct worlds of tiny creatures than researchers realized.

California is home to an astonishing variety of insects, from the deserts of the Mojave to the forests of the Sierra Nevada. But scientists are discovering that the state’s insect diversity is far greater than previously believed.

A new study in Ecography estimates that California supports more than 60,000 insect species, far exceeding earlier estimates. Scientists have formally described only about two-thirds of them. Led by researchers at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, the study also found that nearly every location sampled had its own distinct insect community.

The findings suggest that conserving California’s insect life will require protecting a wide range of habitats. Even places with similar climates and landscapes can harbor different species, making it difficult for any single protected area to represent the state’s extraordinary diversity.

The research is the first publication from the California Insect Barcode Initiative (CIBI), a $6 million project with an ambitious goal: collect and identify every insect species in California. Although insects are the most diverse group of animals on land, they remain underrepresented in large-scale conservation assessments.

Researchers used DNA barcoding on more than one million insect specimens. The technique compares short sections of DNA to help distinguish species, giving scientists a way to investigate diversity that can be difficult to recognize from appearance alone.

The effort brought together the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, California Department of Food and Agriculture, UC Berkeley, UC Riverside, San Diego Natural History Museum, and California Academy of Sciences in San Francisco. Researchers gathered tissue samples from museum collections, deployed Malaise traps across 72 ecoregions, and made collecting expeditions to 454 additional locations statewide.

Museum specimens extended the project’s reach beyond what researchers could collect in the field. Fresh sampling added another essential piece, with volunteers helping keep traps operating week after week. Although Malaise traps capture insects passively, collecting their contents and maintaining them takes sustained effort.

“This is an example of community science. Volunteers stepped forward to help with sampling by managing traps, which we would not have been able to do for continuous weekly sampling,” says study co-author Giar-Ann Kung, the museum’s entomology collections manager.

Kung joined researchers and volunteers across California in setting traps and collecting insects. Some participants maintained sampling sites for years, providing a continuity that the research team could not have achieved alone.

“There are people like Sara Fairchild and Michael Nance who managed a Malaise trap for over three years at a site in the high desert, which is the longest continuous site for the project. That could not have been accomplished without them.”

To explore how insect diversity varies across California, the researchers compared ecoregions, areas grouped by the Environmental Protection Agency according to shared ecosystem characteristics. They used Level 3 classifications, including the Mojave Basin and Range, Southern California Mountains, and Sierra Nevada. Of these regions, the Mojave Basin and Range had the greatest number of insect species.

Although similar environments shared some patterns, each region had its own mix of insects. “The deserts are kind of more similar to each other, and the mountains in northern California are a little bit more similar to each other, but every part of the state hosts a really different insect fauna,” says Dr. Barkdull.

Those differences also appeared at a smaller scale, with individual collecting sites within the same ecoregion harboring distinct insect communities. Together, the findings highlight the need to protect a wide range of California’s wild places.

Reference: “DNA barcoding of more than one million insect specimens indicates that at least one third of California’s insect biodiversity remains undiscovered” by Austin J. #6459. Novel CRISPR therapy is poised to gain first FDA approval to alter genes inside the body

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Heidi Ledford reports for Nature from Seattle, Washington.

The Cas9 protein together with RNA and DNA (orange; artist’s illustration). A new therapy uses the CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing system to treat a rare genetic disease called hereditary angioedema.Credit: Alfred Pasieka/Science Photo Library

A pioneering therapy that edits genes inside a recipient’s body continues to be effective four years after treatment, according to data released by its developer, Intellia Therapeutics.

The therapy, named lonvoguran ziclumeran (lonvo-z), was designed to treat one form of a genetic disorder that causes episodes of painful and potentially dangerous swelling in the throat and other parts of the body. Lonvo-z deploys the CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing system to disable the gene that produces prekallikrein, a protein made in the liver that promotes blood-vessel leakage.

Bigger than CRISPR? A guide to the latest genome editors

Bigger than CRISPR? A guide to the latest genome editors

Intellia, headquartered in Cambridge, Massachusetts, has applied for approval of lonvo-z to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), which is expected to issue a decision by 10 March. If approved, the therapy will become the world’s first CRISPR medicine to be delivered directly inside the body, or in vivo, John Leonard, Intellia’s chief executive, told investors on 12 November. Currently, the only CRISPR therapy approved by the FDA is performed on cells that have first been removed from the body and are subsequently re-infused.

For people with the condition, hereditary angioedema, the gene-editing approach could offer relief from a lifetime of juggling medications to prevent and treat swelling attacks, says Jonathan Bernstein, a hereditary angioedema specialist at the University of Cincinnati in Ohio and an investigator on a lonvo-z trial. “It’s very reassuring,” he says of the four-year data. “That’s what you’re supposed to see.”

The only approved CRISPR therapy is Casgevy, a treatment for two genetic blood disorders, sickle cell anemia and ß-thalassemia. To create a dose of Casgevy, physicians first remove blood stem cells from the recipient, then send them off for gene editing. The edited cells are infused back into the recipient.

The therapy must be made anew for each person, adding time, cost, and complexity. The recipient also has to undergo harsh chemotherapy treatment to make room for the edited cells.

CRISPR makes enhanced cancer-fighting immune cells inside mice

CRISPR makes enhanced cancer-fighting immune cells inside mice

In vivo gene-editing approaches aim to sidestep these concerns by editing genes directly in the body. Lonvo-z, for example, consists of fatty particles that encase mRNA encoding CRISPR-Cas9 components. The particles are infused into the blood and taken up by the liver, where prekallikrein is produced. The procedure takes one day.

In vivo gene editing can introduce other safety concerns, however. The therapy affords no opportunity to screen out cells with unwanted edits at other locations in the genome, or in other organs. Recipients might also have harmful immune responses to the treatment.

Last year, the FDA placed a clinical hold on two other in vivo studies sponsored by Intellia after a participant — an older man with other health conditions — developed liver damage and died after receiving a CRISPR treatment. The FDA lifted the hold this year after requiring added safety measures.

#6458. Scientists Develop a Groundbreaking Rechargeable Battery That Runs on Vitamin B12

The same vitamin found in everyday foods could eventually help store surplus renewable electricity, after an experimental zinc-air battery using B12 completed up to 250 recharge cycles.

The search for safer, more sustainable batteries is leading scientists to some unexpected places, including the chemistry of vitamins. Researchers at the University of Córdoba in Spain have found that vitamin B12, a nutrient essential to human health, can also help power a rechargeable battery. Their experimental design completed up to 250 charge and discharge cycles, opening another possibility for future energy storage technology.

The researchers developed a zinc-air battery, which generates electricity through chemical reactions involving zinc and oxygen from the surrounding air. Unlike conventional batteries that store all their reactive materials internally, zinc-air batteries draw oxygen from the environment. This makes them lighter and gives them high energy density, meaning they can store substantial energy relative to their weight. They are already used in small devices such as hearing aids.

Zinc also offers advantages because it is abundant and recyclable. These batteries use nonflammable, water-based electrolytes, making them potentially safer than conventional lithium-ion batteries, whose raw material extraction raises economic, social, and environmental concerns.

Making zinc-air batteries rechargeable, however, presents a challenge. They need a catalyst, a substance that helps chemical reactions proceed, that can support both the production of electricity and the reverse process needed to recharge the battery.

Vitamin B12, also known as cobalamin, offered a possible solution because its molecular structure contains cobalt (III), a form of the metal cobalt that helps drive these reactions. Although better known for its role in nutrition, B12 is produced naturally by certain bacteria and manufactured commercially for food and pharmaceutical applications. Found in foods of animal origin, it is used to address nutritional deficiencies and has also become popular alongside other B vitamins as a hangover remedy because it can help reduce fatigue.

Researcher Antonio Jesús Fernández Romero explained that vitamin B12 “has proven to meet the necessary conditions to act as a good catalyst because, during discharge, it catalyzes the reduction of oxygen to water and, during recharging, it promotes the production of oxygen”.

The difficulty was keeping the vitamin inside the battery. Because B12 dissolves readily in water, it could not simply be added to a battery that uses a water-based electrolyte. The researchers solved this problem by attaching the vitamin to single-walled carbon nanotubes, extremely thin carbon structures that hold it in place while allowing it to support the chemical reactions. Their approach mimicked “the process by which amino acids bind together in proteins.”

The prototype was developed by the Physical Chemistry research group (FQM-204) at the University of Córdoba’s Chemical Institute for Energy and the Environment (IQUEMA). As study author Manuel Cano Luna explained, “we looked at the properties we can find in naturally occurring materials to use them in new batteries.”

This is the group’s third battery prototype using a biological molecule as a catalyst. Earlier experiments involved hemoglobin, which contains iron (II), and catalase, which contains iron (III). The key advance with vitamin B12 is that the resulting battery can be recharged, completing up to 250 cycles in the researchers’ tests.

Although the prototype remains experimental, the findings suggest that naturally occurring molecules could contribute to cheaper, more sustainable energy storage systems. With further development, rechargeable zinc-air batteries could eventually help store surplus electricity from renewable energy sources, addressing one of the challenges of transitioning toward cleaner energy.

Reference: “A vitamin B12-based air electrode for high-performance rechargeable zinc–air batteries” by García-Caballero, Valentín, López-León, Miguel, G. The Vikings are famous for being warriors, but how often did Viking women take part in battles?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Vikings were explorers, farmers, merchants and, most famously, warriors who launched raids across large parts of Europe.

Stereotypes of Vikings usually conjure up images of muscular men. But over the past few decades, researchers have turned their attention to women of the Viking Age (roughly A.D. 793 to 1066) and the roles they held. For instance, there are stories of "shield maidens" who fought alongside men, and some of these texts mention Viking women who fought in battle. The archaeological record also holds evidence, including graves of Viking Age women who were buried with war-grade weapons and shields.

It's still a matter of debate whether women who lived during the Viking Age could be warriors, but this discussion raises another question: It's one thing to have texts describing female fighters and archaeological records of women buried with weapons, but what can the evidence tell us about how frequently Viking women fought in battle?

The answer, experts told Live Science, largely depends on our interpretation of texts, artifacts, and burials of Viking Age women, which often face higher scrutiny than burials of men who were buried with similar (or even fewer) weapons.

The Vikings used a runic system of writing, but they left precious few texts behind. Instead, much of what we know about the Vikings was written about them by people from other cultures or by their Norse descendants.

One of the most evocative texts was written in the 12th century by the Danish historian and theologian Saxo Grammaticus. In "Gesta Danorum" (Latin for "History of the Danes" and translated by Jenny Jochens), he wrote that "there were once women in Denmark who dressed themselves to look like men and spent almost every minute cultivating [combat] skills." As "if they were forgetful of their true selves they put toughness before allure, aimed at conflicts instead of kisses, tasted blood, not lips, sought the clash of arms rather than the arm's embrace, fitted to weapons hands what should have been weaving, desired not the couch but the kill, and those they could have appeased with looks they attacked with lances."

Another text about the Vikings, the medieval Irish "Cogadh Gaedhelre Gallaibh" ("War of the Irish with the Foreigners"), refers to a woman known as the "Red Lady" leading a Viking fleet in a raid on Belfast in the 10th century.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

There's a lot of uncertainty, said Neil Price, an archaeology professor at Uppsala University in Sweden who has written extensively about the Vikings. The text in the "Cogadh Gaedhel re Gallaibh" that refers to the Red Lady is of debatable accuracy, Price told Live Science in an email.

He suspects that Viking women fought in battle but not frequently. In addition, "female warriors were probably a very small minority," Price said.

A modern-day reenactment depicting Viking warriors.

The account written by Saxo Grammaticus is also contentious. Thomas Kristian Heebøll-Holm, a history professor at the University of Southern Denmark, said Saxo Grammaticus is not a reliable source.

"Saxo Grammaticus does write about female warriors, but only in the parts of his work concerned [with] the legendary past of Denmark," Heebøll-Holm told Live Science in an email. "Furthermore, these writings are not accurate, but moral and fictitious," Heebøll-Holm said, noting that, in some instances, Saxo Grammaticus seemed to be drawing on the stories of the Amazons, a group of legendary female warriors whom the ancient Greeks believed in with stories about them dating back more than 2,500 years.

Archaeological evidence can also be challenging to interpret. Archaeologists know of about 30 Viking Age female burials containing weapons, including three with swords in Scandinavia. Even more Viking Age women's graves have items that could have been used as weapons ‪—‬ including spears, axes and knives ‪—‬ although these tools also could have been used for hunting or tending to farms. Either way, we can't be sure if these women fought in battle.

"The first concern is that the weapons were really used by the deceased and were not merely included as signs of special status or social rank acquired through inheritance," Deborah Shepherd, an independent researcher who holds a doctorate in archaeology and has studied the Vikings extensively, told Live Science in an email. She noted that graves are often not well preserved, making it difficult to gather information.

This 1889 illustration shows a grave at Birka in Sweden. It is now known that the person buried with war-grade weapons and riding gear is a woman.

There were likely "some few female warriors, but they were probably only found in the highest ranking families, and their warrior career was probably short-lived," Shepherd said. "They wouldn't have fought in the great armies of later centuries but possibly did fight in pre-Christian skirmishes." (The Vikings began gradually converting to Christianity between the ninth and 12th centuries.)

There is at least one known case of a Viking woman found with what may be combat-related injuries. A Viking woman found in Solør, Norway, had a head injury consistent with a sword strike. She was 18 or 19 at the time she died, was buried with weapons and lived around 900.

Ole Kastholm, a curator and senior researcher at the Roskilde Museum in Denmark, said there is a lot of uncertainty regarding how frequently Viking Age women fought in battle.

Weapons "do occur as a grave good in a handful of graves with female human remains," Kastholm told Live Science in an email. "Often it is just a single weapon [such] as a spear or [a] battle axe. But we know of at least one example of a female grave with a full set of weapons as well as riding equipment," which is located in Birka, Sweden.

"If this was a man's grave, researchers would have no doubt that it was a warrior grave, and this explanation must necessarily also apply when the interred is a woman," Kastholm said.

That said, there were female warriors in other cultures. "One can also note in passing that female warriors were an almost common feature of central Asian societies for at least a millennium before the Viking Age," Price wrote in his book, "The Sea-King and the Sorceress: Life and Death in the Viking Age" (Basic Books, 2026).

For instance the Scythians are a people who flourished in eastern Europe and Asia and Scythian women have been found buried with horses and weapons. In some cases, the Scythian women suffered combat wounds such as arrowheads and it's been speculated that they may have been an inspiration for stories of the Amazons.

Owen Jarus is a regular contributor to Live Science who writes about archaeology and humans' past. He has also written for The Independent (UK), The Canadian Press (CP) and The Associated Press (AP), among others. Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.

#6453. Brisbane Gets Its Moment in the Sun

Late one afternoon last November, Ty Simon works the room at Golden Avenue. He laughs with a pair of men in suits, tops off the glasses for a table of women in flower-patterned dresses, squeezes shoulders, and nods and smiles his way across the rest of the floor. Waiters ferry wine and coffee and platters of hummus and salads between the kitchen and the split-level dining space. Sheets of bright Queensland sun pour in through the open walls. It's Tuesday, it's lunch, and the place is full, unrushed, and lovely; it feels good to be here. Golden Avenue opened in the middle of last year as the ninth restaurant from Simon and his wife, Milan-born Biànca Marchi-Simon, through their Anyday hospitality group, which started with the Asian-inflected Longtime and went on to include Agnes, a dimly lit open-flame spot that won Australia's Restaurant of the Year in 2023. When Simon returns to our table, I remark on the hospitality that I've just seen. “Here we take a community approach,” he says. “My goal has always been to make sure that the people who like us, love us.”

The community approach may be the key to his city's success. Brisbane—Australia's perpetually distant-third city—has long been reduced by the Aussies to a “big country town.” (Their words—not mine!) Though a good-natured and happy place, it lacked the natural beauty and trendsetting of Sydney and the cultish urban creativity of Melbourne. For decades Brisbane seemed to succumb to the belief that it could never compete. It lacked personality in its Central Business District (CBD) and had pretty much no public transport. Even geography worked against it: In a state prized for its coastline, Brisbane is nearly 50 miles from a surf beach. Locals would often zip overseas or migrate south, perhaps on the assumption that their ambition could never be realized at home. The big country town endured.

The astounding Kith and Kin, from Queensland artist Archie Moore, which won the Golden Lion at Venice’s 60th biennale, on display at GOMA

Then a shift began. The city council embarked on an ambitious rebranding in 2010 to position Brisbane as globally connected and dynamic, giving it the nickname of New World City (“It was about shedding the idea of being the poor cousin,” Simon says). The magnificent Gallery of Modern Art (GOMA) had opened just a few years before, attracting world-class works from the Pacific and beyond. The council leveraged the city's billion-dollar location, just north of the booming Gold Coast, with its high-rises and killer beaches, and south of the covetable Sunshine Coast, with the Great Barrier Reef just off its shores. Millions traveled in from all over each year for what lay on either side of Brisbane, so why not make the city bait for some of their money and time? Many Brisbanites, Simon included, began to grow this place together, creating a city that reflected their own ambitions—and themselves. In the 2010s the city developed sharply designed precincts filled with glamour shopping and higher-level dining, all under year-round sunshine and with Brisbane's noticeable good cheer and friendliness. In 2021 the IOC announced that Brisbane would host the summer Olympics in 2032, following Los Angeles.

And right around that same time, COVID hit. While the rest of Australia struggled with lockdown and tight regulations that dragged on, Queensland fared generally well, with looser rules and relatively low numbers of cases after the initial shutdowns. “We had Melburnians coming into Brisbane just to feel normal again,” says entrepreneur and developer Catherine Malouf.

Malouf may be the most recognizable face of Brisbane's new chapter. Her family is one of the key forces behind the James Street precinct, a fig-tree-studded melange of open-air coffee houses, Champagne bars, and high-end restaurants strung together with designer shops selling top local labels. “I wanted to create somewhere where we could have a good lunch, a glass of wine, and go shopping in a place that felt like the best of Australia,” she says as we eat grilled chicken and salads at her Hellenika restaurant. Stylish and elegant, Malouf exudes the kind of sophistication you may more often associate with the places she formerly called home, like Italy and California, but her good nature and easy friendliness is all Brisbane. In a sense she personifies the version of Brisbane she is invested in creating: global and chic but anchored in hometown charm. “It took me 20 years to come back and realize that this is the place I want to live in, and a lot of people have realized that too,” she says. “It is comfortable. It is easy.”

The precinct's architecture is heavy, concrete, and borderline Brutalist, but not at all ugly. It creates an aura of strength and permanence that's almost symbolic for the next chapter of a city whose heritage architecture was mostly knocked down and whose locals have often fled elsewhere for opportunity. And amid it all is the anchor of the precinct, The Calile, an urban resort hotel whose execution feels Aussie but whose ambition and hospitality would work in any major global city. Its opening—along with its smartly designed rooms and mezzanine-level pool, bars, and restaurants that spill over into the general precinct sidewalks—catapulted the James Street precinct onto the radars of international travelers. “We are very much an Aussie hotel, but we are increasingly hosting people from around the world,” Malouf says.

Designer Heidi Middleton inside her atelier, Artclub

The James Street precinct serves as a gateway to Australia. The stores here, high-end and, for the most part, independent, are nearly all Australian brands such as P. Johnson, St. Agni, and Brisbane's own Gail Sorronda. A centerpiece is Artclub, from fashion designer Heidi Middleton, which launched here last year. Like many of her fellow Brisbanites, Middleton left to start and grow a business whose ambitions, she felt, would never flourish in Brisbane. After spending decades in Europe and selling her globally renowned Sass & Bide, she alleviated her homesickness and moved back. Artclub is a sustainably minded fashion brand that focuses on small production and renewable materials. Middleton remarks that the key to the precinct's success is the curation: high-end and never high street. “They have created a genre that is all their own,” she says.

Brisbane is called the River City for the coffee-hued eponymous waterway that snakes through it. Like the James Street precinct, the river, too, has been a focus for a lot of redevelopment. The work here—walkways, bridges, cycling and jogging lanes, dining districts, and green spaces—has pulled the city together and been a catalyst for a revamped relationship between people and place. On the banks near the James Street precinct, where a once industrial wasteland lay abandoned and uninspired, now sits the reimagined Howard Smith Wharves, alive with breweries, green parks, and restaurants. It's located on the Brisbane Riverwalk, a network of overwater walkways that are dotted with bright red royal poinciana flame trees, which didn't exist 10 years ago. Along the walk sits Stanley, an excellent Chinese spot that conjures a Hong Kong evening parlor and was opened by Louis Tikaram, who made a name on the global culinary stage as executive chef of EP & LP in West Hollywood. A 15-minute stroll away is Supernormal, the only sister restaurant to the hit Melbourne joint of the same name, whose 2024 opening unofficially announced Brisbane as a serious foodie city.

A signature steamed dumpling basket from Stanley

Four new pedestrian bridges have opened to decrease car traffic, promote sustainable living, and solve some of the city's connectivity issues. The latest, Kangaroo Point Bridge, connects the suburb of Kangaroo Point to the CBD, and it's bookended with coffee bars and has green spaces so that pedestrians can relax while looking out over the water. Zigzagging underneath them all is the beloved CityCat ferry, which zips from bank to bank, chartering passengers throughout town and beyond. Stops include the wonderful South Bank cultural district, where you'll find GOMA and the Queensland Art Gallery (QAG). It chugs its way to West End, Brisbane's perennial counterculture neighborhood, which has a funky retro cinema, indie shops selling Japanese crafts and fashion, and solid food.

Take the ferry north and you'll arrive at Brisbane Powerhouse. A hulking industrial building that powered the city starting in the 1920s, it was reborn in 2000 as the city's contemporary art center, complete with sprawling grounds, rooftop areas, bars, restaurants, and untouched industrial spaces that can host interactive exhibitions. It's raw and cool, and its scale is enormous. When I meet Louise Bezzina there, she is in her second week as the Powerhouse's artistic director and CEO. Kind and unassuming, she is the type of person you might casually meet at a mutual friend's birthday dinner and, 15 minutes into the conversation, realize you are sitting next to someone brilliant. “As Australia develops it allows for more cities to grow—it is not just Sydney and Melbourne,” she says. “Brisbane has long been an untapped city of opportunity.”

She is part of the cohort of local leaders drilling into its potential. Prior to the Powerhouse, Bezzina was the creative director of Brisbane Festival, the largest international festival in Australia by attendance numbers, for which she secured the Jean Paul Gaultier show over creative capitals like Melbourne in 2024. “My edgy style suits Brisbane,” she believes. For her first project at the Powerhouse, she launched “Swingers: The Art of Minigolf,” an interactive statement on female empowerment in a male-dominated world, pegged to the origin story of the putting game, which was founded in the 19th century by Scottish women who had been banned from 18-hole golf on account of their gender; each of the nine holes here was designed by a different female-identifying artist. Bezzina has begun ideating plans to partner with Los Angeles and Pacific dance groups in the lead-up to (and handoff of) the Summer Olympic Games.

But to suggest that creativity is new to Brisbane would be misleading. Designer Lydia Pearson is a local loyalist who has long believed in the power of her hometown. “It used to be that if you wanted to be successful, you had to either leave or create it yourself,” she says. She chose the latter. In 1989 Pearson cofounded the fashion brand Easton Pearson with fellow designer Pamela Easton, which focused on circular fashion through textiles and hand embroidery. It took off, showing during Paris Fashion Week in 1999 and selling in 20 countries before the label closed in 2016. The following year the Museum of Brisbane acquired more than 3,000 pieces from the Easton Pearson archive and has put some of the items on permanent display. “The hard part was getting people to believe you could make a brand in Brisbane that wasn't simply a hibiscus-patterned dress,” Pearson says.

We meet in the leafy suburb of Red Hill, where she and her current partner, the artist Shilo Engelbrecht, work diligently to upcycle old fabrics into a new life through their label, ShiloLydia. This could mean turning an antique tablecloth into a sheer, soft dress, or reworking discarded linens into sharp shirts whose silhouettes could compete with any on a global catwalk. The work is slow, careful, and considered—a preservation effort as much as it is a creative one. The results are delicate and beautiful, a quiet and enduring counter to the louder creativity happening across the city.

Their studio sits inside a Queenslander, an old, iconic style of house that started to appear in Brisbane in the mid-1800s. The structures are wood, often colorful but always fragile, with large verandas designed to catch and route cooling breezes through the home. Queenslanders are delightful and charming, and have become recognizable to millions of viewers around the world who tune into Brisbane's most famous export, Bluey. The beloved animated show about Bluey, a blue heeler dog, who is likely known to more people around the world than her real-life fellow Brisbanite Jacob Elordi, is the creation of animator Joe Brumm. The show airs in 28 languages and more than 140 countries. For several years it was the most streamed show in the United States of any genre, and it has an empire worth $2 billion. Brisbane is a main character, and the city is unmistakable via the iconic Queenslander wood homes, the ibis birds pecking around, the sun and steep hills, the hours of imaginative outdoor play that Brumm says is modeled after his own upbringing in Queensland. Bluey resonates with parents and children of the world due to the heart and the humor at the show's core, something Brumm says defines Brisbane. “It is about the cheer that I feel when I come back,” he says. A good reminder, then, that a place's most resonant selling point is often something that can't be built.

True urban resort The Calile Hotel helped put Brisbane on the traveler map. The hotel has a phenomenal pool and fitness space; even if you're not staying here, swing by for its Lobby Bar and excellent restaurants, including Hellenika, which serves Greek favorites.

Inside a restored heritage Queenslander, the intimate Spicers Balfour Brisbane is well-located in New Farm: It's walking distance from the James Street precinct, the Howard Smith Wharves, and Brisbane Powerhouse.

The dimly lit, decidedly grown-up restaurant Agnes, which was named Australia's Best in 2023, is known for its exceptional wood-fired cooking of duck, steak, and more.

Housed inside a former church in West End, August is a nod to the reverence of Sunday lunch, with considerately prepared plates of Noosa snapper and Jerusalem artichoke risotto.

Sleek and light-flooded, the 15-month-old Middle Eastern spot Golden Avenue has great eggplant and grilled meats.

Do an outdoor table and load it up with all the dumplings and noodles you can order at superb riverside restaurant Stanley that feels like high-end Hong Kong parlor dining.

The Brisbane outpost of the hot Melbourne restaurant Supernormal has a glamorous dining room with large water-facing windows and a fun, Asian-inflected menu that leads with local produce and protein.

Located near the funky Fish Lane, Southside is the spot for dumplings and siu mai after strolling the museums of South Bank.

The French Exit, the newest venture from Ty and Biànca at Anyday, has Parisian-style interiors by star designer Tamsin Johnson and cool bars and dining rooms spread over multiple floors in a heritage building.

Brisbane's cultural hub is South Bank, with Gallery of Modern Art (GOMA) and other institutions featuring Indigenous, Australian, and Pacific Island artists. The riverfront Brisbane Powerhouse has ambitious and edgy festivals, exhibitions, and events throughout the year.

For the best Australian labels, head to the James Street precinct for objects from Dinosaur Designs; stylish dresses from St. Agni; and sustainable, one-off fashions from Heidi Middleton's atelier, Artclub. Over in Red Hill, drop into ShiloLydia as well as the other ateliers that share space in the same Queenslander. Shilo Engelbrecht also hosts collage and meditation workshops in her studio out back by appointment.

The best way to see (and travel) Brisbane is the CityCat ferry, which bounces between 22 stops along the river. But the city has made walking easier too. Stroll the overwater footpaths on the waterfront up to the gorgeous City Botanic Gardens. If you‘re keen for a longer walk after checking out the exhibitions at GOMA, find your way to West End for funky vintage shopping and phenomenal food.

There is no shortage of worthy weekend getaways from Brisbane, including the Gold Coast and Noosa on the Sunshine Coast. But drive an hour inland to the artsy, beautiful Tamborine Mountain for a lovely look at a lesser-explored side of Queensland. Stay at the chic, two-year-old Tamborine Boutique Hotel, where a pantry and bar stock local snacks. Have lunch at the petite Picnic Real Food Bar, and don't worry if it's already run out of the plump and delicious pies (everything is worth trying). Then head around the corner for local amaro tastings at Loborn. Restore yourself after mountain hikes at the floating Sol Elements spa, whose soaking baths and salt room all seem to hover over a lake.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.
