#6423. Memory tests may miss clues hidden in the time it takes to answer

Memory tests may reveal more than correct answers, as slower responses in older adults could signal subtle changes.

Getting an answer right on a memory test is usually considered a good sign. But what if it takes someone much longer to reach that answer?

That delay might tell us something important.

New research suggests that the time older adults take to answer memory questions could reveal subtle changes in how their brains work, even when they manage to give the right answers.

Anglia Ruskin University researchers found that older adults with possible mild cognitive impairment (MCI) answered some memory questions more slowly than healthy older adults. Distractions made the gap clearer.

MCI affects memory and thinking beyond normal aging, but people can usually manage daily life. Some later develop dementia, though many do not.

Professor Shahina Pardhan, who worked on the study, thinks measuring answer times alongside memory scores could help doctors spot early changes. The idea needs more testing.

The study brought together 115 people. There were 34 young adults, aged 18 to 30, and 61 healthy older adults, aged 55 or above.

Another 20 older adults had scored below the cutoff on at least one of two standard screening tests. The team placed them in an at-risk group for mild cognitive impairment, or MCI.

Nobody in that group had a confirmed MCI diagnosis. Those screening results were a reason to investigate, rather than proof that someone had the condition.

People with MCI have more difficulty with memory and thinking than normal aging would explain, but can usually get on with everyday activities. Some later develop dementia, though many do not.

In the word task, people watched two or four color words appear briefly in different places. The computer then showed one again and asked whether it was in the place where they’d seen it before.

Participants had to remember each word’s location while ignoring its ink color.

A mismatch between a color word and its ink, such as “red” printed in blue, can create interference known as the Stroop effect.

The at-risk group got more answers wrong than both the young and healthy older groups.

With two words to remember, they took longer to answer too; the timing differences between groups weren’t clear enough to rule out chance with four words.

There was no instruction to hurry. Participants were asked to get the answers right, while the computer recorded how long each response took.

In the arrow task, an arrow could point in one direction while moving in another. For example, it might point left and move right, or point and move in the same direction.

At the time they saw an arrow, participants didn’t know what they’d be asked to recall about it.

Either its movement or the way it pointed could come up in the question, so they had to remember both.

It wasn’t possible to pick one detail and ignore the other throughout the task, as they could with ink color.

Remembering both might have changed how they dealt with a mismatch, the researchers suggested.

With two arrows to remember or four, the at-risk group answered more slowly than healthy older adults.

But unlike the two other groups, they showed no clear extra delay when an arrow’s movement and pointing direction clashed.

Healthy older adults did about as well as young adults with the words, but made more mistakes with the arrows. The two groups answered at similar speeds on the arrow task despite that difference in mistakes.

For young adults and healthy older adults, wrong answers on the word test generally took longer than correct ones.

Perhaps they hesitated because they weren’t sure, the researchers suggested.

The 20 at-risk participants took roughly the same time whether they were right or wrong. One possibility is that they were less aware of making mistakes, though the study didn’t establish this.

And that pattern didn’t carry over to the arrows. All three groups took longer when they gave a wrong answer on that task.

For both older groups, words in matching ink were quicker to deal with than words in clashing ink. Young adults showed little measurable change between those conditions.

The at-risk participants were slowest of all on the conflicting word trials.

They were also slower than healthy older adults on the arrows overall, so the lack of an extra delay from mismatched arrows wasn’t evidence of better performance.

Answers to the word task weren’t clearly less accurate when the ink clashed.

That’s something an accuracy score alone could miss: people could still choose correctly, while needing more time to do it.

The researchers suggested that ignoring the ink took extra effort.

Age can make it harder to keep unwanted information out, and memory and thinking problems may add to that difficulty.

Researchers tested participants once, so they couldn’t link slower answers to later memory loss or MCI. The at-risk group included only 20 people, none with a confirmed MCI diagnosis.

The reasons for the delays remain unclear, and the lab tasks may not reflect everyday memory.

Larger studies following people over time, including adults with diagnosed MCI, could help test the approach.

Professor Shahina Pardhan, who worked on the study, sees promise in measuring response times.

“These findings suggest that measuring reaction times alongside memory performance could help clinicians detect subtle cognitive changes at an earlier stage,” Pardhan said.

“As populations continue to age and dementia becomes an increasing public health challenge, there is a growing need for sensitive, accessible tools that can identify people at greater risk before symptoms become more severe.”

The full study was published in the journal Brain Sciences.

#6422. Earwax’s surprisingly slippery but sticky properties deters insects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Earwax is anything but waxy and may help protect the ear against insect intrusions

This fire ant is struggling to walk on a clump of earwax, a substance that experts think may exist in part to help keep our ears free of insects.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

There are few things more annoying than having a bug fly into your ear. But the body is prepared to fend off these insect invasions, says David Hu, a bioengineer at Georgia Tech.

The goop inside our ears may act as a natural insect repellent, Hu’s team reports 28 October in Soft Matter. What we call earwax is not really waxy at all. Instead, the brownish substance absorbs water, a property that might help it regulate moisture in the ear and keep bugs out, the new analysis shows. “[This] familiar biological material may represent a sophisticated physical defense against small arthropods,” says Stanislav Gorb, a functional morphologist at the University of Kiel in Germany, who was not involved with the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have not studied earwax as much as other body fluids, such as snot, spit or even pee. “It’s a big mystery why we even have [it] in our ears,” Hu says. It can frankly seem like a nuisance. Earwax can build up, clogging earbuds and hearing aids and interfering with hearing, so understanding this substance better may help resolve those problems.

Hu and colleagues analyzed the mechanical and chemical properties of 36 earwax samples from pigs, sheep, dogs, cows, rabbits and humans. They also observed how fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) reacted to both natural and synthetic earwax.

Even though ants seem able to scale kitchen cabinets with ease to invade countertops, they flounder when they attempt to climb earwax. Hu thinks the earwax sucks moisture from the ants’ feet that helps them grip. But earwax also sticks to ants’ bodies, causing the insects to start grooming incessantly trying to get rid of it. “It’s both sticky and slippery,” Hu says.

The chemical analyses provide some clues about the origins of these properties. Dead skin cells make up 60 percent of earwax, along with a smattering of oils and moisture. The earwax contains pores that Hu believes may be shaped like ink bottles to help it absorb twice its weight in water and prevent water from sloshing around in the ear canal. Like snot, earwax has a huge range of consistencies.

Under normal conditions, earwax becomes dry and crumbly in about 10 weeks. As it dries, it’s moved outward by a layer of cells lining the ear canal that act as a cleaning conveyor belt. In this way, the ear maintains just the right thickness of earwax to keep insects at bay, Hu says. “It’s most potent when it’s thin,” he explains. “Too much, and the ants can use their tiny claws to grab hold and climb in.”

Hu admits there’s no practical way to turn earwax into a commercial insect repellent. Each person has a volume of earwax about equivalent to that of a grain of rice in each ear at any given time, says Hu, so even if you add up all the earwax on Earth, “it’s a pretty rare substance.” But, he adds, companies “are trying to come up with biodegradable and biofriendly ways to deal with insects.” And, says Gorb, perhaps earwax “could inspire a new generation of physical, nontoxic pest control surfaces,” that could provide coatings for protecting stored food, agricultural products and technology.

#6420. AI can copy how people write online, but one thing still gives it away

Nine AI models learned the shape of online replies in a new test, but AI-generated text still gave itself away through emotion and tone.

Ask a chatbot to write a reply to a post the way a regular person would, and the result usually reads fine. That is the problem. A reply can sound natural to a human reader and still be nothing like what a real person would have written.

A computer program, however, told the two apart 70 to 80 percent of the time.

Nicolò Pagan of the University of Zurich and Petter Törnberg of the University of Amsterdam ran that test on nine AI language models. The raw material was real conversations from X, Bluesky, and Reddit.

The models learned the shape of online talk well enough. What they couldn’t fake was the feeling behind it, and the harder the team pushed them to sound human, the less they said what the human had actually said.

The stakes go beyond spotting bots. Social scientists have started using these models as stand-ins for people, simulating how crowds might react to a news feed or a policy.

The study asks whether the stand-ins behave like the people they replace.

The team collected replies that real users had posted to real messages. The sample held 275 users on X, 492 on Reddit’s politics forum, and 59 groups of similar accounts on Bluesky, with 20 replies each.

Then they asked each AI model to write its own reply to the same original message, in the style of the same user.

A separate program was trained to look at a reply and guess whether a person or a model wrote it. If the AI replies were indistinguishable from the human ones, that guess would be right about half the time, no better than a coin toss.

The nine models came from six families, including Llama, Mistral, Gemma, and DeepSeek. Most were small by today’s standards, and one, Llama 3.1 70B, was far larger.

All were open-weight models that researchers can run on their own computers, so the biggest commercial chatbots, such as ChatGPT, were not tested.

Christopher Bail of Duke University and Christopher Barrie of New York University and the University of Oxford were co-authors on the research publication.

The standard setup feeds the model a written description of the user’s personality and interests. With that alone, the detector was right at least 87 percent of the time for every model on every platform.

The clearest tells were how long the replies ran, how long the words were, and how toxic the language was. The models wrote longer replies than people did, and the versions tuned to be helpful assistants produced less hostile language than real users.

Several models also stuffed replies with hashtags and mentions that real users almost never used.

On the emotional side, the replies differed from human ones in categories such as positive emotion, negative emotion, and the language of speaking and communicating.

In an interview with Earth.com, Törnberg said the most surprising part was how stubborn those gaps were. “What surprised me most was how persistent the differences were,” he said.

“So in a sense, the models can become quite good at reproducing the form of online conversation, but less so with its feeling.”

The team tried five ways of coaching the models, each one adding to the last.

These were a bare prompt, a prompt with a persona description, ten examples of the user’s past replies, relevant snippets pulled from the user’s history and, finally, retraining the model itself on the user’s writing.

The persona description, which is how most researchers currently do this, made little difference and sometimes made the replies easier to spot. Retraining was unpredictable, and for several models it made detection easier.

The two simplest moves worked best. Showing the model ten real examples cut the detector’s accuracy between about 2 and 10 percent. Adding the user’s past context cut another 2 to 3 percent.

Even the best combinations left the detector right 70 to 80 percent of the time. The bigger model was no better at passing than the small ones, and models tuned to be helpful assistants were generally worse than their raw counterparts.

“I would not assume that newer models will necessarily be better models of human behavior,” Törnberg told Earth.com. He said the training that makes a model helpful and well behaved may be the same training that makes its language less like real human communication.

The study’s second measure asked whether the AI-generated text meant the same thing as the reply the human actually wrote. The team scored that by converting both replies into numbers that capture meaning and comparing them.

The coaching that made replies harder to detect also moved them slightly further from the human reply’s meaning on every platform. The models were learning to write like a person in general, not to say what that person would say.

Next, each model wrote 20 candidate replies, and the team picked one in two ways. Choosing the reply that best matched the human’s meaning roughly doubled the similarity score but did not reliably make the reply harder to detect.

Choosing the reply most likely to fool the detector trimmed its accuracy by 5 to 10 points but left the meaning no closer. The two methods picked the same reply only 5 to 10 percent of the time, about what chance would give.

Asked by Earth.com what else stood out, Törnberg pointed to that trade-off. The team could make replies harder to tell from human writing, he said, but doing so often made them less similar in meaning to what the real person wrote.

Every message in the dataset had only one real human reply, so the meaning score measured closeness to that one reply, not whether the AI’s reply was a reasonable one.

On X, the comparison between two humans answering the same post rested on only 18 pairs, which the authors treated as exploratory.

The models also saw less of each conversation than the human replying had seen. And the detector was more likely to flag a real person as a bot than to miss a bot.

Whether future models close the gap is an open question, the authors wrote, and their test is built to keep asking it. Even a model that passed every statistical check, they added, would not necessarily hold the attitudes behind a human reply.

Törnberg said the fix for researchers is to validate a simulation against real human behavior in the specific setting being studied, rather than trust that it sounds right.

And getting the feeling right, the authors wrote, may take new training goals that target emotional expression directly instead of copying style.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Julie Elie, an ethologist at the University of California, Berkeley, tells Live Science's Kenna Hughes-Castleberry about using AI to decode the vocalizations of zebra finches.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Bird calls are far more than pleasant sounds in nature. They are complex forms of communication that can reveal how birds think, learn, cooperate and respond to their surroundings. From intricate songs used to attract mates to alarm calls that warn others of danger, vocalizations offer valuable clues about avian intelligence and social organization.

Julie Elie is an animal behavior researcher and associate project scientist at the University of California, Berkeley. She recently won the 2026 Coller Dolittle Challenge for Two-Way Interspecies Communication for her work in studying and deciphering zebra finch communication.

For more than a decade, Elie observed the social behavior of birds, recording thousands of sounds and using machine learning combined with behavioral experiments to decode specific calls.

In this interview, Elie discusses how zebra finches learn and use vocalizations, what their calls reveal about intelligence and social relationships and how artificial intelligence (AI) contributed to decoding birdsong.

Dr Julie Elie is a computational neuroethologist who studies how social animals communicate. Her research combines behavioral experiments, neuroscience, and computational tools to reveal how animals produce communication sounds, what information they transmit in their vocalizations and how they perceive the meaning of vocalizations.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry: What made you study birds and birdsong?

Julie Elie: The beginning of my work with birds dates from my Ph.D. I've always been super interested in animal behavior in general. But I think as a young person, I was more attracted by animals that we relate more easily to, which are mammals, right? Dogs, cats, horses.

I wanted to do a Ph.D. on animal behavior and, more specifically, on relationships between animals. I was interested in how animals interact with each other and what kind of social organization they establish.

[Someone suggested I] work on the zebra finch, and I said, "OK, I've never taken the time to really observe birds very well; might as well start now."

I realized that it's difficult to observe birds because they're not close to you. They can fly wherever they want. When you are out and about in town, in the countryside, and you see birds, they're here, and then they're gone. You don't get to see a lot of their vocal interactions or a lot of their social interactions.

So here I was, studying the zebra finch in cages where they were fully interacting with each other. And the question was, what kind of social organization do they have?

I realized quickly that they were not doing a dominance hierarchy [which was previously thought to be the case], but instead, the most important thing in their life was their partner. They were doing pair bonds, and that's the core of their social organization, [with] males and females pairing for life.

Studying birdsong can help researchers like Elie better understand how the birds navigate their complex environments.

KHC: Why is it important to study birdsong, and what can it teach us about intelligence and behavior?

JE: A level of complexity we were trying to understand was, what are the neural mechanisms that enable those birds to do this process of listening to something and copying it, and reproducing it, and doing a comparison between what they're producing and what they're hearing?

The zebra finch is a just-right middle ground level of cognitive ability that is interesting, where you see this pattern of copying vocalization and producing it. But you can look through the avian kingdom, and some species show more complex behaviors.

We know that there are some species that are able to not only imitate their own vocalizations from their own species, their dad, but they're able to copy other species. So, here in California, for instance, a mockingbird is a bird that is really known to be able to reproduce a bunch of different sounds and is actually incorporating this in their vocalizations.

Parrots are also well known for that because we have them as pets, and they're able to reproduce our own vocalizations as humans. This is kind of crazy, when you think about it, because they don't have the same vocal tract as we do. It's smaller, and they have a different system. I think a high cognitive level is when an animal is able to reproduce a sound that is not in their "native language," let's say, and use it for a goal. We do see this in parrots ‪—‬ they're able to ask you for something or even ask the dog to shut up sometimes, which is interesting. They're able to really use those vocalizations, such as "This is not mine, but I communicate with another species this way."

It shows you how smart they can be, and by studying vocal communication in animals, we are getting a window of what cognitive abilities they have and how the usage reveals their level of smartness.

KHC: Could you walk me through how you ended up decoding bird vocalizations?

JE: I spent countless hours observing zebra finches, and I realized that I could progressively do a match between the social context and the acoustic characteristics of the sound produced. I could recognize these sounds and understand what they "mean."

It's like at home with your cat or dog: Within a couple of months, you figure out every time the cat is doing this kind of sound —‬ "meow" — ‬it means he wants to get out or he's hungry, or he wants to cuddle. Same thing with the dog. It's the same process, but instead of doing this with cats or dogs, I did this with birds and constituted the first acoustic dictionary of zebra finch calls.

However, how do you know you are correct? That you correctly identified the sounds that correspond to the "words" in that species?

Pet owners can often differentiate between different vocalizations in their pets, such as different meowing noises for their cat.

I thought that the best confirmation of whether I was right or not could only come from the zebra finches themselves. Up to now, nobody had found a way to systematically go through the vocal repertoire of an animal and confirm if each identified call type was indeed perceived as a word in that species' language.

To achieve this somewhat impossible discussion with a bird, we designed an operant conditioning experiment where the bird is asked to classify vocalizations that were previously recorded from other zebra finches. The game is simple and relies on two rules. The first one is that every day, only the recordings corresponding to one call type are rewarded by seeds, while the recordings from the other call types in the repertoire are not rewarded. The second rule is that the bird can interrupt recordings and skip to the next one whenever they want, like how you skip through songs on your favorite music app.

The bird is placed in a cage that has a button or a little infrared sensor that it can activate with its beak. Each time it does so, the recording of a vocalization randomly drawn from the library of call types is played. Four out of five times, birds trigger the playback of a call type that will not give them access to seeds. Because they are slightly food deprived, they only really want to listen to the rewarded playback, so they interrupt the nonrewarded calls and only listen for the calls that are going to be rewarded.

Every day, the bird has to find out which call type or "word" is rewarded. They usually figure it out pretty rapidly and then start interrupting the playback of all the other call types. Using this task, we could test a different call type every dayIf they had not been able to do it, it would tell us that the call type we had identified was in fact not existing in their language. If they were able to do it ‪—‬ and spoiler alert, they were! ‪—‬ it meant that we had correctly identified that call type.

The birds told us yes, basically —‬ the organization that you're proposing is correct.

But then we made a surprising discovery. We noticed that birds were making some rare and systematic mistakes. We wondered if these mistakes were coming from the acoustic similarity of the call types — how you might mistake, for instance, the word "glove" for "love" or "hurt" for "heart." Or if they were coming from the semantic similarity of the call types — you could maybe mistake "love" for "heart" if you are remembering about the general meaning of the rewarded word today, which is "love.".

In that last case, it would mean that birds truly have an understanding of their call types' meaning. We found out that birds' errors could be better explained by the meaning [the semantic similarity] of the call types. That is a big discovery in the field of animal communication.

I'm thinking that the first species we might be able to communicate with, interact with vocally, might be a bird.

KHC: Do you think we are headed toward actually being able to communicate with birds, or do you think it's more that we're still testing the waters and we still need to learn the rest of the language before we get there?

JE: When we say "talking with birds," I think we need to understand that it's not going to be a language. Right now, I am studying the zebra finch; it doesn't mean that I would be able to communicate with a crow once I have a repertoire. So there's this component of when we talk about birds, there are many different species.

I think there's more traction in this particular part of the animal kingdom than in other parts, just because birds are really talkative. Birds use a lot of their vocalizations to communicate with each other. So because of that, I'm thinking that the first species we might be able to communicate with, interact with vocally, might be a bird, just because they are very talkative.

For now, I found all those words. But we need to understand how those words are [strung] together. So it's not necessarily the case that we need to understand the rules of the dynamic exchanges between individuals or how fast you're responding, but how you are responding and whether that makes sense or not.

They [also] have [body] postures. They have specific displays at the same time they're producing the vocalizations. And if we really want to achieve full communication with another species, we need to get to that level.

It's not tomorrow for sure, it's probably not next year, but I think in the range of 10 years we should get there. Especially with how fast the domains of AI and robotics are. I have some hope that we should be able to get to that point.

KHC: Is there one takeaway you would want our readers to know about your work?

JE: Just one. The most important thing for readers that are not specifically scientists is to realize that, by studying animal behavior more generally, researchers are discovering the intelligence of animals. This is opening our eyes to other species and realizing that we're not the only species that is intelligent on this planet.

This is a lesson to us as another species on this planet, that we are not the only ones that are smart and we need to take this into account in how we are evolving.

We need to realize how we're affecting them and realize that they also have their own internal lives, and maybe we should start to respect them a little bit more.

Editor's note: Some of this interview was conducted via email as part of a follow-up conversation. The interview has been edited lightly for clarity and length.

#6418. When AI does the work, what happens to our skills?

Relying on AI may quietly erode professional skills, a new paper argues, calling for shared safeguards to preserve human expertise.

Letting an AI tool draft a report or read a scan feels like getting help.

But handing over those tasks may gradually weaken the skills needed to do them independently, and people may struggle to notice the change.

Kaisa Kärki of the University of Helsinki makes the case in a new paper on what researchers call deskilling.

The word covers both losing a human skill and never developing it, because the task has been handed to artificial intelligence.

Her conclusion is that professions, not professionals, should decide which skills stay in human hands.

The paper is an argument built on published studies, not a new experiment, and it draws most of its evidence from medicine.

Most human skills need regular use to survive, Kärki wrote, citing what psychologists call the “use it or lose it” principle.

In one study of surgeons she cites, every skill measured decayed after a long break, and complex tasks done by novices suffered most, while heavily practiced skills held up best.

AI changes what counts as a break. A professional who does a task with an AI assistant doesn’t think of herself as having stopped doing it, Kärki noted.

So the skill can decay while the job appears to go on as before.

The same goes for skills never learned. In a programming study she cites, people learned far more without AI help because they had to find and fix their own errors.

In medicine, trainees may lose chances to learn when the tool does the hard part, and people can struggle when it is taken away.

People are poor judges of their own abilities, Kärki wrote.

Across many studies, self-ratings line up only moderately with measured ability, and most people rate themselves generously.

So professionals may not reliably recognize when their skills are fading.

The studies reviewed by Kärki suggest that experienced professionals are also vulnerable.

Very experienced radiologists reading mammograms showed deskilling, though far less than inexperienced ones.

After endoscopists began using AI, their colonoscopies performed without it detected adenomas – potentially precancerous polyps – in 22.4% of patients, down from 28.4% before AI was introduced.

Accountants who had worked for more than a decade without AI tools showed heavy skill loss once they had them.

“One of the problems with deskilling is that professionals have difficulty noticing it in their everyday lives, partly due to biases about AI reliance,” Kärki said.

“When we converse with large language models and they respond convincingly, it easily leads to overreliance. However, these models also make mistakes.”

Doctors are not oblivious. In a survey Kärki cites, 74% of physicians said they worried about their own deskilling.

Worry is not measurement, though, and the loss usually shows up only when the tool is switched off.

Kärki’s central point is about responsibility.

Philosophers have generally held that people answer for what they do knowingly. A bias you can’t see in yourself doesn’t fit that picture.

“The inconspicuous biases associated with AI use pose something of a challenge to these viewpoints: after all, we don’t notice our own biases or, say, tendency to rely too much on AI,” she said.

“It’s therefore unclear whether we can be held responsible for the insidious deterioration of our skills and the mistakes that will result.”

The mistakes can be serious. In one test she cites, the best large language models answered 85% of cancer-care questions correctly.

More than 80% of the wrong answers carried a high chance of moderate to severe harm.

In Kärki’s view, holding individual doctors responsible may overlook the wider changes in training and practice that contribute to skill loss.

If a whole field relies on AI, Kärki wrote, the field can lose the ability to teach its own basics, a problem earlier authors called the fragility of the system.

No single surgeon knows how many other surgeons are relying on a robot for the same step. A professional body can find out.

So the first job, in her view, belongs to professional communities. They should decide, from inside the field, which skills are core and which tasks should stay at least partly in human hands.

After that come the tools, such as regular skill checks, stretches of training with no AI, and making the human decision before looking at the AI’s answer.

Pilots already train for autopilot failure and log manual flying time, she wrote.

The European Union’s AI Act recognizes that people over-trust automated systems, but Kärki pointed out that it says nothing about the skill loss that follows.

“In medical education, it has already been argued that training in basic skills should include a stage where AI is not used,” she said.

“For instance, diagnostic reasoning is a skill central to medical practice, as is general understanding of the field and the associated tasks.”

Deskilling is hard to measure, Kärki noted. It builds gradually and may become apparent when the AI is removed, and its effects on judgment and critical thinking are hard to count.

Most of the evidence comes from medicine, and Kärki wrote that other fields need the same scrutiny, along with studies that follow the same professionals for years.

Nor is it settled which skills are safe to hand over and which are not, or whether a professional who lets a skill lapse is ever to blame.

According to Kärki, those are the next questions for philosophers, but regulators should not wait for the answers.

“Deskilling involves major risks that humanity and professions should pre-emptively consider before skills decay at the community level,” she said.

Until professions draw those lines, each worker is left to notice a loss that the research says is hard to notice alone.

The full study was published in the journal Human Affairs.

#6417. Our Universe Is Held Together by Invisible Galactic Glue—And We Wouldn’t Exist Without It

Its transformative emergence might have occurred within the very first seconds of time, physicists say.

Dark matter isn’t like other matter. It doesn’t interact with visible light or any other electromagnetic force. And yet, it seems to push around regular matter through its gravitational influence. Dark matter rules the universe, maybe holding galaxies together, but we still don’t know what it is.

A battery of cosmological probes has revealed clues to the presence—and influence—of dark matter in the universe: Stars orbit galactic centers far too quickly. Galaxies zip around clusters with excessive velocities. Massive objects bend the light passing by them with more gravitational force than we can account for with visible observations. And the history of the universe has revealed the incredibly speedy growth of gigantic structures.

The conclusion is that there’s something more to the universe than our traditional electromagnetic measurements can detect. Yet this thing simply doesn’t emit or absorb light. What could it be?

What we know is that it’s cold, heavy, and slow. Yet, new research suggests that it may have once been the complete opposite: hot, light, fast … and insignificant.

How do you turn dark matter from zero to hero? The answer lies in the strange and wonderful physics of superconductivity, which lets electricity flow with zero resistance. In a new paper, theoretical physicists Guanming Liang and Robert Caldwell from Dartmouth College outline a hypothetical scenario for flooding the universe with dark matter when it was mere seconds old.

For decades, cosmologists have been following one particular compelling idea to explain dark matter, known as WIMPs, for weakly interacting massive particles. These are hypothetical particles that only interact with the rest of the universe through gravity and the weak nuclear force (which rules subatomic particles’ behavior). But searches for WIMPs have so far come up empty.

To fill the gaps, theorists have been busy, generating dozens of new theories every year to unravel the mystery of dark matter. The vast majority of these ideas come from the land of high-energy physics, invoking this-or-that exotic process or super-theoretical particle that we might see someday in a collider. These massive machines smash high-energy subatomic particles together in the search for new particles.

But Liang and Caldwell took a different tack, turning instead toward condensed matter physics. This branch of physics makes major breakthroughs all the time, but without as much public fanfare as the high-energy work.

At a fundamental level, condensed matter physics is the study of stuff. It gives us an understanding of how everyday things work on subatomic levels—from why glass is transparent to how heat flows through new materials. And it’s also the study of everyday materials under extreme conditions, which leads to completely counterintuitive behaviors.

For example, take electrical resistance. Electrons flowing down a wire bump into each other, which saps energy out. This is why we can’t, for instance, have solar arrays in the desert that can pipe their electricity all around the country.

But if you cool some materials down to nearly absolute zero, the electrons bind up together in a new state of matter. And when they do that, all the resistance disappears, and electricity can flow uninterrupted. This is known as superconductivity, and it’s through superconductors that we’re able to harness tremendously large currents to drive technologies like MRI machines and maglev (magnetic levitation) trains.

In Liang and Caldwell’s model, dark matter starts out as a hot soup of fast-moving, massless particles in the extremely early universe. But as the universe expands and cools off, the dark matter particles pair together, the way electrons do in a superconductor. When they do that, the dark matter particles undergo a radical transformation, emerging on the other side with a brand-new set of properties. The pairs become slow-moving, heavy—and dark.

However, the model revealed an unusual quirk: that if the dark matter particles start out with even a tiny bit of mass, then not all of them bind up together as pairs. Most of them stay in the background, where they soak up all of spacetime. This behavior might provide an explanation for another mysterious ingredient in the cosmos, dark energy, which is responsible for causing the accelerated expansion of the universe.

So far Liang and Caldwell’s idea is just that: a guess as to how the universe might actually work. But it’s a testable one. The properties of these paired-up dark matter particles may leave behind a subtle signature in the appearance of the cosmic microwave background. That’s the light left over from when the universe cooled from a plasma to a neutral state, when it was around 380,000 years old.

To be fair, the idea is probably wrong. But that’s okay. We have no idea what dark matter is, and we need to flex every analytical and creative muscle we have to solve a puzzle that spans the entire universe. And we need to draw from as many sources of inspiration as possible, whether it’s high-energy physics, condensed matter physics—or even something else.

We never know when we’re going to be right. It’s only by searching in the dark that we’ll find out.

Paul M. Sutter is a science educator and a cosmologist at Johns Hopkins University and the author of How to Die in Space: A Journey Through Dangerous Astrophysical Phenomena and Your Place in the Universe: Understanding Our Big, Messy Existence. #6416. Even remote wildlife can’t escape microplastics in their blood

Scientists found microplastics in the blood of wild tapirs and giant anteaters in Brazil, including animals living far from human development.

As the afternoon sun began to fade over Brazil’s countryside, a team of researchers drove along dusty dirt roads searching for giant anteaters.

Two spotters rode in the back of the truck, scanning the landscape for signs of movement. When they spotted an anteater, the team approached on foot with two long-handled nets.

Capturing the animal usually took about a minute, but the information gathered would help answer a much bigger question: How far has plastic pollution spread into the natural world?

The researchers were investigating whether wild animals living closer to human activity had more microplastics in their blood.

Their findings revealed a clear connection between human disturbance and plastic exposure.

But one discovery was particularly concerning.

Even in Brazil’s remote Pantanal, the world’s largest tropical wetland, every animal sampled had microplastics in its blood, despite living more than 40 miles (65 kilometers) from the nearest development.

The results suggest that plastic pollution is reaching wildlife even in places that appear largely untouched by humans.

Scientists had widely assumed a connection between human activity and plastic in wildlife.

To test it, the researchers needed several records for the same animals, namely blood samples, GPS movements and detailed maps of human disturbance.

Study co-author Justin Calabrese of the Center for Advanced Systems Understanding (CASUS) described the difficulty of getting all those records together.

“Such integrated datasets simply did not exist,” Calabrese said.

Marcia de Almeida Monteiro Melo Ferraz and Michael Noonan, both at the University of British Columbia Okanagan, conceived the study.

Teams from two long-running conservation programs in Brazil did the fieldwork.

From February 2021 to November 2022, those teams collected blood from 26 lowland tapirs and 21 giant anteaters.

The animals lived at a soy farm on the Amazon’s deforestation frontier, farmland in the Cerrado savanna and a cattle ranch in the Pantanal.

For the anteaters, the work took place near two federal highways, where the Anteaters and Highways Project studies collisions between vehicles and wildlife.

Each blood sample went into a glass tube, which the field team sealed with aluminum foil to prevent contamination.

To record where the animals went, adult tapirs wore GPS collars that logged an hourly position. The anteaters wore GPS trackers as well.

Once in the lab, each sample went through a chemical treatment to break down the blood. The team collected the solids left behind on a filter.

Raman spectroscopy then identified the materials from the way they scattered light from a laser.

When the team had checked all 47 blood samples, 43 contained microplastics. The particles averaged about 0.0004 inches (10 micrometers) in length.

Pieces of that size need a microscope to be seen.

Counts for individual animals ran from zero to more than 1,200 particles in a milliliter of blood. The average for all the animals was about 74, and a milliliter is roughly a fifth of a teaspoon.

For comparison, the average fell within the range already reported in human blood by other studies using spectroscopy.

The tapirs had about 99 particles per milliliter on average and the anteaters about 43. The difference between the species was not statistically significant.

GPS records provided more than 440,000 locations, allowing researchers to map the home ranges of 40 animals.

To describe the land within those areas the researchers used the Human Footprint Index.

This global map has scores running from zero for undisturbed land up to 50 for the most heavily modified.

An animal did not need to live across uniformly disturbed land for a link to appear.

The team found more particles in blood when the most heavily modified spot in an animal’s range had a higher footprint score.

Average footprint scores across entire home ranges were not significantly associated with microplastic levels.

The distance comparisons also pointed to less plastic in animals living farther from development, which here meant urban areas, mines and power plants.

The same was true of animals living farther from waste management facilities.

Calabrese said the paper “is the first to demonstrate this linkage for terrestrial mammals,” meaning mammals that live on land.

The researchers also checked how much the highest values influenced the findings. They ran each test again without the animals making up the top 10% for that measure.

For the distance tests, that meant leaving out the animals living farthest away.

After that check the footprint link remained, while neither distance link was still statistically significant.

Animals with more farmland in their home ranges did not have higher microplastic levels in their blood.

The authors suggested that farmland may add less direct exposure to microplastics than other kinds of human disturbance.

The types of plastic offered another comparison between sites, with differences the authors described as consistent with local land use.

Animals at the Amazon farm carried more polyamide, the main material in fishing nets and ropes, than animals on Cerrado farmland.

The Cerrado animals had more PVC, a material used in irrigation pipes, than animals in the Pantanal.

The authors described the site comparisons as case studies, with uneven numbers of animals at each site.

For the animals at the cattle ranch in the Pantanal, the distance from the nearest waste facility was about 70 miles (112 kilometers). Each of them still carried microplastics in its blood.

The researchers also obtained a value of about 10 particles per milliliter of blood from their model for land with a footprint score of zero.

The authors suggested that the value may partly reflect limitations of the model.

Even so, they wrote that direct contact with land changed by people was unlikely to be the only route into wildlife.

The authors identified wind and water as likely routes carrying microplastics into remote habitats. Cities, industry and farms supply airborne microplastics that may settle far away.

Runoff, rivers and seasonal floods provide ways for particles to move far from their sources as well.

Microplastics in the water and sediment of the Pantanal were already known from previous studies.

The highest measurements in those studies came from places near rivers flowing out of urban areas.

This observational study found associations between human disturbance and microplastic levels in blood, but it cannot establish cause and effect.

The researchers had a single blood sample from each animal. Their method could not identify particles smaller than about 0.00004 inches (one micrometer).

Future studies could collect blood, soil and water samples from the same locations to help trace the particles’ sources.

The team did not collect those environmental samples and could not yet match the plastic in blood to its source.

The measurements also concern the amount of plastic, without examining its effects on the health of these wild animals. Laboratory experiments have shown that microplastics can harm animals.

For the years 2001 to 2020, the increase in Brazil’s average footprint score was 42%, whereas the worldwide increase was 26%.

Thus, as land development continues, the authors suggested that the plastic levels in land animals would continue to increase.

They described keeping wildlife farther from development and waste facilities as a possible way to lower the amount the animals carry.

The study is published in the journal Nature.

#6415. Little Ice Age cooling in Europe may have raised the risk of rickets

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Skeletal remains with signs of vitamin D deficiencies hint at how climate change impacted health

A volcano-fueled chilly climate during the 18th and 19th centuries may have made winter in England so bad, as depicted in this 19th century painting of a man collecting wood, that it raised the risk of kids getting rickets, a condition caused by vitamin D deficiency.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

England isn’t renowned for its weather. But just a few centuries ago, climate change–fueled conditions may have been so bad that they put children’s health at risk.

Calcium mineralization in the teeth and skeletons of people who lived in rural northern England suggests that children growing up during the height of the Little Ice Age routinely developed vitamin D deficiencies, researchers report November 5 in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. In the worst cases, these deficiencies developed into rickets, a bone disorder that can occur when people don’t get enough ultraviolet light.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Previous skeletal studies suggest that rickets became more common among Europeans during the 18th and 19th centuries. One culprit may have been the Industrial Revolution, when many Europeans lived in UV-poor polluted cities and often worked indoors. The unusually cold climate may have added “an extra layer of difficulty” to getting enough sunlight, says Ellen Kendall, a bioarcheologist at Durham University in England

The Little Ice Age was a period of global cooling from the 13th to 19th centuries caused by extreme solar cycles and a series of volcanic eruptions, which can cool the planet by ejecting aerosols into the atmosphere that block sunlight. In the last 200 years of the era, 18 major eruptions helped spur a temperature drop of 2 to 3 degrees Celsius over northern Europe.

Kendall and colleagues wondered how this cold climate affected health. They examined calcium deposition — how the essential mineral is incorporated into bones — in the remains of 21 people buried from 1711 to 1829 in the town of North Shields. Calcium often doesn’t fully mineralize in people with vitamin D delicacies, leaving voids in teeth as they grow.

The team found bands of failed calcium mineralization in the teeth, suggesting seasonal spates of vitamin D deficiencies. Some skeletons also showed signs of rickets. North Shields was a small rural town that hadn’t yet undergone industrialization, so these deficiencies probably weren’t due to bad air conditions.

The unusually cold weather may have changed people’s behavior during the winter, Kendall says. Residents may have kept their kids indoors or bundled them up so that little skin was exposed when they did go outside, preventing them from getting enough UV light, she says.

However, climate was still just one factor among many — including gender roles, diet and pollution — that shaped vitamin D deficiencies at the time, says Kendall. “Humans are very messy to study,” she says. “That’s one of the things that makes them so very fascinating.”

#6414. ZWO Seestar S30 Plus review

We tested the brand-new ZWO Seestar S30 Plus, an all-in-one smart telescope for beginners and hobbyists that makes astrophotography accessible to everyone.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There's much to enjoy about the Seestar S30 Plus. The image quality is great, it's easy to use, and it's compact and lightweight enough to take it anywhere. It's not quite as good as the more expensive S30 Pro, but it's a nice middle-ground option between the S30 and the S30 Pro that gives you a lot of features for the money.

Seestar app is reliable and easy to navigate

All-in-one workflow from shooting to sharing

2K image quality is better than we expected

Editing controls could be a little more responsive

Not suitable for smaller planetary nebulas

Why you can trust Live Science Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best ones for you. Find out more about how we test.

ZWO has just released the newest member of its smart telescope range: the Seestar S30 Plus. This all-in-one smart telescope is designed for beginners and hobbyists who want an affordable way into astrophotography that won't leave you scratching your head, and lets you capture, process and share your images in one simple workflow. It sits between the Seestar S30 and S30 Pro, and is priced at $499 for its release.

With 2K image quality, a light pollution filter and a user-friendly interface, it's a smart telescope that anyone can enjoy, regardless of your experience level, and regardless of whether you're shooting from your city balcony or a dark sky site. Like the other models, it uses dual cameras to capture a wide range of subjects, including deep-sky objects with the telephoto camera, and constellations, star trails and the Milky Way with the wide-angle camera. It's lightweight and easy to travel with, and it even comes with a separate solar filter for solar imaging and eclipse time-lapses.

We got our hands on an advance copy to test ahead of its release, so we put it through its paces on several different celestial subjects.

The Seestar S30 Plus is one of the smallest, most compact smart telescopes on the market, weighing just 3.63 pounds (1.65 kg) and measuring 8.3 x 5.5 x 3.2 inches (210 x 140 x 80 mm). Its sleek, matte white design looks identical to the other Seestar models (we compared it to our S30 Pro), except for the branding on the unit itself.

It comes in a padded soft carry case and includes a small tripod (although we always prefer to use our own), a solar filter, a 40-inch (1 meter) USB-A to USB-C charging cable, a removable shoulder strap for the carry case, and a quick-start guide. With its accessories and case, the whole setup weighs 4.89 pounds (2.22 kg).

On the unit itself, you'll find just one button, which powers it on, plus the USB-C port on the side. Super simple, although we'd have liked the USB-C port to be covered to prevent moisture or dust from getting in.

It comes with a carry case, strap, USB-C cable and solar filter.

The set-up process couldn't be easier. When you turn the telescope on, you'll hear a double beep and see the power button light up alongside the red dots on the black screen to indicate the battery level. Four dots mean the battery is full. The telescope will tell you when it's ready to connect, at which point you can sync it up to the app on your smartphone or tablet. To turn it off, you just select "Shutdown" in the app, which closes the arm and turns the unit off.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

It also features an anti-dew heater, which we've found works quite well in mild to moderate humidity. On a couple of our shoots, we noticed a tiny bit of condensation forming on the unit when the humidity was higher, so we wouldn't feel confident leaving it unsupervised for long periods on a particularly dewy evening. (We used the Clear Outside app to monitor the humidity levels.)

The Seestar App is user-friendly and easy to navigate, with just the right amount of controls: you have plenty of options to choose from but it doesn’t become overwhelming. The main Seestar page is where you'll likely spend most of your time, as this is where you can search for celestial objects to shoot, access your album, plan a shoot and read up on what objects Seestar recommends based on your time and location.

The Stargazing section is where you can select or search for the subject you want to shoot. You can use the search function to find a specific target or browse Tonight's Best, and you can also search through different types of subjects like galaxies, nebulas, clusters and more. From here, you can also select planets, track comets and photograph constellations using the wide camera.

Click on a subject and the app will display information about it, including its current altitude and coordinates, which help determine what time is best to shoot that particular object. It automatically applies the appropriate filters and settings, but you can override these if you want to.

There's very little to complain about when it comes to using the app. It has lots of information for beginners, so you don't need a ton of knowledge about the night sky, and everything is fairly self-explanatory. There were a couple of occasions when it failed to calibrate itself (for example, when we tried to locate the Pleiades, which had just risen above a tree), and other times when we chose a new target and it slewed the long way round instead of only having to move slightly. But otherwise, the app worked well.

The AI Enhance section has some good editing tools to bring out the best from your photos. You can reduce the stars, adjust the brightness, contrast, saturation and RGB curves, apply denoise and eliminate any satellite trails — although we'd love a dehaze slider to bring out some of the fainter nebulosity of certain objects. The sliders could do with being a little more responsive, especially the RGB curves, but overall, it does a pretty good job of editing your pictures to get a pleasing result.

We had about 10 days to test our review unit before its release, so we could only capture as much as the weather permitted in that time. We'll add more images to this review over the coming weeks. All our tests were conducted from our backyard in a Bortle 4 region, and captured before moonrise to eliminate as much light pollution as possible. Due to these time constraints, we aimed to capture our images for a total of 60 minutes each, although we'd have ideally aimed for longer in some cases.

Now for the fun part — the images. The Seestar S30 Plus has a focal length of 160mm, which is advantageous for capturing large subjects like the Andromeda Galaxy, the North America Nebula and the Pleiades. Large emission nebulas are where it really shines; however, the focal length is too short to capture smaller apparent objects.

For this review, we aimed to capture as many different types of objects as possible. All our images were edited in the Seestar app with, in some cases, a few minor tweaks in Lightroom. You also have the option to download the individual files to your computer to process them yourself in dedicated astrophotography software, which is advantageous if you're a more experienced user.

Everyone's favorite star cluster, the Pleiades, was one of the first targets we wanted to capture. We could see the faint blue nebulosity after as little as 15 minutes of integration time, and it only improved over time. After 60 minutes, we had a really nice image and could easily bring out the blue haze via the editing tools in the app. However, we got a much more impressive result after tweaking our image a little further in Lightroom, bringing out even more haze and reflective dust.

The Andromeda Galaxy is a perfect target for the Seestar S30 Plus. It takes up a large portion of the frame, and with long integration times, it can reveal beautiful details in the faint outer arms. We shot for around an hour in our tests due to weather and time constraints, but we still got an impressive image. As we approached 60 minutes, there was a lot of cloud cover, and we noticed it struggling to stack images toward the end of the session, so we stopped the integration at 57 minutes.

Andromeda is certainly going to be the most impressive galaxy for the Seestar visually, as most others will appear smaller in the frame and will need longer integration, so make sure you have a clear, dark night for it.

Large emission nebulas are where the Seestar S30 Plus thrives, and the North America Nebula is a great target. It covers the whole field of view, and the red hydrogen gas easily comes to the forefront of the image.

The Eastern Veil Nebula is another lovely target where you can bring out the beautiful red and turquoise hues in as little as 15 minutes, but longer integration times will yield brighter, more colorful results.

Planetary nebulas are where you will see the limitations of the Seestar's 160mm focal length. Most planetary nebulas have a very small apparent size — we've previously captured the Dumbbell Nebula and Cocoon Nebula with our S30 Pro, and they were a tiny dot in the middle of the screen. We tried the Helix Nebula, and even though it's one of the largest apparent planetary nebulas, it's still fairly small on the Seestar S30 Plus. You can still get a decent image of it, but if you want to focus on imaging planetary nebulas, you'll need a bigger scope. Because it was very low in the sky and there was some interfering cloud, we stopped integration at 27 minutes.

The Seestar S30 Plus is an affordable entry point into deep-sky astrophotography without the confusing settings and expensive setup. It's ideal for beginners, although more experienced users will likely want to upgrade to the superior image quality and extra features of the S30 Pro.

Still, for under $500, we can't complain. Not only is the Seestar S30 Plus easy to navigate and use, but it teaches you about space in a fun and interactive way, and you don't need to spend hours stacking individual frames on your computer to process — although you still can do that if you want more control over your editing.

If you can stretch your budget, the S30 Pro is a worthy upgrade. It produces 4K images and offers more pro-level features.

To see deeper into space, the Seestar S50 Pro has a longer focal length of 260mm and a larger 50mm aperture, making it better for smaller apparent objects.

If the imaging aspect doesn't interest you, the Celestron StarSense Explorer range of telescopes connects to your phone to guide you around the sky, but you observe the cosmos through an eyepiece instead of capturing it on your phone.

Her photos have been featured in a number of national magazines, including Digital Camera World and Cosmopolitan. #6413. A Massive Cave Held Sculptures From 18,000 Years Ago. It Might Be Hiding Secret Chambers, Too.

The mysterious cavities may connect to the main cave—and archaeologists are itching to finally dig in.

Southern Italy’s Apulia region gained a measure of fame in 1966, when archaeologists discovered bone figurines dating to at least 18,000 years ago tucked inside the Cave of Venuses. Now, experts believe the cave may hold new archaeological surprises after detecting what could be additional cavities, spaces that have gone unexplored and unknown for untold millennia.

According to a study published in the journal Digital Applications in Archaeology and Cultural Heritage, researchers conducted a geophysical survey at the site in Parabita, in the heel of Italy’s boot. Using ground-penetrating radar and electrical resistivity tomography, they identified a series of anomalies that they interpreted as cavities.

“The results are surprising and show different areas with the presence of cavities in the vicinity of the same cave,” the authors wrote. “Results show a probable unexplored zone of the cave.”

The cave first burst onto the archaeological scene in 1966, when experts announced the discovery of two figurines inside it. The figurines measure 3.5 inches and 2.3 inches long and were carved from either cow or horse bone. Both are classified as Venus figurines, which depict a female figure and likely celebrate pregnancy. They resemble others found throughout Europe, including the famed Venus of Willendorf in Austria. Their age of at least 18,000 years places the Italian find well within a glacial period of the Upper Paleolithic.

That discovery confirmed the presence of Paleolithic humans at the site and led to further excavations in 1968, which revealed stone tools, decorated bones, and remains from the Neolithic and the Metal Ages. Together with a burial of a man and a woman dated to around 28,000 years ago, these finds showed that people used the cave over a very long period.

Ironically, the fame of the ’66 finds indirectly led to the latest discovery. Teams from the University of Malta and the Institute of Heritage Science of Italy’s National Research Council conducted the surveys ahead of a project to turn the site into a tourist attraction. Before that project could move forward, contractors needed to know how strong the limestone was throughout the area.

To find out, the researchers used two complementary techniques. Ground-penetrating radar, which works somewhat like sonar, sends pulses of radio waves into the ground. Depending on the material the waves hit, such as solid rock or empty space, different patterns reflect back to the instrument. Electrical resistivity tomography serves a similar purpose: it sends an electrical current through the ground and measures how easily the current travels. Using the two technologies together helps researchers cross-check results and reduce false readings.

“The geophysical data confirm that there are actually a series of cavities—not known until now—that could be connected to the main cave,” the authors wrote. “The resulting model provides the necessary parameters—depth and volumes—for the design of a series of direct investigations by archaeologists.”

So far, archaeologists haven’t dug into the ground to inspect the anomalies directly, but the voids in separate areas around the known cave could be additional cave passages. However, the data could also reflect heavily fractured rock, which would be a weak point in the cave rather than a new cavity. Even that would be valuable information for crews planning the tourist attraction.

Next, experts hope to excavate and explore the previously undocumented cavities. These could connect the Cave of Venuses to additional chambers and possibly yield new evidence of southern Italy’s prehistoric past.

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. #6412. Dancing may shape how the brain responds to other people’s emotions

Ballet dancers show different brain responses to emotional faces, without identifying emotions more accurately than people without training.

Ballet dancers spend years training their bodies to move with precision.

A new study suggests that the same training is also linked to how the brain responds when a dancer sees fear or happiness on someone’s face.

When ballet dancers looked at photos of fearful, happy, and neutral faces, their brain activity differed from that of people with no dance training.

The differences appeared in brain areas that process vision and in areas that process touch.

Beatriz Calvo-Merino worked with lead author Vasiliki Meletaki and Bettina Forster at City St George’s, University of London’s Centre for Cognition and Neuroscience.

“The impact of dance expertise goes beyond movement and taps into social perception mechanisms, such as face processing and emotions,” said Calvo-Merino.

The team compared 26 professional or trainee ballet dancers with 26 people of similar age and sex who had no dance experience.

The dancers had been dancing for about 17 years on average.

Both groups judged the emotions about equally well, but their brain signals differed in timing and pattern.

Earlier brain-scanning studies, including work by Calvo-Merino, found increased activity in the brains of expert dancers when they watched familiar dance movements.

Nearly all of that research looked at how dancers perceive movement and bodies, the authors wrote.

The team used faces to test whether dancers’ brains also differ in other, everyday kinds of perception.

The test is based on an idea about emotion.

According to this idea, people perceive someone else’s emotion partly through their own body’s sense of that emotion, and not through vision alone.

Researchers describe this as an embodied view of emotion.

Earlier experiments found that the brain area receiving touch and movement signals from the body is involved when people look at emotional faces. That area is the somatosensory cortex.

Professional dancers develop a refined awareness of their own bodies through long, precise training, the authors wrote.

Dance training might also refine the body’s part in perceiving emotion, the team reasoned. If so, dancers’ brains should respond differently to emotional faces as well as to dance.

Each volunteer wore a cap fitted with 64 electrodes. The electrodes recorded the brain’s electrical activity, a method called EEG.

The faces came from a photo collection called the Karolinska Directed Emotional Faces. The team used 60 black-and-white photos, half of them male faces.

Each face stayed on screen for 600 milliseconds, a little over half a second.

In one task, a question about emotion sometimes followed a face, such as “Is s/he fearful?” In the other task, used as a comparison, the question asked whether the face was male or female.

Half of the time, a blunt-tipped device gave a brief touch to the tip of the volunteer’s left index finger.

The touch came 105 milliseconds after a face appeared, and volunteers were told to ignore it.

The touch served as a probe. The team recorded the brain’s response to a face with a touch and to a face alone, then subtracted the second recording from the first.

The subtraction helped isolate the brain’s response to touch. Differences between facial expressions could then indicate that emotional processing was influencing that response.

In the dancers, the touch response differed between fearful and neutral faces at the earliest stage the team analyzed.

That stage was about 143 to 173 milliseconds after the face appeared, less than a fifth of a second.

The response to happy faces didn’t differ from the response to neutral faces at that stage. The early effect was specific to fearful expressions, the authors wrote.

In non-dancers, the touch response didn’t differ by emotion at that first stage.

Their touch responses did differ by emotion at later stages, but at a narrower set of recording sites than in dancers.

“What is particularly interesting is that dance expertise appears to influence how the somatosensory cortex responds to emotions expressed by others,” Forster said.

“This suggests that our own bodily experiences can shape how the brain processes other people’s emotions, providing further evidence for the embodied nature of emotion perception.”

Electrodes over the visual areas at the back of the head recorded a second set of differences.

One difference appeared between about 150 and 200 milliseconds after a face came on screen. In dancers, visual responses to neutral faces differed from responses to both fearful and happy faces.

In non-dancers, visual responses at that stage were different for each of the three expressions. Those differences were also stronger on the right side of the brain, a pattern that earlier face studies have typically reported.

In dancers, the differences were spread across both sides. The authors called the two patterns distinct styles of telling emotions apart.

Both groups processed fearful faces in a distinct way. The authors linked that result to the priority the brain is known to give fear.

The authors also wrote, as an anecdote, that fear is an important tool in dance training. Dancers learn to feel comfortable performing in front of an audience, for example.

The study found no clear advantage in dancers’ ability to identify facial emotions.

During the recordings, dancers answered 94% of the emotion questions correctly. Non-dancers answered 95% of them correctly, a gap too small to rule out chance.

Dancers did score higher on a questionnaire about awareness of signals from inside the body. Their average score was 3.69, compared with 2.71 for non-dancers.

Body awareness may be part of how dancers process other people’s emotions, the authors suggested. They proposed exploring that relationship further.

Each group had 26 people, a size chosen to match earlier studies. The authors sugg that future studies should calculate in advance how many participants they need.

Scalp recordings also couldn’t show precisely where in the brain the differing touch responses arose.

The study compared the two groups at a single point in time, so it can’t show how the differences developed.

The next question is whether the brain differences are accompanied by differences in behavior.

Future studies could add behavioral tests of emotion recognition, the authors wrote.

New studies could also explore how the touch area’s response to emotion changes across stages of dance training, from advanced trainees to professional performers.

The full study was published in the journal Cerebral Cortex.

#6411. Record-low temperature created on China’s space station

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A Bose-Einstein condensate reached about 10 trillionths of a kelvin

An experiment on China's Tiangong space station (rendering shown) reached a record-low temperature in a state of matter called a Bose-Einstein condensate.

Shujianyang/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Science has reached a new low. Temperature, that is.

Scientists cooled a collection of atoms to about 10 picokelvins, or 10 trillionths of a kelvin. That’s barely a smidge above absolute zero (−273.15° Celsius). The atoms formed a Bose-Einstein condensate, a quantum state of matter, colder than any before, researchers report November 5 in Science.

To achieve that record-low chill, scientists took their work to space. The atoms orbited Earth aboard China’s Tiangong space station. There, researchers used laser-based traps to contain 20,000 rubidium atoms and reduce their motion, thereby cooling them. At an atomic level, temperature is tied to motion: Atoms and molecules in the air around us move more slowly when it’s colder. Similarly, in systems of cold atoms, scientists can define an effective temperature based on how slowly the atoms spread apart when they are allowed to expand.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

On Earth, gravitational forces cause clouds of atoms to sag, reducing the effectiveness of cooling. But on the space station, the atoms experienced microgravity, the apparent weightlessness of an object in free fall.

To make a Bose-Einstein condensate, a disorderly gaggle of atoms is cooled until the atoms all take on the same quantum state, acting as one entity. By experimenting with ultracold atoms, researchers can study exotic states of matter and other mysterious physics. And they can test fundamental concepts, such as the equivalence principle — the idea that explains why objects of different masses fall at the same rate in a vacuum.

Spacefaring Bose-Einstein condensates were previously made on the International Space Station, at effective temperatures as low as 52 picokelvins. And an experiment on Earth, in which atoms were dropped down a tower to induce weightlessness, reached 38 picokelvins. But drop tower experiments are limited by the time their free fall lasts. That’s not an issue for experiments in Earth’s orbit. So cold atoms in space are really taking off.
