#6410. A Remote Island Holds a Major Warning Sign for the Future of Humanity

A 180-year accidental experiment on a barren volcanic rock could show us how to reverse deserts—or how to break nature.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The word “terraforming” is typically reserved for discussions of other worlds. Sci-fi writers dream up vast galactic empires where humans have bent entire planetary ecosystems to their will while, in the real world, the world’s richest man contemplates a similar future. But on the remote island of Ascension in the South Atlantic, an accidental 180-year-long experiment shows what happens when you terraform our own planet. Some see the story as a small slice of hope for areas around the world facing desertification in the face of climate change, while others see the history of Ascension Island as a warning about humanity’s impact on the natural world.

Around one million years ago, volcanic eruptions along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge pushed the island up out of the Atlantic. It went unseen by humans until 1501, when Portuguese admiral João da Nova came across it. Two years later, Portuguese navigator Afonso de Albuquerque found it again on the Christian holiday of Ascension Day, which is how the island got its name. However, neither of these expeditions set up shop on the island, and it wasn’t until 1815 when Napoleon Bonaparte was exiled to St. Helena, an island located some 800 miles away, that the United Kingdom finally established a military outpost Ascension to keep tabs on him (a good idea since he’d escaped exile once before).

Some of the most colorful descriptions of Ascension come from naturalists arriving at the island in the decades following British settlement. Among these voices was a young Charles Darwin, who arrived on the island in the summer of 1836 and described it as possessing a “naked hideousness.”

“Those who have beheld a volcanic island, situated within an arid climate, will be able at once to picture to themselves the aspect of Ascension,” Darwin wrote. “To complete this desolate scene, the black rocks on the coast are lashed by a wild and turbulent sea.”

However, a little less than two centuries after this bleak description, the island is now a lush tropical cloud forest filled with eucalyptus, bamboo, banana plants, araucaria, and Cape bramble—all plants from three separate continents. So how did this happen? Well, the short answer is humans, but the slightly longer answer is the work of the British botanist Joseph Hooker. In 1847, Hooker persuaded the Royal Navy to bring plant specimens from the Kew Gardens in London to catch rain, reduce evaporation, and improve soil health, according to El Pais.

The introduction of these plants, along with more humans (who brought with them insects, rats, and cats, in a cyclical parade of invasive species), essentially terraformed the island, turning a once desolate landscape into something more suitable for human habitation.

Some scientists see this history as a possible blueprint for fighting desertification, which is spreading as climate change threatens vulnerable ecosystems. Among them is Victor Maull, who recently finished a Ph.D. at Pompeu Fabra University focused on the island.

“In the laboratory we are working to make minimal models that can explain changes to ecosystems,” Maull said in a press statement. “Normally, we model ecosystems that degrade, but with Ascension we have the opportunity to understand the reverse process and see if we can invert the collapse.”

However, other experts who spoke to El Pais have a different interpretation of Ascension island’s ecological history—one that stresses caution rather than celebration. Although Darwin had little positive to say about the island on his visit, endemic species did live on the roughly 34-square-mile island back then. Today, those native species are being crowded out by invasive plants that now cover almost the entire island. One of those natives, the Ascension Island parsley fern, was thought to be extinct until 2009, when researchers found four plants clinging to a cliff.

“What remains today is an unusual combination of species—bamboo, eucalyptus, ficus and others—that would never have grown or evolved together naturally in an ecosystem,” Tiffany Simpson, director of Conservation and Fisheries for the Ascension Island Government, told El Pais. Because of this mismatch, even some of the invasive plants are struggling to establish roots in the shallow, volcanic soil, causing many trees to topple over during fierce storms.

Whatever one makes of its history, Ascension offers two lessons. It shows that deliberate intervention may help hold back advancing deserts, and it warns of what can be lost when humans reshape a one-of-a-kind ecosystem to suit their own needs, whether on this planet or another.

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

A fresh look at Einstein's equations suggests that gravity can sometimes snap and reconnect, similar to magnetic field lines on the sun. The findings hint at a new way that gravity and matter can trade energy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Magnetic reconnection — the process behind the sun's most violent outbursts — may have a counterpart in gravity.

According to a new theoretical study, sheet-like structures in the gravitational field can break apart and reconnect in new arrangements, much like the magnetic field lines that unleash solar flares.

Built entirely on Albert Einstein's theory of general relativity, the study spells out when this "gravitational reconnection" can happen. It also offers a way to measure how fast the theoretical reconnection proceeds, and suggests a change to how gravity and matter trade energy. The process could even play a role in black hole collisions, the researchers suggest.

Magnetic field lines are normally "frozen" into plasma — the hot, electrically charged gas that makes up stars — and carried along wherever it flows. The lines can be stretched and twisted, but not cut. Where this rule breaks down, they can snap and rejoin in a process called magnetic reconnection, releasing pent-up energy in explosive bursts such as solar flares.

"In plasma physics, reconnection has become an essential part of our understanding of how magnetic fields reorganize and exchange energy with matter," Luca Comisso, an astrophysicist at Columbia University and first author of the study, told Live Science via email. "Could something similar be true for gravity?"

"Gravity and magnetism describe very different aspects of nature, so there's no obvious reason to expect them to behave alike," Comisso said. "But when we express Einstein's equations in a particular mathematical form, some of the same principles that govern magnetic fields also emerge in gravity. We wanted to understand whether those similarities extended to reconnection itself."

Comisso and study co-author Felipe Asenjo, a physicist at Adolfo Ibáñez University in Chile, used a mathematical framework known as the tetrad formulation. "Einstein's theory describes gravity through the geometry of space-time," Comisso explained. But in the tetrad formulation, "certain aspects of gravity can be expressed through quantities resembling electric and magnetic fields."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In a prior study published in the journal Physical Review Letters earlier this year, the researchers applied this framework to gravity. That study suggested that gravitational fields can form two-dimensional structures called gravitational field sheets. Of the sheets' two dimensions, one stretches through space and the other through time — so each sheet is the trail a line leaves as time passes. A snapshot at any instant therefore catches each sheet as a line, akin to the field lines drawn around a magnet. And, like magnetic field lines frozen into a plasma, "under certain conditions, these sheets evolve without breaking or changing how they are connected," Comisso said.

An illustration depicting the sun’s magnetic field lines over an image taken by NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory. When magnetic loops get stretched to their limit, they snap and reconnect, triggering solar flares.

In the new study, published Oct. 28 in the journal Physical Review D, the researchers found that this is not always the case. "Gravitational field sheets can break and reconnect in a different arrangement, much like magnetic field lines do in plasmas," Comisso said.

The researchers showed that breaking the frozen-in rule doesn't, by itself, guarantee reconnection. Sometimes, the sheets merely slip relative to the flow that carries them, staying intact because they remain frozen into a different flow. Genuine reconnection happens only when no such alternative flow exists.

"We also derived equations describing how quickly this reconnection can occur and how it can affect the transfer of energy and momentum," Comisso said. In general relativity, gravity and matter can trade energy and momentum, with only their combined total conserved. The study shows that reconnection changes the local rate of that exchange.

Reconnection also alters gravitational helicity, the gravitational counterpart of a quantity that measures how twisted and interlinked magnetic field lines are. Frozen-in sheets keep their helicity fixed, but reconnection can create or destroy it.

The findings don't require new physics. "Everything follows from Einstein's general relativity," Comisso said.

"Einstein developed his theory more than a century ago, and it has passed an extraordinary number of experimental tests," he added. "Yet even after more than a century, there are still new insights to be gained from those same equations."

What could trigger gravitational reconnection in nature remains an open question. Among the candidates the researchers suggested are the singularities thought to lurk at the hearts of black holes and the combined effect of gravitational ripples that are too small to track individually. Quantum effects linked to Hawking radiation ‪—‬ the faint glow that black holes are predicted to emit ‪—‬ could also play a part.

"We're still at the beginning, but one of the most interesting possibilities is that gravitational reconnection could play a role in extreme events, such as the merger of two black holes or the collision of neutron stars," Comisso said. "These are environments where gravity is extremely strong and the geometry of spacetime changes dramatically."

Such collisions send out ripples in space-time called gravitational waves, which detectors such as LIGO (the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) have been recording since 2015. "We'd like to understand whether gravitational reconnection could contribute to transferring energy, and whether it might leave a recognizable signature in gravitational waves," Comisso added. "We don't know the answers yet, but these are questions that we can now begin to investigate."

Comisso, L., & Asenjo, F. A. (2026). Reconnection of gravitational fields. Physical Review. D., 114(8). https://doi.org/10.1103/lmqy-pf9k

#6408. Could a nuclear blast save Earth from an asteroid? Good aim will mean everything

Computer simulations reveal how an asteroid’s shape could affect efforts to push it off course with X-rays from a nearby nuclear blast.

A nuclear blast set off near a dangerous asteroid could, in theory, push it away from Earth. But if the asteroid has a lumpy, uneven shape, how hard it gets pushed depends on which side the blast hits.

In new computer tests, hitting one side of an oddly shaped asteroid instead of another gave it nearly five times as much push.

So a real defense mission could depend on knowing an asteroid’s shape before anyone chooses where to aim.

Nathan Moore, a physicist at Sandia National Laboratories, led the research. “We expected aim to matter,” he said. “What surprised us was how much.”

No asteroid was blasted for this work. The team ran every test in computer simulations, using the shapes of real asteroids.

In this kind of defense, a nuclear device would go off some distance from the asteroid, not on it.

The blast sends out a burst of X-rays that heats one side of the asteroid and turns part of its surface into vapor. That vapor rushes off into space, and the pressure it puts on the surface pushes the asteroid the other way.

The goal is to push the asteroid, not smash it. Breaking it apart could turn one big threat into smaller pieces that could still be deadly.

A nuclear blast is a different approach from crashing a spacecraft into an asteroid, which NASA’s DART mission tested in 2022.

Moore has worked on this question since a 2024 experiment at Sandia’s Z machine, a lab device that produces intense bursts of X-rays.

That experiment showed for the first time that X-rays could push a small piece of asteroid material.

Next, he wanted to know how a full-size asteroid would respond. Most researchers had treated asteroids as perfect spheres because that made the math easier, he said.

Real asteroids have irregular shapes that a perfect sphere cannot capture.

“You can make estimates that way, but asteroids come in all kinds of odd, lumpy shapes,” Moore said.

He found a way forward in a colleague’s work on how objects in space give off gas.

“I think we had an aha moment when we realized we could do this,” he said. “No more spheres. We would be able to model deflection for any asteroid.”

Moore built the new model by joining two computer programs that Sandia already used for very different jobs.

One usually simulates fast, high-energy events, such as experiments on the Z machine. The other usually handles weak forces that change slowly, like the drag the solar wind puts on a satellite.

In the new model, the first program works out how the X-rays heat the surface and turn part of it to gas.

The second follows that gas as it spreads across the asteroid’s real 3D shape, and it calculates the pressure on every part of the surface.

“The key innovation here was figuring out how to combine the two simulation approaches,” Moore said.

He also pointed to speed. “Our new algorithm is over 1,600 times faster, which was critical to this breakthrough,” he said. “With the old models, computers just couldn’t handle it.”

To use the model, the team loads in an asteroid’s shape, which can come from detailed 3D images taken by passing spacecraft.

They then set the size of the blast, how far away it goes off, and which side it hits.

The program maps how much of each part of the surface turns to vapor. From that map, it works out how hard the asteroid gets pushed and how fast it spins afterward.

The team tested the model on three real asteroids with very different shapes. Bennu is the asteroid NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft sampled in 2020. The other two were Itokawa and Golevka.

For each one, the researchers tried blasts at close range and farther away. They also changed which way the asteroid was facing when the X-rays arrived.

In the simulations, orienting Bennu at its most favorable angle, instead of its worst, gave it up to nearly twice as much push.

The difference was larger for the other two, at up to nearly four times for Itokawa and five times for Golevka.

In one simulation, the blast changed an asteroid’s speed by about 0.15 inch (3.9 millimeters) per second from one angle. From another angle, it was only about 0.03 inch (0.8 millimeter) per second.

The asteroid and the blast were the same both times, and only the side facing the X-rays was different.

The aim also affected how fast an asteroid spun after the blast. For one asteroid, the change in its spin rate varied 17-fold depending on which side faced the blast.

“Our study shows how important it is to aim carefully,” Moore said. “Pick the right side and you win. Guess wrong and it could be a bad day.”

To run the model, the team needs a fairly accurate picture of an asteroid’s shape from every side. In a real emergency, there might not be time to get one.

Placing a nuclear device at the right distance, on the right side of an asteroid speeding through space, would also be hard.

Another unknown is what happens to the whole asteroid.

“Right now, our computer model only considers breakup of rocks on the surface,” he said. “We can’t predict breakup of the entire asteroid body accurately yet.”

When the researchers applied the blast pressures to a loose, Itokawa-like pile of boulders, the rock thrown off was lopsided, just like the vapor.

Predicting whether a whole asteroid breaks apart will take more research and better modeling tools. An X-ray blast would set off many effects at once, and those effects could change one another.

That full calculation is what Moore and other scientists are working toward.

The full study was published in the journal Icarus.

#6407. Editor's Letter: Introducing Our Winter Travel Issue

It was a long and hot summer, and I welcomed the cooler weather as soon as the leaves started to turn. My closet full of coats and jackets had sat sadly neglected for many months; the new boots I bought in April on a clearance rack are only now about to get their moment. I'm excited for the Christmas lights in London and New York, the festive trees, chestnuts roasting on street corners—and yes, my Christmas wish list (featuring a dangerous number of watches and pieces of jewelry) is ready too. There is something about the winter that still feels exotic and enthralling to me. I saw snow a few times in Kashmir as a kid, but the first real blizzard I encountered was when I was a freshman in college in Pennsylvania. It was late at night, but my roommate dragged me out of bed to make snow angels. I still remember lying on my back, waving my arms around—the sensation of cold all along my body was surreal, as was the way in which white feathery bits floated down from the sky. I recall thinking, What a strange but wonderful feeling! I discovered two things quickly: One, I was a terrible skier. And, two, I loved après-ski—to be nursing hot chocolate by crackling fireplaces and snuggled in blankets.

Our story on Banff perfectly encapsulates the promise of winter: the adventure, the exhilaration, the romance of a landscape transformed overnight. But equally seductive is the prospect of winter sun. Come January I'll happily trade snow boots for sandals and fly to Tenerife, Spain, or Boracay, in the Philippines, or Brisbane, Australia. That dose of vitamin D is essential by then, when the Christmas lights have come down and everything seems gray and empty. At that point I need a beach—and something colorful and sparkly to wear on it. So often I close my eyes and return to the end-of-year trips I've made to Maldives, Indonesia, Mexico, and remembered the sunrises, the sound of the waves, the palm trees swaying in the breeze, the fiery red chiles, and fresh coconut water. It's been a strange year. But as we navigate the final months ahead, this issue is filled with reasons to feel excited about what comes next. I hope it gives you plenty to dream about—and somewhere to go.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. #6406. Plant roots have a clever way to tell good and bad fungi apart, even though they both give off the exact same molecules

Good and bad fungi release the exact same chemical signal but plant roots still know which one is dangerous

A fungus growing on a crop sounds like bad news, but not all fungi are harmful. Plants also rely on helpful fungi to take up nutrients through their roots.

Attackers and partners alike are built from the same material, a sugar chain called chitin. Fragments of it end up in the soil whenever a fungus grows or breaks down.

A new study shows how a receptor on legume roots sorts those fragments by length.

Receptors tightly grip long chitin chains, the kind that come with a fungal attack, and raise the alarm. Short ones, the kind that partner fungi shed, barely register.

Kira Gysel and Kasper Røjkjær Andersen of the Department of Molecular Biology and Genetics at Aarhus University in Denmark led the work.

Simon Boje Hansen and Henriette Rübsam are the first authors, with co-authors at the University of Copenhagen and the French research center CERMAV. The experiments were done in two small legumes used as laboratory models, not in crops.

In an interview with Earth.com, Gysel said the puzzle was that chitin looks the same along its whole length.

“It’s the same sugar repeated, like a string of identical beads, with nothing to tell one part of the chain from another,” she said.

Chitin is the main building block of a fungal cell wall. When a fungus grows or gets broken down, pieces of the chain of different lengths end up in the soil. Roots read these fragments of fungi to keep track of the microbes around them.

Long fragments usually come with an attack and, in legumes, they set off a much stronger defense than short ones. Short fragments come with the helpful fungi that plug into roots and exchange nutrients with the plant.

How a root told the two apart was the open question.

The team produced the outer part of a root receptor called CHIP13 and tested how hard it holds chitin chains of different lengths. It held an eight-sugar chain more than 1,000 times more tightly than a five-sugar chain.

Then they froze the receptor into crystals with the long chain attached and mapped it, atom by atom.

The receptor holds the chain at three points. Two are standard chitin-binding pockets found in related receptors. The third sits between them, and the team named it the bridge domain, because it spans the middle of the chain.

Gysel told Earth.com that the structure answered the question at a glance.

“CHIP13 holds the chain at three main contact points, and the central one, the bridge domain, is what coordinates binding of the long chitin chain,” Gysel said.

“Only chains long enough to reach all three are held tightly and can activate the plant’s immune response. It’s really a molecular measuring tape.”

Swapping out two amino acids near the bridge cut the receptor’s grip 100-fold. In a second legume, barrel medic, mutant plants given a version of the matching receptor with the same two swaps didn’t regain their response to chitin.

Legume roots also need a second receptor, CERK6, to respond to chitin, and CERK6 can barely hold chitin at all. Boje Hansen said that had been a puzzle.

“It turns out the two receptors split the work: one recognizes the signal, the other passes it on. Neither can do the job alone,” he said.

In leaf cells engineered to carry both receptors, CHIP13 pulled in CERK6 only once chitin was bound. The weakened version of CHIP13 didn’t recruit it at all.

The team’s model is a pair of CHIP13 receptors holding chitin and recruiting two CERK6 partners, which then pass the alarm into the cell.

To test the receptors in a living plant without altering its genes, the team raised nanobodies – tiny antibody-like proteins made by immunizing a llama – that plug each receptor’s chitin-binding site.

They soaked intact seedlings of the model legume Lotus japonicus in them. When asked by Earth.com what else about the research stood out, Gysel pointed to that experiment.

“We simply applied them to plants from the outside, and we weren’t sure it would work at all,” she said. “We thought the plant cell wall would block the nanobodies from reaching the receptors on the surface of the plant cells.”

The nanobodies reached the receptors. Seedlings treated with the CERK6 blocker responded to chitin about as weakly as plants missing that gene, and the CHIP13 blocker cut the response sharply too.

Both legumes are laboratory models, and the measuring tape hasn’t been checked in a crop. The bridge domain can be predicted in many related receptors across higher plants, but a predicted domain isn’t a tested one.

Gysel said the two receptors are only a glimpse of a larger immune system. Plants use many related receptors to monitor soil microbes. How those receptors work together, and whether others read signals by length, is what her group wants to find out next.

The stakes she described are agricultural. Strengthening the chitin alarm could make crops more resistant to fungal disease, but only if it doesn’t also fire at the fungi the roots depend on.

“Knowing how the long chitin chains are read helps us improve crops without tipping the balance, so we don’t weaken their defenses to make room for helpful fungi, or the other way around,” Gysel said.

Which crop receptors carry a bridge domain, and whether they measure chitin the same way, is the next thing to check.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#6405. How octopuses squeeze through tiny openings, step by step

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The cephalopod how-to guide involves three or four moves, depending on a hole’s size

Octopuses are famous for fleeing tanks by squeezing through narrow slits and impossibly tiny holes. Now scientists have studied the sequences some cephalopods like this Mayan octopus use to make such great escapes.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Octopuses have made many a great escape. Remember Inky, who fled from New Zealand’s national aquarium?

The cephalopods can Houdini their way out of tanks and off boats by squeezing through narrow slits and incredibly tiny holes. Now researchers know exactly how some octopuses pull it off. These masterful getaways involve a consistent, step-by-step game plan, researchers report November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

Octopuses are mostly squishy muscle, allowing them to shape-shift, though they do have some rigid body parts. Not many scientists have studied how these animals squirm through small openings, says Robyn Crook, an evolutionary biologist at San Francisco State University who was not involved in the research. “It’s one of the most characteristic behaviors of octopuses in popular awareness, but the strategies octopuses use have not really been examined systematically.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Sneaking through small spaces isn’t just a party trick for octopuses, says Michael Kuba, a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy. The animals use that skill to find hidden food and to avoid becoming food themselves.

Kuba and his colleagues observed how three common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) and four Mayan octopuses (Octopus maya) approached small holes. For each individual, the team measured the distance between the octopus’s eyes as an indicator of the size of their most rigid cartilage around their brain. Then the researchers designed acrylic boxes with holes that were slightly smaller or larger than that eye-to-eye measurement. They plopped the octopuses inside and watched what happened.

Octopuses have slightly different escape how-tos, depending on the size of the hole they are squeezing through. Here, a common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) wriggles through a space just a little bit bigger than their most rigid body parts. It takes just three steps for the octopus to free itself from the acrylic box.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Common octopuses used one of two escape strategies depending on the hole’s size. When the hole was wider than the distance between their eyes, the octopuses pushed themselves through it in three steps. First, they snuck one or two arms through the hole and then threaded a couple more arms through. Finally, they used the arms that they had already snaked through the hole to push against the box and yank their head and the rest of their arms through in one fell swoop. The whole operation took a few seconds.

When the hole was narrower, common octopuses added a fourth step. They shoved all of their arms through the hole first and then squished their head and bulbous mantle through.

When a hole is smaller than their most rigid body parts, common octopuses add a fourth step to wrestle their bodies through an opening.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Mayan octopuses behaved more cautiously than the common octopuses. When confronted with the narrower hole, Mayan octopuses didn’t even attempt to fit inside of it. They usually ignored it. This difference between the species could stem from their biology or how they’ve adapted to their environments, Kuba says. Mayan octopuses live in sandy, rocky areas, so while they might disappear under rocks, they don’t often need to cram through holes, he says.

The team hopes these escape artists will inspire new soft robots that can morph their shape to fit through tiny spaces, says Wenci Xin, a robotics researcher at the National University of Singapore. “This incredible capability could enable robots to overcome environmental limitations and enter spaces that are difficult to reach.”

Studying how octopuses navigate different types of holes may provide additional clues for robots, Crook says. For instance, the cephalopods may take a different tack for openings that are more like slits or tubes than holes.

Currently, robots built to fit through tiny holes tend to be snake-shaped, but further research on these eight-armed contortionists could unlock other configurations.

#6404. Scientists Have Hunted Dark Energy for Decades. They May Be Chasing a Cosmic Ghost.

A new study finds a mathematical solution for the universe’s expansion within the original work of Albert Einstein.

In 1916, Albert Einstein published his foundational paper on the General Theory of Relativity in the German-language science journal Annalen der Physik. Now, 110 years later, scientists are still debating just how right Einstein’s conception of the universe really was, especially as it relates to the accelerated expansion of the universe. Of course, at the time of his revolutionary publication, the world still didn’t know that the universe was expanding, so a year later, Einstein introduced a “lambda” cosmological constant to his equations to form a stable, non-collapsing universe.

Thanks to the pioneering work of Edwin Hubble in 1929, the world learned that the universe was actually expanding, and in response Einstein discarded lambda, calling it his “greatest blunder.” What Einstein couldn’t have known was that, decades after his death, lambda would make a comeback. When astronomers discovered in the late 1990s that the universe’s expansion was speeding up, the constant became central to the modern model of the cosmos, known as “Lambda-Cold Dark Matter,” or ΛCDM. Rising along with the renaissance of the cosmological constant was a concept known as dark energy, the force that made this accelerated expansion possible.

This ΛCDM is a pretty tidy description of the universe with one glaring plot hole—we’ve never directly seen or measured dark energy. Because of this lack of evidence, some scientists have searched for other possible explanations, even disregarding Einstein entirely, but a new study by researchers at the University of California, Davis takes the opposite approach. According to their research, published earlier this year in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society A, Einstein was actually more right than he ever knew.

To build their case for a universe without dark energy, UC Davis mathematics professor emeritus Blake Temple and his colleagues turned to Friedmann spacetimes. These are a family of solutions to Einstein’s field equations originally developed by Alexander Friedmann, the Soviet mathematician who first proposed that the universe is expanding.

“The Friedmann family of spacetimes describe a uniform three-dimensional Universe of galaxies expanding in time from an initial Big Bang singularity at a rate determined by Einstein’s field equations,” the authors write in the study.

The researchers rewrote Einstein's equations in a “self-similar” form, meaning the equations keep the same structure at any scale, much like a fractal. This version of the equations let them test a key question: if the smooth, even spread of matter in a Friedmann universe gets slightly disturbed, does it settle back to normal or move further away from it? They found that the small disturbances don’t fade away. Instead, they grow, at both large and small scales. In other words, a perfectly uniform Friedmann universe can’t stay that way.

“Unstable solutions in physics and science are considered not physical. You’ll never observe them in nature,” Temple said in a press statement. “The instability of all Friedmann spacetimes to accelerated expansion suggests a simpler, more natural explanation for the acceleration of the universe than dark energy.”

That instability is the heart of the argument. Einstein’s own static universe had a similar flaw: it was so delicately balanced that the slightest nudge would tip it over. “We prove that, like Einstein’s static model, the Friedmann spacetimes are all unstable to radial perturbation at large length scales,” Temple added. As the universe drifts away from a perfect Friedmann state, the team argues, its expansion naturally speeds up. That would mean Einstein’s original equations, without lambda, may explain the acceleration we see today, without dark energy.

The work is purely mathematical, though, and it comes with a catch. The team’s model has a center, so we’d need to live near a special spot in the universe for it to match what astronomers see. That goes against a basic assumption of modern cosmology. Temple argues that ΛCDM has the same problem, however.

For now, scientists around the world continue to probe for the elusive dark matter and dark energy that presumably dominates the universe (with some detectors reporting encouraging results). But the study raises an intriguing possibility: we might be chasing a cosmological ghost.

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#6403. Can more snow save Antarctica’s ice? A new study weighs the odds

Antarctica is likely to lose ice through 2100 even with sharp emissions cuts, as extra snowfall struggles to offset losses driven by warmer seas.

Predicting how much ice Antarctica will lose means weighing two competing effects. Warmer air can bring more snow, adding ice to the continent, while warmer seawater speeds ice loss along its edges.

A new study suggests Antarctica is very likely to lose ice overall by 2100, even if emissions fall sharply.

Extra snowfall is very unlikely to make up for the ice that the ocean removes, and the researchers found that very high emissions would probably lead to greater losses.

The author leading the work is Yucheng Lin, an assistant professor at City University of Hong Kong, who worked with colleagues in Australia, New Zealand, the United States and the United Kingdom.

Their study used a machine-learning program to examine existing computer simulations of the Antarctic Ice Sheet and check them against the satellite record.

The Antarctic Ice Sheet contains enough ice to raise global sea level by about 190 feet (57.9 meters), and its losses accounted for roughly 10% of global sea-level rise between 2006 and 2018.

How much emissions will alter the losses during this century has been a source of disagreement, something the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change drew attention to in its 2021 assessment.

One large international comparison included some simulations in which Antarctica lowered sea level by more than 2.8 inches (seven centimeters) by 2100 and others in which it raised sea level by more than 15.7 inches (40 centimeters).

All of these simulations assumed very high emissions.

Making these models involves deciding how easily ice slides over the bedrock beneath it and how quickly seawater melts floating ice from below. It also requires choosing a climate model to provide the warming projections.

Different research groups make different choices about each of these things.

Counting each model equally also gives more influence to choices that appear in more models, Lin’s team wrote, and those common choices may not be the ones that best fit observations.

Their approach was to compare the choices with Antarctica’s recent behavior.

The team used 340 simulations produced by 16 research groups. They recorded the modeling choices behind each simulation, then trained a machine-learning program to predict how those choices affected the results.

Running a full ice-sheet simulation takes a lot of computing power, but the trained program could turn out about 30,000 projections a second on a laptop, so the team could try 100,000 combinations.

To judge them, the researchers used the GRACE satellite record, which showed an average loss of about 174 billion tons (158 billion metric tons) of ice a year from 2002 to 2021.

They gave greater importance to combinations that produced losses close to what the satellites measured, reducing the range of projected sea-level rise by 30% to 42% depending on the emissions scenario.

The middle estimate moved up by 15% to 25% as a result.

With the satellite record helping to decide how much importance each combination received, the estimated chance of Antarctica losing ice overall by 2100 went from 80% to 92% in the lowest-emissions case.

For very high emissions, the researchers put the chance of an overall loss at no less than 95%.

The middle estimate for Antarctica’s contribution to sea-level rise by 2100 was 1.3 inches (3.4 centimeters) under the lowest emissions and 2.4 inches (6.1 centimeters) under very high emissions.

There was an 89% chance of very high emissions producing more sea-level rise from Antarctica than the lowest-emissions scenario, the team calculated.

“We have to transform our energy system to cut every emission we can, and we must do it quickly,” Lin said.

One set of simulations showed how much the extra snow could matter, with a net gain of ice in Antarctica even though the climate model they used produced the most warming this century out of the five models in the study.

More snowfall, together with only modest warming of the surrounding ocean, accounted for the gain. But it did not last in simulations that continued beyond 2100, when losses to the ocean overtook the added snow.

For people planning infrastructure that has to last a long time, including nuclear power stations, the team also examined the outcomes with the most sea-level rise.

These were the top 1% under very high emissions, and all still matched the satellite record.

In this selected group the middle estimate for Antarctica’s contribution by 2100 was 6.2 inches (15.7 centimeters), with one in 20 outcomes exceeding 10 inches (25.4 centimeters).

The sea was the starting point in these simulations, with strong warming melting the floating ice shelves quickly from below.

Ice on land then moved into the sea faster as the shelves thinned or collapsed and lost their ability to hold it back, particularly where the ice could slide easily over bedrock.

For these highest losses the team was looking at the very high emissions case, which the authors described as increasingly implausible given current climate policies.

Researchers cannot use this program to learn what happens in a process that the original simulations never included.

Among the processes that most simulations leave out are flows of water beneath the ice sheet and a still-debated way in which ice shelves might rapidly collapse, both of which could speed up ice loss, the authors wrote.

The satellite record covers only about 20 years, offering limited insight into processes that have caused little ice loss so far but could become important later.

The researchers stopped their projections at 2100 because the available simulations for the following century are too few to capture the sharper changes that begin then.

Of all the choices researchers make when building these models, the authors identified three that need stronger evidence.

These are how ice slides over bedrock, how ice shelves melt and which climate model is used.

Lin pointed out that researchers have limited resources, so they need to work out which details of an ice model matter most.

The authors suggested collecting new field observations and studying records of past climates to help narrow these choices.

Future simulations that include the missing processes could also provide new data to train the program.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Geoscience.

The new Peerium architecture aims to power hyper-efficient computers capable of training AI models with up to 40 trillion parameters.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Engineers in China have built a new computer architecture they say can one day make up to a million artificial intelligence (AI) chips work as one. For comparison, Elon Musk's AI company, SpaceXAI (soon to be SpaceXSI), describes its Colossus cluster as the world's most powerful AI training system, comprising 200,000 interconnected chips.

Traditionally, the AI chips used to train foundation models are housed in separate servers and communicate over a network to share data and divide workloads. But the new architecture, Peerium, uses a high-speed interconnect system designed to maintain efficient communication between chips across multiple racks, even as the number of chips scales into the hundreds of thousands.

Huawei unveiled the new architecture Sept. 17 at the company's annual CONNECT conference.

Representatives from Huawei said in a statement that computers powered by Peerium could train models with up to 40 trillion parameters. For comparison, competing hardware, like GB200 NVL72 from NVIDIA and CS-3 from Cerebras, have reported training at the trillion-parameter scale, rather than the tens-of-trillions.

"Over the next two years, there will be roughly 6 or 7 frontier AI labs in China, and all will aim at training foundation language models of sizes ranging from 10 to 40 trillion parameters," Liao Heng, chief scientist for Huawei's chip design arm HiSilicon, told the Associated Press. "So you need such a scale of infrastructure to train these models."

Peerium's performance relies on three elements: nested parallelism, unified memory addressing, and peer-to-peer interconnects, Huawei representatives said in the statement.

Nested parallelism allows workloads to be broken into smaller tasks and organized across hierarchical groups of chips that work in parallel. It's similar to how a company breaks down work into departments and then smaller teams, all of which coordinate their efforts toward a common goal. Unified memory addressing allows processors to access memory across other servers, as opposed to only that attached to the processor's own server. Peer-to-peer interconnects allow components to communicate more directly with one another, rather than relying on an intermediary.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

All three principles are designed to make more efficient use of computing resources so that a single system can coordinate larger numbers of chips to handle demanding AI workloads.

According to Huawei, existing interconnect technologies — which link processors and servers to enable them to communicate — cannot support the Peerium architecture at the scale it envisages. For instance, NVIDIA uses NVLink for communication within racks and InfiniBand for communication between racks. The inter-rack communication bandwidth in this setup is 200GB per second, Eric Xu, Huawei's rotating chairman, told the AP.

"With such a low inter-rack communications bandwidth, there is no way you can make one million processors work as one computer," he said.

Huawei instead developed its own interconnect technology, UnifiedBus, which the company says delivers inter-rack communications bandwidth of up to 800GB per second.

"When one million processors work as one computer, this lays the foundation for better and more efficient AI training and inference," Xu added. "Therefore, I see UnifiedBus as the path for the future AI era. I believe, in the years to come, other players would certainly follow suit."

Alongside Peerium, Huawei also announced the Atlas 950 SuperPoD, a computing system built on Peerium and powered by more than 8,000 Huawei Ascend 950DT AI accelerator chips.

Xu said testing for AI training is underway on these SuperPoDs and that results show that they use their available computing power for AI training more efficiently than AI computing clusters that aren’t based on Peerium and UnifiedBus.

Huawei expects to begin supplying the SuperPoDs by early next year, at the latest, before its SuperClusters, which link multiple SuperPoDs to form a larger AI computing system, based on Peerium, eventually come online. Representatives said that one SuperCluster with 256,000 computing cards — hardware modules that add processing capacity — is currently being deployed and tested.

Models with large numbers of parameters demand greater computing resources and infrastructure, which isn't always desirable as it increases costs. In the summer, researchers used an IBM quantum computer to reduce the perplexity of Meta's Llama 3.1 8B language model — a measure of how well it predicts the next word or token — while keeping the number of parameters almost unchanged.
